outcomes.statement: ST30.1 Select, use and assess a variety of strategies to interpret American Sign Language messages.
outcomes.printedWith: * For further information and suggestions for additional strategies, see Appendix A.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Use and assess a variety of metacognitive strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- independently execute a plan to engage in a new language learning task;
- assess communication process by being aware of own strengths and weaknesses, identify needs and goals and organize strategies and procedures accordingly; or,
- keep a learning log to evaluate their own performance or comprehension at the end of a task and assess which language learning strategies are most effective.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate and assess a variety of interactive and affective strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- collaborate with others to identify how patterns and relationships in signs assist in interpreting meaning;
- summarize the point reached in a discussion to help focus the talk and ask follow-up questions to check for understanding; or,
- recognize nuances in facial expressions as essential components of communicating in ASL.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Practise and assess a variety of interpretive strategies* to enhance language learning, such as:
- view a variety of video recordings to compare and contrast regional, cultural and gender signing variations;
- assess own information needs and prepare questions or a guide to note information found in a signed text; or,
- perceive and note down unknown signs and sign-expressions, noting also their context and function.

outcomes.statement: Select, use and assess a variety of strategies to express oneself in American Sign Language.
outcomes.printedWith: * For further information and suggestions for additional strategies, see Appendix A.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Use and assess a variety of cognitive strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- assess similarities and differences between aspects of ASL and students’ other languages;
- group together sets of signs (e.g., vocabulary, structures) with similar characteristics and use induction to generate rules governing language use; or,
- make information easier to understand and remember by using reference points and initiatives like classifiers and body shifts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate and assess a variety of interactive and affective strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- participate cooperatively in conferencing, brainstorming and debating and invite others into the discussion;
- initiate or maintain interaction with signers who are deaf, deafened or hard of hearing; or,
- use a range of fillers, hesitation devices and gambits to sustain conversations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Practise and assess a variety of productive strategies* to enhance communication, such as:
- employ rhythm and symmetry in signs and use familiar patterns appropriate for various genres;
- revise and improve expressive communications by using knowledge of patterns and structures in ASL to form new sentences; or,
- rephrase difficult structures or strategically use circumlocution to clarify communication.

outcomes.statement: Construct, independently, the meaning of a variety of signed texts in American Sign Language.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Watch, interpret and comprehend fluently signed texts in familiar and unfamiliar contexts such as global community and history or celebrating language and culture.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of the five parameters of ASL (handshape, movement, palm orientation, location and facial expression) to interpret the meaning of different signs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize several common variations in signing (e.g., age, gender, ethnicity) and effectively interpret non-manual markers (e.g., facial expressions and body language) to aid in interpreting information and feelings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply important social conventions in everyday interactions (e.g., turn-taking, calling for attention, interpersonal space).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: View and understand multiple visual elements in a variety of media.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the organizational structure of a variety of signed text forms, including Plains Indian Sign Language, Langue des Signes Québécoise (LSQ) and Black American Sign Language.

outcomes.statement: Produce, independently, a variety of signed texts in American Sign Language.
outcomes.printedWith: *For further information and suggestions for additional grammatical elements, see Appendix B.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Combine a variety of complex sentences and phrases using accurate grammar in familiar and unfamiliar contexts such as activities in the community or groceries and meal preparation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express language with sufficient structural accuracy and vocabulary to communicate in spontaneous situations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply the five parameters of ASL (handshape, movement, palm orientation, location, facial expressions) to effectively express information and feelings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Employ several common variations in signing (e.g., age, gender, ethnicity) and non-manual markers (e.g., facial expressions and body language) to effectively communicate information and feelings.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Express meaning using a variety of visual and other media and communication forms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply grammatical elements* such as rhetorical questions, relative pronouns or indefinite pronouns, appropriately and fluently in conversations about familiar and unfamiliar contexts.

outcomes.statement: Apply knowledge of American Sign Language, in a familiar and unfamiliar situations and for a variety of purposes to receive information, extend knowledge of the world, achieve objectives and for enjoyment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate comprehension of the main idea presented in a signed text and explain how the language techniques chosen were effective in conveying the intended meaning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Organize information from signed texts to indicate steps in a procedure or directions to follow.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine causes and effects of decisions made by characters in fiction and non-fiction texts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Summarize the definitions, comparisons or examples used in a signed text to clarify intended meaning and support a position on an issue.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Gather information on a topic from a variety of ASL sources (e.g., human, videos, media) and organize and summarize the information in writing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Attend to signed speeches with a variety of purposes (e.g., inspirational, political, factual) and summarize their intent in writing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine perspectives present in signed texts and share opinions with others.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interpret humour in ASL by identifying examples of puns and jokes and examining their construct and purpose, such as gentle criticism and audience involvement.

outcomes.statement: Apply knowledge of American Sign Language, in familiar and unfamiliar situations and for a variety of purposes, to impart information, share emotions and personal perspectives, achieve objectives and for enjoyment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express thoughts and ideas on familiar and unfamiliar topics such as global events and issues or journeys with growing fluency by coherently linking phrases and sentences together.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide suggestions, advice, warnings and feedback in a variety of situations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inquire about and express in conversations: agreement and disagreement; approval and disapproval; interest and lack of interest; and, satisfaction and dissatisfaction.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe personal experiences and predictions about the past, present or future.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Narrate and retell others’ stories or create unique narratives with the aid of various visual mediums such as dramatization, art or displays.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct research to respond to inquiry questions such as “What are the reasons that cultures and individuals create narratives of their experiences?”.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Present a factual report on a chosen topic, supported with researched information and visual aids that add to its effectiveness for a particular audience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Persuade others to support a position on global events or issues through the use of definitions, comparisons and examples.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Facilitate and contribute to group work by soliciting and offering ideas, seeking input and reformulating others’ ideas to enable consensus.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use ASL creatively and fluently for aesthetic purposes, to express humour and for personal enjoyment.

outcomes.statement: Explore Deaf culture in the world by examining historical and contemporary elements of Deaf culture and investigating the cultural and linguistic diversity of Deaf culture.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Formulate questions about elements of Deaf culture such as “How does language help build relationships and a sense of community?” and conduct a student-led inquiry to find answers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in, and help facilitate, activities and experiences involving the Deaf community and Deaf culture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how society’s perceptions of people who are deaf, deafened or hard of hearing have changed over time and relate how they are reflected in the evolution of supports available to the Deaf community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare aspects of students’ other languages and ASL, identifying how and why languages borrow from one another.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify elements of Deaf culture (e.g., key historical events) and their influence on contemporary ways of life and cultural values.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of diverse elements of Deaf culture in interactions with people who are deaf, deafened or hard of hearing.

outcomes.statement: Research and share findings about personal and career opportunities available within the global Deaf community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify global impacts and contributions to the arts, sports, and/or work force made by the deaf, deafened, and hard of hearing community.

outcomes.statement: Apply injury prevention principles to ensure safe work performance in the autobody trade.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1D: Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE), including dust masks, approved respirators, coveralls, chemical resistant gloves, eye and hearing protection and footwear.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify, label, store and handle hazardous materials according to Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the fire plan for the work area, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits and procedures, and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess hazards and apply appropriate safety procedures when working in a confined space.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Disconnect batteries and other power sources prior to undertaking autobody repairs where appropriate.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or material and equipment damage as a result of unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the proper procedures to follow to report a workplace injury.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply safe and fair work practices, including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the ergonomic design of the work space and implement appropriate procedures to ensure safety.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Implement a plan for a safe and healthy classroom and shop environment.

outcomes.statement: Estimate the damage and time required to carry out repairs on an automobile.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Estimating Repair Costs (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze the role of insurance in the autobody trade in Saskatchewan and elsewhere including:
- describing insurance, liability, waiver, total loss, premium, deductible and package policy;
- examining the role and responsibilities of the insurance adjuster/broker, automobile appraiser, automobile owner(s) and autobody repair shop; and,
- comparing original equipment manufacturer (OEM), recycled, remanufactured and after-market parts to repair an automobile.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Estimate damage repair costs including:
- detailed description of all labour operations that must be performed;
- complete list of parts and materials needed for the repair; and,
- total price including labour, parts, materials and applicable taxes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Interpret technical service bulletins about potential issues that could result in the need for automobile repairs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the extent of the damage from outside the automobile and work inward and list everything by section that is bent, broken or missing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the conditions that make an automobile a total loss.

outcomes.statement: Examine the evolution and characteristics of structural components in each section of the automobile.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Advanced Automobile Structural Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the history of automobile structural design including major changes and characteristics of selected components.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify front (e.g., cowl, shock towers, radiator and supports, fire wall, fenders, hood), centre (e.g., floor pan, pillars, rocker panel, rear shelf, doors, glass, hinges, side impact beam, roof panel, instrument panel, dash) and rear (e.g., trunk floor, trunk lid, quarter panel, lower rear panels, rear shock towers, inner wheel housing, upper body panel) section components of an automobile.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the construction and safety features of plastic bumpers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify part numbers, prices, installation time and procedures using original equipment manufacturer (OEM) specifications and software and/or manuals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe proper safety procedures used by certified technicians to disable an automobile air bag sensor system.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the properties of dissimilar automotive materials (e.g., carbon, fibre, plastic, stainless).

indicators.label: a

e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: i

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of science.
To develop students' abilities to access knowledge.
Appreciate the basic principles of chemistry which are involved in life processes.
Recognize that organisms are made of atoms.
Realize the relationship between the electron structure of atoms and the type of bond which forms.
Understand the relationship between chemical bonds and stored energy.
Recognize the importance and ongoing nature of various chemical reactions in the body.
Discuss a chemical reaction — the reactants, products and energy either required or produced.
Illustrate with examples the similarities and differences between synthesis and decomposition reactions.
Describe some relationships which exist between synthesis and decomposition reactions in relation to the functioning of the body ie., dynamic balance (homeostasis).
Investigate the properties of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins.
Explain how carbon-based molecules interact with each other through hydrogen bonding.
Compare mono-, di-, and polysaccharides and then provide examples of their usefulness to a living system.
Describe the relationship between fatty acids and fats by providing examples to illustrate when they are useful to a living system.
Describe the relationship between amino acids and proteins with reference to the peptide bond.

Discuss enzymes using a series of key words which should be included in a concept web with the heading of proteins. (The key words are substrate, enzyme—substrate complex, lock and key, catalyst, factors affecting enzyme activity [temperature; relative concentration of substrate], enzymes, and coenzymes.)
Indicate the component parts of a fat molecule.
Recognize the value of proteins by using examples from the human body.
Describe the structure of nucleic acids.
Describe the similarities and differences in the structure of DNA and RNA.
Describe the processes of replication and transcription.

units.name: Cell Structure and Function
factorsEmphasized: E3 using equipment safely page for expla abou see s 81-82 an nation t webs.

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of ecosystems.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
Describe the structures and functions of cell components.
Review evidence for the existence of cells.
Observe, sketch, and describe a representative sampling of plant and animal cells.
Describe the structure of a cell membrane.
Describe the functions of the organelles found in eukaryotic cells.
Contrast the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Explain how the processes of diffusion, active transport, photosynthesis, and respiration are accomplished in a cell.
Identify the factors which influence the rate and direction of diffusion.

Examine the mechanisms of active transport by identifying and explaining the two processes. (Process one involves the expenditure of energy where a carrier molecule takes a substance from one side of a membrane to the other side of the membrane. Process two involves the inpocketing of material by a membrance -- pinocytosis and exocytosis.)
Recognize how the ATP-ADP system, and the NAD-NADH system, transfer energy within a cell.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic metabolism.
Describe the processes involved in photosynthesis and then compare the process of photosynthesis with respiration.
Examine how the structure of the leaf is adapted for the processes involved in photosynthesis.
Identify how osmosis is related to diffusion and the value of osmosis to living organisms.
Compare the similarities and differences between active and passive transport.
Indicate the importance of the light and dark reactions in the process of photosynthesis.

items.text: To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structure and forms of expression which characterize the study of biology.
To develop a contemporary view of technology.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To contribute to the development of "strong sense" critical and creative thinkers.
To develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups.
Explain the significance of Mendel's experiments and observations, and the laws derived from them.
Explain the concept of independent events.
Understand that the probability of an independent event is not altered by the outcomes of previous events.
Describe Mendel's experiments and observations.
Describe the relationship between genotype and phenotype.
Use the concept of the gene to explain Mendel's laws.
Describe the ideas of dominant and recessive traits with examples.
Consider the value of the punnett square by creating examples of mono and dihybrid crosses.
Explain the law of segregation.
Discuss the relationships among chromosomes, genes, and DNA.
Describe how the genetic code is carried on the DNA.
Outline the process of replication.
Compare mitosis and meiosis.
Describe the process of transcription.
Describe the functions of mRNA, tRNA, amino acids, and ribosomes in protein synthesis.
Describe the causes and effects of both chromosome and gene mutations.
Consider the purposes and techniques of gene mapping.
Examine incomplete dominance, alleles, sex determination, and sex-linked traits in the context of human genetics.
Discuss several human genetic disorders such as hemophilia, sickle-cell anemia, Down's syndrome, and Tay-Sach's disease.
Discuss the similarities and differences between sex chromosomes and somatic chromosomes.
Using examples from living organisms discuss the importance of asexual and sexual reproduction to their growth and survival.
Delineate the impact of biotechnology on our society.
Describe the basic processes involved in the production of recombinant DNA.
Discuss examples of current uses of recombinant DNA technology in the agricultural and pharmaceutical industries.
Discuss the techniques of genetic screening.
Consider the implications of genetic screening of adults, children, and fetuses.
Discuss the application of population genetics to the study of evolution.
Describe the concepts of the deme and the gene pool.
Consider the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
Describe the factors which influence genetic drift.
Consider the relevance of the gene pool and the idea of mutations to the concept of evolution which will be studied later in unit 5.

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of biological systems.

To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.

Describe how nutrients and oxygen are moved to the body cells.
Review the principles of diffusion and active transport.
Contrast passive transport systems, as in the cnidaria, with active transport systems, such as the human blood circulation system.
Compare open circulation systems, as in the grasshopper, with the closed systems of vertebrates.
Compare the efficiencies of hearts with one, two, three, and four chambers.
Describe the blood circulation pattern and vessels in the mammalian systems.
Explain the functioning of the human circulation system.
Describe the functions of the heart, lungs, kidneys, and liver in the circulation system.
Describe the ABO and Rh typing systems for human blood.
Consider the role of the blood in the immune system and the effect of the human immunodeficiency virus on the T4 cells of the blood.
Research the use of artificial hearts, heart transplants, the and circulation machines used during open-heart surgery.
Discuss respiration by relating the activity to the physical structure like the lungs and blood and the cells fed by the blood.
Describe the functions and functioning of nervous systems.
Describe the structure of a neuron.
Explain how neurons transmit impulses within and between themselves.
Compare the complexity of nervous systems in the planaria, earthworm, and human.
Contrast the functions of the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system in humans.
Compare the structure of the brains of reptiles and humans.
Explain how the human endocrine system influences body development and maintenance.
Describe the general structure of hormones.
Describe the influence of the pituitary gland on body processes and on other glands.
Discuss the relationship between insulin and the body's control of blood sugar levels in the two forms of diabetes.
Outline the functions of hormones produced by several other glands.
Compare reproductive strategies among animal phyla.
Contrast the advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction with those of sexual reproduction.
Compare external fertilization with internal fertilization.
Describe fertilization in the earthworm.
Compare the amniotic egg of reptiles and birds with the structures which form in the uterus of a pregnant mammal.
Describe the production of semen in humans.
Describe the human female reproductive cycle from ovulation to either menstuation or implantation.
Trace the major developmental events from implantation of a fertilized egg to the birth of a human baby.
Identify the biofeedback mechanisms which are important in the regulation of the female reproductive cycle.
Describe how the use of the hormones found in birth control pills alters the reproductive cycle.
Discuss the relationship between the diet and health of the mother and the development of the fetus.

Investigate some technologies related to reproduction, such as in vitro fertilization, use of fertility drugs, birth control, amniocentesis, genetic screening of prospective parents, sperm banks, etc.

Explain how Darwin's observations led to his inferences about evolution.
Compare the development of theories of evolutionary change (some examples - Lamarck, De Vries, Weisman).
Recognize evidence of evolution.
Discuss the use of the fossil record in the creation of lines of phylogeny.
Examine data from comparative anatomy and comparative embryology.
Describe instances of evolution documented in earth history.
Discuss the theory of continental drift and how that might have contributed to the changing variety of organisms that exist today. Where possible consider examples.
Examine broad climatic changes during the earth's history (ice ages, melting of the ice caps) and consider how these changes may have contributed to the changing organisms.
Examine the effects of migration and mutations on evolutionary change.
Discuss how evolution proceeds.
Compare gradualism and punctuated equilibrium.
Discuss the implications of the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
Describe the role of isolation in speciation.
Identify both pre-mating and post-mating barriers to recombination and reproduction.
Consider the speciation and development of humans.

notes: Structure as printed: for each core unit, 'Factors of Scientific Literacy Which Should be Emphasized' (codes defined in the guide's Dimensions of Scientific Literacy section; kept as printed in factorsEmphasized), 'Common Essential Learnings Foundational Objectives' (code = CEL abbreviation as printed), and 'Biology Foundational and Learning Objectives' (bold numbered foundational objectives, decimal-numbered learning objectives).
The guide says learning objectives 'can be selected from those listed or can be developed by the teacher and students' (p. 3 printed); they are not all mandatory.
Biology 20: 4 core units (78 h minimum) + optional time; Biology 30: 5 core units + optional time. Optional Plans pages list suggestions only (no objectives) and are not extracted.
The guide states 'Biology 20 is not a prerequisite for Biology 30' (printed p. 82).
Codes like '1' and '1.1' restart in every unit; they are only unique within a unit (and level).

Text extracted with pdfjs-dist (legacy build) from a 1992 WordPerfect-generated PDF; two-column pages split at x=300. Bullet glyphs (WPTypographicSymbols '!') and box-drawing dashes (WPBoxDrawing ')') were mapped to '•' and '—'.

indicators.text: Discuss the importance of probability in predicting the likelihood of inheriting particular traits. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish among patterns of inheritance (e.g., dominant and recessive alleles, sex-linked traits, codominance, incomplete dominance, multiple alleles and polygenic inheritance) of heritable traits. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine an organism's phenotype from its genotype, and where possible, its genotype from its phenotype. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses using P1 genotypes (i.e., homozygous and heterozygous) to determine genotypic and phenotypic frequencies for F1 and F2 generations. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe how gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection influence the frequency of alleles within a population. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize that scientists now understand chromosomes to be the mechanism of Mendel's laws (i.e., law of segregation, law of independent assortment and law of dominance). (STSE, A, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of meiosis, including crossing-over, in creating genetic variation in gametes and non-disjunction in creating chromosomal abnormalities. (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the types of chromosomal mutations (duplication, deletion, inversion, and translocation) that can occur during genetic processes. (K, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify, using karyotypes, nondisjunction mutations (e.g., Klinefelter, Down, and Turner syndromes) that can occur during genetic processes. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Investigate how genetic information is stored, transmitted and expressed at the molecular level.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Appreciate how the discovery of the DNA molecule as the chemical basis of inheritance has fundamentally transformed the field of biology. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the nature of the predominant scientific culture when scientists such as Erwin Chargaff, Rosalind Franklin, Maurice Wilkins, James Watson and Francis Crick were investigating the chemical basis of inheritance. (A, STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the importance of the structure of the DNA molecule to its ability to store, transmit and express genetic information. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Model molecular genetic processes of DNA replication and protein synthesis (i.e., transcription and translation), including the roles of DNA, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the types of point mutations (base pair substitution, insertion, deletion) and the effects of these point mutations (missense, nonsense, and neutrality), including the role of reading frame and frameshift effects during additions and deletions of one or two bases. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the value of DNA proofreading and repair and its role in preventing genetic mutations. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the role of genetic mutation in the process of evolution. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe how environmental and epigenetic factors influence genetic expression. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Model or simulate common techniques (e.g., agarose gel electrophoresis, polymerase chain reaction, DNA sequencing and DNA fingerprinting) used by molecular geneticists. (S, K, A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore the impacts of historical, current and emerging biotechnologies on self, society and the environment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify examples of historical, current and emerging biotechnologies (e.g., selective breeding, applications of fermentation, genetic engineering, cloning, gene therapy, assistive reproductive technologies and synthetic biology). (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how societal pressures such as food, energy and resource shortages can drive the development of biotechnologies. (A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research a medical (e.g., 3-D bio printing, personalized medicine, genetic testing and screening and gene therapy) or industrial (e.g., use of recombinant DNA, biofuels and bioremediation) application of biotechnology. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore potential positive and negative impacts of a specific biotechnology (e.g., the use of stem cells, genetically modified and synthetic organisms and synthetic DNA) on individuals and society. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how the use and misuse of antibiotics has led to increased bacterial resistance, including the emergence of superbugs. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Critique how individuals and groups use and misuse scientific information to support their positions regarding biotechnologies such as vaccines. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the media's role in crafting public perception related to biotechnologies (e.g., vaccines, genetically modified organisms and genetic screening). (STSE, A, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the role of regulation and legislation in providing a level of public safety pertaining to applications of biotechnology. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Defend a position related to intellectual property rights in biotechnology such as genome ownership and whether patents should include owning the rights to organisms or parts of organisms. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the Human Genome Project (HGP) as an example of a collaborative scientific endeavour. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement:
Extend understanding of functions including:
- algebraic functions (polynomial, rational, power)
- transcendental functions (exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric)
- piecewise functions, including absolute value.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify functions as algebraic, transcendental, and piecewise from their graphs and from their equations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify functions as being even, odd, increasing, decreasing, one-to-one, and many-to-one from their graphs and from their equations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The graph of an absolute value function will be located entirely above the x-axis.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the domain of a function from its equation and from its graphical representation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the range of a function from its equation and from its graphical representation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and express the domain and range of a function using set and interval notation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining characteristics including symmetry, direction, and end behaviour of functions from their equations and from their graphs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze rational functions to determine conditions where x intercepts, vertical asymptotes, and holes exist by identifying the values of the domain that produce values which are zero, undefined, or indeterminate.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If the denominator of a rational function equals zero at $x = a$, then the rational function has a vertical asymptote at $x = a$.”

outcomes.statement:
Extend understanding of factoring, absolute value, and solving inequalities to include:
- rational expressions
- double inequalities
- absolute value inequalities.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Extend and apply factoring by greatest common factor (GCF) to include negative and rational exponents.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Extend and apply factoring over the set of rational numbers to the set of real numbers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “All polynomials can be factored.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for factoring sum of cubes, difference of cubes, and $x_^n-y_^n$ (where n is a positive integer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving inequalities containing rational expressions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving double inequalities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving rational equations which include absolute value expressions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving absolute value inequalities containing rational expressions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of limits and continuity.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and explain the meaning of a limit.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the difference between the limit of a function and the value of a function.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function has a limit of L as x approaches a, then as x-values get close to a, the y-values of the function will get progressively closer to L.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Determine the value of a limit and express the value using limit notation when given:
- a graph
- an algebraic expression.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the graph of a function to determine if it is continuous.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the equation of a function to determine if it continuous.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining if a function is continuous at a given point.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the type of discontinuity (removable, jump, or infinite) when given:
- a graph
- an algebraic expression.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies (e.g., direct substitution, factoring, simplifying, rationalizing) to determine limits, at real numbers and infinity, of functions including absolute value, root, and piecewise.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the conditions under which a limit does not exist.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of differentiation based on slope as a rate of change.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and explain situations in which slope is used to describe a rate of change.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Interpret and explain the difference between average rate of change and instantaneous rate of change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving average rates of change and instantaneous rates of change.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the slope of the tangent line at a particular point by finding the slopes of secant lines.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply the following definition of a derivative: $\lim_{h→0}{f(x+h)-f(x)}/h$

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply rules of differentiation:
- power
- product
- quotient
- chain.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply two or more differentiation rules to a function.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “It is possible to differentiate any function with the rules that we have studied.”

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the value(s) of x where a function is not differentiable.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function is continuous, then it is differentiable.”

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply the process of implicit differentiation.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Determine the equation of the tangent line and normal line at a specific point on a function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Express derivatives using a variety of notations such as $f'(x)$, $y'$, $d/d_\x$, and $d_\y/d_\x$.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The $f'(x)$ notation for the derivative is superior to the $d_\y/d_\x$ notation.”

outcomes.statement: Extend understanding of curve sketching by applying differentiation and limits.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for finding higher order derivatives and their notations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for using the first derivative to determine:
- critical points
- increasing and decreasing intervals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for using the second derivative to determine:
- points of inflection
- concavity intervals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the difference between relative and absolute extrema.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the first and second derivatives to determine relative and absolute extrema.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze graphical representations of $f(x)$ to identify critical point(s), increasing and decreasing intervals, point(s) of inflection, and concavity intervals.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of $f(x)$ when given the graph of the first derivative and/or second derivative.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of $f(x)$ when given descriptions of the first derivative and/or second derivative.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply understanding of limits to determine vertical and horizontal asymptotes.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of a function with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “An absolute maximum or minimum value occurs at $x=a$, if and only if $f'(a) = 0$.”

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the application of derivatives to solve problems including:
- optimization
- rates of change
- related rates.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving optimization as they apply to topics such as area, volume, and cost.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving rates of change as they apply to topics such as business, motion, and science.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving related rates by the application of implicit differentiation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If the rate of change of the radius of a circle doubles, then the rate of change of the area will also double.”

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of transcendental function derivatives and their applications.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop an understanding of e using limits.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize the squeeze theorem to evaluate limits involving trigonometric functions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies to determine derivatives of the following transcendental functions:
- exponential and logarithmic functions using any base
- sine and cosine functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Apply first and second derivatives to sketch graphs of:
- exponential and logarithmic functions using any base
- sine and cosine functions
- composite transcendental functions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “A function and its derivative are always different.”

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving the derivatives of transcendental functions.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of indefinite and definite integration:
- by sight
- by substitution
- as used in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between indefinite and definite integration.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function can be differentiated, then it can be integrated.”

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine indefinite integrals by sight.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine indefinite integrals by substitution.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals by sight and by substitution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving integration.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The integral of $f'(x)dx$ equals $f(x)$.”

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the area bounded by:
- a curve and the x-axis over [a,b]
- two curves.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “To integrate any power, we apply in reverse the power rule for differentiation.”

outcomes.statement: Compare the impact of federal and provincial legislation on workers in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14C: Employment Standards C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List examples of industries (e.g., inter-provincial and international services such as railways, pipelines, shipping and shipping services; radio and television broadcasting; air transport; banks; most grain elevators, flour and seed mills; uranium mining and processing; and most federal crown corporations and the federal public service) that are federally regulated by the Canada Labour Code.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List examples of industries that are provincially regulated by The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios that demonstrate ways of managing anger and negotiating and resolving conflict in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop an employment contract that outlines working conditions for a specific workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways to address workplace disputes such as a worker not being paid overtime.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: List community agencies that can provide information about employment standards.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of rights and responsibilities in relation to workplace safety.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15C: Workplace Safety – Rights and Responsibilities (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research employer and worker responsibilities with respect to health and safety standards as required by law in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios to demonstrate how to properly refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019 and associated Regulations, and how they affect safe workplace practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how workers can participate in and support health and safety activities in the workplace. (e.g., Occupational Health and Safety Committees, professional development, training and following safety procedures).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents, dangerous occurrences, injuries, or illnesses immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

outcomes.statement: Explore workplace hazards and injury prevention.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16C: Workplace Safety – Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how a workplace injury might affect the injured worker and others such as the employer, supervisor, work colleagues, family and friends.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between a workplace hazard and risk.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among the four Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazard categories including physical (e.g., heavy lifting, repetitive motion, slipping/tripping, working at heights, working alone, cuts and burns), chemical (e.g., chemicals, fumes, vapours and gases), biological (e.g., viruses, fungi, bacteria, mold; bodily fluids; sewage; animal/pet waste; and influenza), and psychological (e.g., harassment and bullying, stress, fatigue and shift work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of potential workplace hazards in the five major categories.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, workplace inspections and following safe work practices, and provide examples of each for a variety of industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in a variety of environments including home, school, and workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore safety statistics related to young workers in the workplace in Saskatchewan and Canada and compare the statistics to those of workers in other age brackets.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe current prevention programs or agencies (e.g., Mission Zero, Work Safe Saskatchewan and Saskatchewan Safety Council) in Saskatchewan that are designed to raise awareness of and prevent workplace incidents.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain health and safety regulations common to a specific occupation of interest.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify employer responsibilities in relation to safety hazards.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss the need for health and safety legislation and regulations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) is and its purpose and scope in the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between general education and workplace training in regards to WHMIS 2015.

e

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define life/work balance and how it relates to maintaining personal wellness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the prevalence of mental illness in Canada and the resulting impact on the workplace.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how areas of stress, including personal financial stress, impact productivity in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of a psychologically healthy and safe workplace to employees and employers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research employers’ responsibility for establishing a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe practical ways that employees can contribute to a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research employers’ duties and responsibilities about workplace mental health as outlined in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research accommodations (e.g., modification of work duties, flexible hours, job sharing and modifications to the work environment) that employees experiencing mental health problems or issues can request.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research employers’ ‘duty to accommodate’ as outlined in the Canadian Human Rights Code.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss barriers (e.g., lack of awareness that accommodations may be possible, lack of awareness of where to find supports and lack of confidence in requesting accommodations) that employees face in disclosing a mental health problem or illness and/or in requesting accommodations.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research sources of support (e.g., Human Resources Department, union, Saskatchewan Health Authority, Canadian Mental Health Association, Mental Health Commission of Canada and Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety) for those experiencing mental health problems or issues in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Examine how personal, cultural and societal beliefs affect relationships in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Diversity in the Workplace (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how workplace relationships can benefit when diversity is acknowledged, accepted and incorporated in the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the cultural diversity within one’s community and the impact on local workplaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how discrimination based on factors such as ancestry, nationality, creed, gender diversity, sexual orientation, age, religion and disability can affect the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate issues faced by underrepresented groups (e.g., persons with disabilities; ethnic or cultural groups; and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and Two-spirit persons) face in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of an open discussion to establish workplace standards and norms that foster respect, mutual understanding and inclusion within the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on personal beliefs and unconscious bias, and their potential impact on relationships in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Examine fair and ethical practices and privacy rights in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Workplace Ethics and Privacy (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of ethical (e.g., responsibility, honesty and confidentiality) and unethical (e.g., conflict of interest, abuse of substances, sexual harassment, bullying, theft, falsifying documents and reports, and misrepresentation) behaviours on the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of unions in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the role of unions in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss common expectations for union members in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of being employed in a workplace where workers are unionized.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the term harassment and discuss the potential effects of harassment on mental health and wellbeing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss ways to deal with harassment of self or others in the workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the code of ethics for school with a code of ethics for a workplace.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare employers’ and employees’ expectations with respect to fair and ethical workplace practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research employee and employer rights and responsibilities that foster a culture of privacy in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Explore factors that contribute to a successful work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80C: Work Study Preparation A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify safety hazards that could potentially be encountered during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Compose a list of questions related to workplace hazards and safety to ask of the work placement employer such as:
- What physical, chemical, ergonomic or biological hazards should I be aware of in my work placement?
- When will I receive job safety training and orientation before I begin work?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear or other clothing am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify employment standards (e.g., use of a uniform) that may pertain to one’s work placement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s right to know, right to participate and right to refuse while in the work placement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop personal and learning goals for the work placement in consultation with the parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff member and employer.
