outcomes.statement: Examine Catholic teachings regarding the nature, role and influence of the Holy Spirit.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Discuss the mystery of the Holy Spirit using experiences and teachings such as:
- Holy Spirit as third person of the Trinity
- Holy Spirit in key moments of Jesus' life (e.g., Annunciation, conception, baptism by John, ministry of Jesus, Paschal Mystery)
- Holy Spirit in one's life and the Church (e.g., grace; Sacraments; the sense of the faithful; Magisterium; one holy, Catholic, apostolic Church; Church councils and synods)
- Holy Spirit in society (e.g., revealed in beauty; influencing feminine theological discourse; guiding organizations such as Society of St. Vincent de Paul, The Catholic Women's League of Canada, Knights of Columbus).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Represent ways the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit may be expressed in one's life (e.g., represent through class projects, digital formats, arts expressions).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways the Holy Spirit affects individuals, groups, institutions and society (e.g., hearing, heeding, indifference, rejection).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research individuals who, although flawed and marginalized in their time, have now been recognized by the Church as having been guided by the Holy Spirit (e.g., Saint Mary McKillop, Mary Ward, Saint Mother Teresa, Dorothy Day, Catherine Doherty, Blessed Oscar Romero, Saint Kateri Tekakwitha).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe ways the "new evangelization" raises awareness about the role of the Holy Spirit in contemporary life (e.g., conveying Catholic messages through websites, podcasts, videos, graphic novels, modernized traditional hymns, praise and worship music, films).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a representation to show how individuals, the Church and society can be drawn into community through the Holy Spirit (e.g., artistic, written, verbal, digital).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Investigate what individuals and institutions have said about the influence of the Holy Spirit on their lives and work, including topics such as:
- cultural infusion (e.g., First Nations, Polish, or Filipino culture within the Latin Catholic church; Ukrainian Catholic church; Chaldean Catholic church)
- ecclesial traditions (e.g., local and international pilgrim events or religious art) such as:
- Saskatchewan pilgrimages to the Shrine of St. Laurent or the Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes in St. Peter's Colony and the artwork of Father Henry Metzger
- international pilgrimages to World Youth Day or famed pilgrim trails such as the Camino de Santiago (i.e., Way of St. James)
- local religious art in Saskatchewan churches such as the dome of St. Mary's Ukrainian Catholic Church in Yorkton painted by Stephen Meush and Our Lady of Sorrows Church decorated by Count Berthold Von Imhoff in Paradise Hill
- international religious art in churches throughout the world such as St. Sophia's Cathedral in Kiev and Cathédrale Notre Dame de Paris
- religious movements (e.g., L'Arche, Madonna House, Focolare Movement, Knights of Columbus, Catholic Women's League, Catholic boys and girls clubs such as Conquest or Challenge).

outcomes.statement: Examine the Catholic understanding of discernment in response to God's vocational call to each individual.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the Catholic meaning of discernment as being a decision-making process in life including vocational decision-making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss influences on one's discernment processes such as:
- humility
- prayer
- advice from friends and/or family
- expectations of others
- personal interests and passions
- suffering or illness (e.g., physical, mental, emotional, spiritual)
- trust in God
- vocational vows (e.g., obedience, poverty, chastity).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine the benefits, responsibilities and challenges associated with the traditional Catholic vocations (i.e., priesthood, religious life, marriage, single life) including discussions of:
- spiritual development
- service
- chastity
- loneliness versus being alone
- family and community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how important vocational decisions can be guided by various religious and spiritual approaches including Catholic discernment, First Nations and Métis traditions and other practices (e.g., meditation, prayer, Elder advice, retreats, candle-lighting ceremonies).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate how the priesthood and religious life influence society through ways such as:
- reflecting the Beatitudes
- demonstrating Gospel values
- representing and giving witness to Jesus.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Examine the Catholic understanding of the vocation of marriage through topics such as:
- matrimony within the vocation of holy orders (e.g., married deacons, married priests such as Ukrainian Catholics or those of the Chaldean Church)
- differences between civil law marriages and the sacrament of holy matrimony (e.g., Canon law, Council of Trent, Sacrament of Crowning in Eastern Churches, covenants versus contracts)
- differences between civil divorce and declaration of nullity of marriage (i.e., annulment)
- implications of the recalling of the gift of children within Eastern rite matrimonial ceremonies and the Latin rite two-fold question (i.e., Will you lovingly accept children from God? Will you raise them in the faith of the Church?)
- married life and family dynamics (e.g., communication, Natural Family Planning, artificial contraceptives, parenting strategies, domestic responsibilities, charity, play and leisure)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe personal responses to the vocational call of God.

outcomes.statement: Examine the daily commitment involved in responding to Jesus' invitation to live in covenant with God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the Catholic understanding of a God who calls.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Describe what can be learned about the commitment required for living in a covenantal relationship with God through:
- the call and response of St. Peter
- the call and response of St. Paul
- Catholic teachings of Pentecost
- the commissioning of the disciples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Investigate difficulties one might encounter in hearing and heeding the call of God such as:
- apathy or indifference to spirituality
- negative associations with religion or religious institutions
- the prevalence of atheism in contemporary society
- the presence of various non-religious views (e.g., agnosticism, humanism, relativism)
- conflicting religious views
- daily distractions (e.g., social media, mass media saturation, fads, trends, sensory overload, financial and other pressures).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Investigate how a person's daily efforts to hear and heed God's call can be supported in various ways by considering the ideas of:
- spiritual counsellors (e.g., clergy, teachers, theologians, Elders, men and women religious, evangelists, parents, family, friends)
- artists whose subject matter is spiritual (e.g., sculptors, painters, architects, poets, musicians, playwrights, filmmakers, dancers)
- the digital world (social media, internet)
- retreat houses, leaders and facilitators
- missionary disciples
- social justice and service agencies (e.g., Development and Peace, Catholic Family Services).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of the `new evangelization' on one's own life and contemporary society.

outcomes.statement: Investigate influences on the development of conscience and its effect on individuals and society.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe influences on the sensitization and desensitization of conscience (e.g., family, friends, grace, formal and informal education, media, cultural traditions).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the extent to which one's conscience and moral beliefs influence one's actions (e.g., resistance to peer pressure; moral relativism; environmental, economic and social sustainability; cohabitation; digital behaviours such as sexting and cyberbullying).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the difference between doing good and avoiding evil including the role of silent majorities and unquestioned obedience (e.g., Nazism, KKK, slavery, ISIS, Edmund Burke's statement: "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good people to do nothing").

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Examine and represent (e.g., through presentations or arts expressions) ideas about conscience and morality such as:
- I am part of a community so my actions affect others
- faith informed by reason; reason informed by faith
- a good intention can never justify an evil act.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of conscience in moral judgment through the three sources of Catholic morality (i.e., the moral object, the intention and the circumstances).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss personal implications and responsibilities stemming from the Church teaching about the concept of primacy of conscience.

outcomes.statement: Examine ethical implications of freedom.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine ethical implications of limitless freedom (e.g., personal and corporate greed, human trafficking, abuse of power, sustainability issues, discriminatory practices).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Generate and investigate inquiry questions for the following:
- foundations for moral decision-making (i.e., moral agency)
- concepts of 'can versus should' or 'able versus ought'.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine Paul's understanding of freedom as being set free from something and set free for something.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the Catholic paradox of freedom involving obedience (e.g., finding freedom within the will of the Father, freedom to fulfill the purpose for which one is created).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Examine the Christian conviction of Jesus as Truth which will set one free including interpretations such as:
- Jesus as fulfillment of Mosaic law (i.e., Jesus provides freedom from prescribed Mosaic laws to pursue the law of the heart)
- Jesus' teachings shifting morality away from legalistic approaches to relational ones.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research diverse views on human dignity and limits on freedom (e.g., Catholic, traditional First Nations and Métis, Buddhist, Hindu, Evangelical Christians, atheists, moral relativists, religious extremists).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Express personal perspectives on the ethical implications of freedom.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the morality and effects of bioethical decisions and other dignity of life issues.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe Catholic teachings pertaining to dignity of life including the concept of human value versus human usefulness (e.g., euthanasia, abortion, marginalization of the vulnerable).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research views of prominent bioethicists regarding the value of human life (e.g. Dr. Moira McQueen, Sr. Nuala Kenny M.D., Margaret Somerville, representatives of the National Catholic Bioethics Centre).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine and describe how personal views are influenced by Catholic teachings on bioethical issues (e.g., cloning, stem-cell research, in-vitro fertilization, organ donation and transplants, eugenics, designer babies, abortion, transhumanism, euthanasia, suicide).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine and describe how personal views are influenced by societal perspectives on bioethical issues (e.g., traditional First Nations and Métis, Evangelical Christian, Hindu, Buddhist, moral relativist, popular culture and atheist).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss ethical implications and effects of health and wellness practices, programs and experiences such as:
- current medical interventions (e.g., palliative care, abortion, organ transplantation, sterilization)
- past medical interventions (e.g., the Alberta Eugenics Board operating from 1928 – 1972, the Weyburn Mental Hospital operating from 1921 – 1971)
- use of artificial contraceptives or Natural Family Planning
- medical research techniques using generated or harvested stem cells
- federally funded universal Medicare program
- health issues resulting from marginalization and poverty including those occurring in First Nations and Métis communities (e.g., high incidents of diabetes, HIV and suicide).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Using Church teachings expressed in documents such as "A Church Seeking Justice", research and represent Cardinal Bernardin's principle of the 'Seamless Garment of Life' (e.g., homelessness, gender and sexual diversity issues, artificial contraceptives, militarism).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the benefits of being both spiritual and religious.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe perspectives on faith, spirituality, religion and church from Catholic and diverse spiritual, religious and secular points of view.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Debate anthropological and psychological theories that human beings are naturally spiritual and religious.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Compare one's own spiritual practices to those within the Catholic Church such as the:
- Thomistic path of intellect
- Augustinian path of devotion
- Franciscan path of service
- Ignatian path of asceticism
- Theresian path of mysticism
- Benedictine spirituality of prayer and work
- spirituality of Saint Mother Teresa
- prayer of the heart (e.g., the Jesus Prayer, practicing the presence of God in all things).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe one's own role in the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops' five actions supporting the mission of the Church (i.e., proclaiming Christ, worshiping Christ through the sacraments, forming a communion of people, giving witness, serving).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine spiritual and religious tension and conflict within society as it affects relationships.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss and represent what it means to live in the world, but not of the world (i.e., Jn. 17:16).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the Catholic concept of martyrdom with religious extremism.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss similarities and differences between being spiritual and religious recognizing people can be either, neither or both.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Discuss benefits and challenges faced in spiritual and/or religious growth using topics such as:
- relationship with God or a higher power
- gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit or other spiritual beliefs
- witnessing to your faith in all situations (e.g., respect versus stereotyping)
- growing in one's identity (e.g., inner peace and strength versus concerns over reactions of others)
- prayer and meditative practices
- community involvement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe benefits of private and communal prayer (e.g., Mt. 6:6, Mt. 18:20).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Explain the Catholic perspectives of:
- faith and spirituality being more personal than private (e.g., Mt. 28 16-20, Rm. 1:12, 1Cor. 11: 1-2)
- religion and church membership being more communal than public (e.g., Mt. 6:1-5, Rm. 15: 7, Mt. 5:13-16, Mt. 22: 37-40).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the effect reported miracles have on faith and religious expression.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the centrality of the miracle of the Resurrection of Jesus to the Christian religion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express personal perspectives on the wondrous and miraculous nature of life and the mystery and power of God (e.g., music, painting, digital presentation, expressive writing).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss artistic expressions inspired by the life, miracles and teachings of Jesus and the effects of these works on personal faith and religious beliefs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Research and express viewpoints about miracles authenticated by the Church such as:
- miracles within Scripture
- Marian apparitions at Fatima (e.g., the day the sun danced) and Guadalupe (e.g., the tilma of St. Juan Diego)
- stigmatists (e.g., St. Francis of Assisi and St. Padre Pio)
- healings (e.g., 1958 healing attributed to the intercession of St. Brother André, healings at Lourdes attributed to the intercession of Mary)
- incorruptible corpses (e.g., St. Francis Xavier, St. Bernadette of Lourdes).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Describe or represent (e.g., written, visual, digital) how personal faith is impacted by miracles such as those involving:
- Moses (e.g., burning bush, plagues, parting of the Red Sea)
- Jesus (e.g., water to wine, healing, commanding weather, casting out demons, raising the dead)
- Pentecost (e.g., the miracle of the tongues)
- Church authenticated miracles in modern history (e.g., Fatima, Lourdes, St. Padre Pio, the tilma of St. Juan Diego).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine effects on one's personal faith of the miracle of transubstantiation within the celebration of the Eucharist.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss implications for one's faith, religious practices and life if one were to witness a miracle (e.g., others' interpretations of the event, radical changes in one's life, Thomas' experience in John 20:24-29).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Debate the question: What is the greatest miracle (e.g., the transformation of a human heart, a simple life lived in freedom and faithfulness, the Resurrection of Jesus, life and creation)?

outcomes.statement: Examine significant changes in the Catholic church over time and propose ideas for future growth.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Conduct an inquiry examining the degree to which church teachings, practices or relationships have evolved over time such as:
- teachings on suicide, slavery, or priest celibacy
- practices involving the roles of laity or women within the Church
- relationships with Indigenous peoples, scientific communities, or people who are gender and sexually diverse.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the evolving nature of the Mass and the sacraments of the Church.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Describe how relationships evolve through dialogue such as:
- ecumenical (Evangelical Christians, Anglicans)
- interfaith (Buddhists, Hindus)
- secular (Atheists, Agnostics, Relativists).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Analyze the Catholic teaching that private revelation continues salvation history and reveals God's message through examples such as:
- St. Hildegarde
- St. Bridget of Sweden
- St. Vincent Ferrer
- St. Juan Diego
- Marian apparitions (e.g., Akita, Lourdes, Fatima).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate the mission and characteristics and predict future roles of Catholic religious orders such as:
- priestly orders (e.g., Spiritans, Jesuits, Basilians, Missionary Congregation of St. Andrew the Apostle)
- orders of priests and brothers (e.g., Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate, Redemptorists)
- male and female orders (e.g., Carmelites, Order of St. Benedict)
- female orders (e.g,. Ursulines, Sister Servants of Mary Immaculate, Sisters of the Precious Blood, Grey Nuns, Sisters of St. Joseph, Sisters of the Presentation).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Research and debate influential theological views on topics such as:
- the doctrine of the Trinity
- the union of Christ's humanity and divinity (e.g., hypostatic union, Incarnation, heresies including Arianism or Gnosticism)
- reformation theology (e.g., marriage, divorce and indulgences)
- contemporary issues (e.g., female clergy, same-sex marriage, 'restored order' of sacraments in the Roman rite, distribution of Eucharist to civilly divorced and re-married Catholics).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to propose ideas to ensure the future relevance of the Church.

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence of ecumenical and interfaith dialogue on one's faith, religious communities and society.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare distinctive features among various faiths (e.g., moral codes, religious or spiritual expressions, concepts of God, artistic representations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Investigate examples of how dialogue fosters co-operation and acceptance amongst diverse faith traditions such as:
- sharing traditions through the arts
- Pope Francis' 2015 meeting with Hindu, Buddhist, Muslim and Christian communities in Sri Lanka
- Evangelicals and Catholic Together, an ecumenical document, developed in the United States in 1994
- Pope Benedict XVI's 2009 meeting with National Chief Phil Fontaine expressing sorrow for residential school abuse and support for Truth and Reconciliation
- annual National Day of Prayer in Solidarity with Indigenous Peoples established December 12, 2002
- annual Week of Prayer for Christian Unity
- The Common Witness Project
- various local and school-based initiatives.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on the development of one's spiritual beliefs and examine how effective dialogue influences faith and deepens understanding.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss personal religious and spiritual beliefs with individuals or groups of various faiths (e.g., in-class sharing, meetings with Elders, digital exchanges, exchanges through Saskatoon Centre for Ecumenism).

outcomes.statement: Examine how Catholic faith and teachings can support individuals and communities in positively transforming society.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Evaluate how individual and societal values and beliefs are influenced positively and negatively by popular culture (e.g., raising awareness, documenting the human condition, stereotyping, desensitizing, desiring fame and celebrity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss the Catholic culture of encounter as a means of transforming the world through, for example:
- developing Catholic virtues (e.g., cardinal virtues such as justice and courage, theological virtues such as charity, cardinal virtues such as humility and generosity)
- scriptural studies and church teachings (e.g., John 17:14-19, Luke 10:25-37, culture of love espoused by Saint Pope John Paul II, teachings on the preferential option for the poor)
- community and global action (e.g., church youth group, L'Arche, Chalice, Development and Peace).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how society is affected by the values demonstrated by organizations and social structures (e.g., business supporting community, media promoting social justice, government cooperation, reverence for life in health care, gender inequality in families, corporate social sin, abuse in sport, inequities in education).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe ways that individuals can influence organizations and social structures by promoting Christ-centred values.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Respond to the work of diverse artists who represent Christian stories and teachings considering how the work may help deepen faith and transform society.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how the Church's support for the arts throughout history has affected development of faith and understanding of Church teachings (e.g., funding architecture, sculpture, stained glass, paintings, music and poetry).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Explain how the Catholic responsibility to bring Christ to culture (i.e., ushering in the Kingdom of God) leads to involvement in the 'new evangelization' though personal and communal actions such as:
- service
- social justice
- giving witness to Christ
- forming Christ-centred families, local and global communities.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the assertion that dialogue is foundational for peace and unity in the world.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the Catholic understanding of dialogue as a relationship in which the dignity of the person is respected and rooted in Scripture and Tradition.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the Catholic interpretation of 'peace' as being more than the absence of war.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Discuss the concept of 'unity in the world' from diverse viewpoints including:
- the holistic nature of First Nations' worldviews, medicine wheels, tipi teachings
- the call for Christian unity in Scripture by St. Paul (e.g., Eph. 4:1-6) and others (e.g., John 17:20-21
- the Dalai Lama's teachings of compassion as the pillar of world peace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Evaluate the morality and effectiveness of using physical and psychological violence to achieve peace or unity using examples such as:
- religious extremists
- misuse of religion through proselytizing, religious wars, residential schools and other assimilation practices
- cults
- war and genocide
- imperialism
- force used by democratic and non-democratic nations.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish between freedom fighters and terrorists, research examples and evaluate diverse perspectives.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Research and evaluate the effectiveness of ecumenical, interfaith and non-religious dialogue as a means for peace and unity through historic examples such as:
- Lester Pearson's unity and peace initiatives (e.g., mobilizing United Nations Emergency Forces leading to Nobel Peace Prize, universal health care, abolishing capital punishment)
- Brian Mulroney's role in South African anti-apartheid initiatives leading to 2015 Order of the Companions of OR Tambo.
- South African and Canadian Truth and Reconciliation processes
- Father Albert Lacombe's mediation with First Nations (e.g., peace between Cree and Blackfoot, Canadian Pacific Railway through Blackfoot territory)
- St. Pope John Paul II's multiple statements and meetings to promote unity and peace through dialogue
- Pope Francis' meeting with the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew of Constantinople
- scientific and religious collaboration (e.g., Father Georges Lemaître's Big Bang Theory, papal support of evolutionary theory, papal statements on the mission of the Vatican Observatory).

outcomes.statement: Describe how one's experience in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat affects one's spiritual development and religious life.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create, in collaboration with one's peers and teacher, a plan for participation in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the planned Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat might affect one's life, spiritual development and religious life.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact of faith-motivated service and communal endeavors on individuals and communities.

courses.name: Chemistry 20, 30

legacyEvidence.reason: 1992 guide; not in the site's menus; its 30-level part is replaced by the renewed Chemistry 30 (id 69)
evidence: Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its objectives under 21 headings: “Introduction to Chemistry”, “Laboratory Activities”, “Independent Research”, “Atoms and Elements”, “Molecules and Compounds”, “Chemical Reactions”, “Mole Concept and Stoichiometry”, “Optional: Behaviour of Gases”, “Optional: Consumer Chemistry”, “Optional: Organic Chemistry”, “Optional: Teacher Developed Unit”, “Review of Basic Principles”, “Laboratory Activities”, “Independent Research”, “Case Study”, “Solubility and Solutions”, “Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions”, “Reaction Kinetics”, “Equilibrium”, “Acid-Base Equilibria”, “Oxidation and Reduction”.

courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum; the objectives are taken from its curriculum document (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=70); see `document`.

notes: Structure as printed: each unit has one heading 'Foundational Objectives for Chemistry and the Common Essential Learnings'. Bold statements are foundational objectives; the Common Essential Learnings ones end with the CEL abbreviation in brackets, e.g. '(COM)' (also copied into `cel`). Bulleted statements under each are learning objectives (`parent` = index of their foundational objective in the unit's items). Nothing is numbered in the source, so `code` is null.
Units whose heading starts 'Optional:' are optional units as printed.

Text extracted with pdfjs-dist (legacy build) from a 1992 WordPerfect-generated PDF; two-column pages split at x=300. Bullet glyphs (WPTypographicSymbols '!') mapped to '•' (and stripped from the start of learning objectives); WPBoxDrawing ')' used as a dash mapped to '—' (in sub/superscripts, where it is a minus sign, to '−'). Subscripts/superscripts (e.g. chemical formulas) are flattened inline, so 'H2O' may appear where the print has H₂O.

indicators.text: Sing with breath support (e.g., practise appropriate breathing technique and recognize how it helps support sound production, vocal health and characteristic tone quality).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers, with teacher guidance, to develop criteria for high quality singing considering cultural context.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discern pitch variances and make appropriate adjustments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create own vocal warmup sequences for purposes related to the repertoire.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Practise healthy ways to expand own range.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the difference between performance range versus singable range (e.g., singable range might be A# or B but would not use that range in production).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate effective transition in accessing different registrations and evenness of tone throughout the range (i.e., passaggio).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply, with guidance, a well-supported characteristic tone quality as appropriate to the repertoire.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Enact principles of vocal anatomy and terminology (e.g., how does one support breathing, the role of articulators and resonators in enunciation).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Consistently demonstrate appropriate diction required of the language and repertoire demands.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the importance of proper posture and body alignment for singing.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate choral blend through vowel unity and modifying intonation with diverse repertoire.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify factors and apply techniques for maintaining vocal health.

outcomes.statement: Apply decision-making abilities, skills and practices for improving ensemble singing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Adjust vocal techniques as appropriate within the context of the ensemble, such as:
- adjusting dynamics
- blending vowels
- placing consonants
- adjusting vibrato
- maintaining own part.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate personal and interpersonal skills necessary for ensemble music making including:
- etiquette
- rehearsal protocols
- leadership.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate interpretation abilities through versatility of voice (e.g., inflection, tone, emulating instrumental sounds).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain accurate pitch when singing harmony.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate fluency and growth in vocal techniques and musicality when singing advanced vocal ensemble repertoire.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine and apply processes (e.g., focusing on a specific part, experimenting with phrasing, running through from start to finish, working on sections, isolating variables, making group choices), independently for collective practise, rehearsal and performance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify musical functions of own and others’ parts in a song (e.g., melody, harmony, bass line).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Incorporate movement in ensemble work (e.g., use movement to experience music concepts) recognizing how singing involves the whole body.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to respond to the conductor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate ability to interpret, with increased accuracy and expression, music using various visual (e.g., standard and/or non-standard notation, written musical scores, graphic score) and aural music systems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate, with increased accuracy, the ability to respond to notation systems such as letter names, solfege, scale degrees, aural cues when singing in the context of the repertoire studied.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate increased ability to read, notate, understand and interpret written musical scores and various notation systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sight sing a short passage (e.g., at a lower difficulty level than the repertoire studied).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to learn and lead others in learning music through aural transmission (e.g., picking own part out of harmony, learning by listening to others, matching with others in same section, using another part as a reference for singing own part, learning a melody through repetition).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret expressive terms and music symbols within the context of the repertoire (e.g., tempo, dynamics, form, style, articulation, graphic symbols).

outcomes.statement: Improvise, arrange and compose with purpose for meaning.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate ways that music elements (e.g., tempo, rhythm) can be used to express musical ideas.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Take creative risks when creating and refining work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Embellish, ornament or improvise on a melody.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with stylistically appropriate group improvisation (e.g., with chords/harmonic background).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore and examine composition and arranging techniques (e.g., What is the composer doing musically in relation to the text? What is a compositional hook?).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compose, arrange or improvise a phrase or passage (e.g., develop a counter melody or descant).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on individual and group compositions and arrangements, identifying strengths and challenges encountered.

outcomes.statement: Refine stylistic practices within various forms of vocal and choral music traditions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Refine vocal characteristics and stylistic features that are typical in diverse music genres (e.g., spirituals, jazz, blues, opera).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sing (e.g., warm up, excerpt, repertoire, short folk song) in a minimum of two languages.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate stylistic features reflective of the socio-cultural contexts of the choral repertoire being studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Engage (e.g., online, in person) with artists from diverse cultural backgrounds.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how the choral music being studied has changed over time (e.g., role of choir, changing styles or genres).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how choral music has changed or developed through various eras.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine various purposes (e.g., sacred, celebratory, entertainment) of choral music and how those purposes may change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss why the content (e.g., text, subject matter within a genre, theme, message) of choral music may change over time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how aural traditions are maintained or changed in choral music.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ways that choral music can include or exclude people (e.g., audition processes, lack of site reading ability, financial barriers, marginalized populations, access to education).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Co-create a symbolic representation (e.g., visual, vocal, digital) of Saskatchewan choral music.

outcomes.statement: Examine contemporary Indigenous vocal music and composers.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research (e.g., reference materials, personal interviews) contemporary Indigenous music and vocalists.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Engage with Indigenous singers to learn about contemporary music expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research social and cultural influences (e.g., family life, legacy of residential schools, languages, personal experiences growing up, traditional stories, global issues) on contemporary Indigenous singers and their work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how specific selections of contemporary Indigenous music, local and global, incorporates traditional and/or innovative singing styles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze how the work of contemporary Indigenous singers may be influenced by cultural traditions and global change (e.g., treaty education outcome SI12 - investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community and society in relation to the importance of honouring the spirit and intent of treaties).

outcomes.statement: Create a plan for continuing engagement in choral music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore and research pathways and benefits of continuing engagement in choral music.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into opportunities and benefits for continuing lifelong engagement in choral music (e.g., community choirs, musical theatre).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research career avenues and investigate opportunities (e.g., scholarships, entrance requirements, music schools) for continuing study at the post-secondary level.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Make connections between choral music and other areas of study (e.g., literature, math, science, social sciences, physical education, other arts).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and discuss the roles that choral music plays in Saskatchewan including First Nations and Métis traditions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research supports for musicians such as unions, professional associations, agents, Elders and Knowledge Keepers, provincial and federal grants (e.g., funding for creation, touring and recording).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Seek opportunities to hear (live and recorded) and participate in choral music performances.

outcomes.statement: Analyse and discuss societal standards (e.g., legal, ethical, community norms and values) and cultural sensitivities related to choral music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the selection of repertoire and issues of community norms (e.g., appropriateness for audience, singing secular or sacred repertoire, lyrics).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into questions related to censorship and community sensitivities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss text issues/references in choral music.

outcomes.statement: Assess and refine own process for improvement as individual singers and as an ensemble.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss ways to conduct constructive critiques (e.g., identifying what is going well and how we can build on that; examine how we can pull from one area to make another better?)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine criteria collectively for critiquing own ensemble rehearsals and performances.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Take ownership of the rehearsal process (e.g., What do we need to spend more time on later?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify opportunities for improvement through various approaches (e.g., small ensembles, soprano sectionals).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore different choral structures or models for small ensembles (e.g., rotate the section leaders, conductorless singing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the process of polishing a piece including how to refine a rehearsal (formative) or a performance (summative).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Co-develop criteria for evaluating the quality and effectiveness of music performances and compositions and apply the criteria to personal listening, composing and performing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine performance spaces including acoustic properties (e.g., reverb, tone, volume) and make necessary adjustments (e.g., singing techniques, microphones).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on, and document, rehearsals and performances to achieve artistic intent and support ensemble and individual musical growth.

outcomes.statement: Critique a variety of live or recorded choral ensemble performances.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Seek out and select examples of choral performances to critique.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss components of a performance critique (e.g., analyze technique, assess interpretation, make informed opinions).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generate appropriate criteria for critique.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique different arrangements of the same choral text.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate among various genres and styles of choral performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate critical thinking during critique.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Contribute to dialogue and common understanding of the selection.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Probe and challenge assumptions about the selection.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine the aesthetic qualities of the work.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine and discuss interpretive decisions that reflect a particular musical style.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research, document and share information about various choirs, conductors, choral leaders and vocalists in Saskatchewan (e.g., Saskatchewan Choral Federation, Choral Canada).

outcomes.statement: Explore the concept of religion.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define religion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define spirituality.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify the relationship between religion and spirituality.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Examine the role of religion related to triumphs and challenges within societies past and present.

outcomes.statement: Investigate various world religions, including Judaism, Islam, Sikhism, Hinduism, Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss origins of various world religions, including the story, the context and the location.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify contemporary geographic concentrations of various faith groups.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research holy figures, founders, deity or deities, hierarchy and leadership structures of various world religions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe beliefs and practices (sacred scripture/texts and symbols, worship/rituals, conduct, purpose of life, prayer life, afterlife) of various world religions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Depict significant events in the histories of various non-Christian religions, such as Judaism, Islam, Sikhism, Hinduism, Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore themes common to various world religions including Christianity (e.g., belief system teachings, practices depicting personal expressions of faith, rituals, ceremonies of celebration).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how the study of various religions facilitates the understanding of self and others.

outcomes.statement: Explore traditional spiritual belief systems of Indigenous peoples in Canada.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Conduct an inquiry regarding the spiritual teachings and beliefs of:
- the peoples of a selection of Saskatchewan First Nations;
- Métis peoples of Saskatchewan; and,
- Inuit peoples of Canada.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the significance of the medicine wheel within Indigenous cultures of Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the Circle of Courage and tipi teachings as they relate to values, morals and lifestyle choices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research various traditions and ceremonies of spiritual significance to Indigenous cultures of the local area.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Explore the New Testament.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation showing chronology of the establishment of the early church as described in the book of Acts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between God, Jesus and the Holy Spirit in Scripture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the role of the Holy Spirit in the development of the Early Church.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the genres of the New Testament, including the Gospels, Acts of the Apostles, Letters/Epistles and Apocalyptic.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the genres of the New Testament in terms of the chronology, authorship and thematic structures.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between the New Testament and the Hebrew scriptures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain ways in which contemporary Christian ceremonies and rituals reflect connection to the Hebrew scriptures and the New Testament.

outcomes.statement: Appraise how the New Testament can influence contemporary Christian life.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how individuals in the New Testament bear witness to the nature and character of God.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the significance of the Holy Spirit within Christian Communities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the possible role of the Holy Spirit in some Christians’ personal faith journeys.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how teachings gleaned from an event within the New Testament can be applied to a contemporary situation such as inclusion, welcome or dealing with the oppressed.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the discipline of apologetics.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define apologetics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between absolute truth, objective truth and subjective truth.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how 1 Peter 3:15 impacts the discipline of defending a Christian’s faith.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize the process and benefit of logical reasoning as it relates to Christian religions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explore a variety of questions about Christianity such as:
- Does God exist?
- Is there life after death?
- Why is there evil?
- What is the role of judgement?
- What is the role of forgiveness? and,
- Is science at odds with Christianity?

outcomes.statement: Explore contemporary challenges and opportunities facing current Christian congregations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the role of Christianity in the colonization of parts of North America, Central America, South America, Africa and Asia.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research various Canadian Christian denominations’ approaches to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission Calls to Action.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define the concepts of racial privilege and gender privilege.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the role of privilege and fragility as it has manifest historically in the Church.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify opportunities that church congregations have to lead movements for social justice, equity and fairness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify trends in 21st century Church membership, and how various Christian denominations are responding to these trends.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of immigration on various Chrisitan Church congregations in Saskatchewan or Canada.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the varying views of missions in contemporary Christian beliefs and practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe how past histories regarding social issues such as corporal punishment, capital punishment, marriage, conversion therapy, abortion, healthcare directives are addressed by contemporary Canadian Christian religious groups.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact of the Doctrine of Discovery (1493) on colonialism, Indigenous spiritualities and Christian religions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the concept of Doctrine of Discovery.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of the Doctrine of Discovery on Indigenous peoples in various world locations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how the Doctrine of Discovery influenced actions of the Christian church.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the results of the Doctrine of Discovery in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the response of faith groups in Canada to calls for repudiation the Doctrine of Discovery.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss why many Indigenous peoples and organizations view repudiation of the Doctrine of Discovery as important to reconciliation in Canada.

outcomes.statement: Assess the impact of religion and spirituality on personal conduct.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Identify relationship between personal beliefs, ethical and moral standards, and the teachings of the Christian faith.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how one might reconcile potential differences between personal beliefs and the teachings of the Christian religion.

outcomes.statement: Engage in an action project that fosters a faith journey beyond the local community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Plan an action project of personal interest (e.g., worship, prayer, mentorship, leadership, healthy relationships, service, equity work, environmental, poverty) including:
- the purpose and goal of the action project
- the components within the project plan;
- the materials or research necessary to actualize the plan; and,
- financial or cost factors associated with the project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Implement the action project.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text:
Assess the implementation of the action project in terms of:
- achievement of the intended outcome;
- effectiveness of the plan; and,
- the impact of the project.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consider how the action project might influence or impact one’s future faith journey.

outcomes.statement: Create a quilt using advanced quilting techniques.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select a pattern (e.g., log cabin, pattern with diagonal block) for use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of the quilt pattern and cutting of fabric (e.g., cutting, notions, fabric and fabric amounts).

indicators.label: c

outcomes.statement: Investigate the evolution of clothing fashion.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze trend forecasting and how it affects what will be available to consumers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine cultural influences (e.g., First Nations and Métis, African, Asian) on Western fashion designs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry of influential designers and their companies at a local, national or global scale.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate major events or factors in history and their influences on fashion trends (e.g., world wars, evolving roles of women).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the influences of fast fashion (i.e., inexpensive mass market clothing) in relation to one’s ethical conscious.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ethical issues around cultural appropriation in past and present clothing and accessories fashion trends.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze significant fashion characteristics from a specific historical period (e.g., Early Renaissance, Victorian, Roaring 20s, 1960s) and their influences on present day fashion.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate subliminal messages in fashion advertising and clothing.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how fashion could cause oppression of people’s body shapes and sizes and contribute to eating disorders and use of diets.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how changes in fashion trends influence the consumer (e.g., spending habits, mental well-being, social status).

outcomes.statement: Create an item that promotes waste reduction.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Evaluate the life cycle of a garment with consideration to resources (e.g., environmental sustainability, natural/manmade materials) used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how clothing fulfils physical, psychological, social and aesthetic needs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss alternate ways of acquiring clothing such as thrifting, clothing swaps, rentals, altering and creating.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct an item (e.g., re-usable sandwich bags, cosmetic pads, food wraps and covers, totes and bags) that promotes waste and plastic reduction by replacing a single use item.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?

Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c

indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

- aspirations.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Present information on a topic of interest (e.g., advocacy, role models and reconciliation) using a variety of visuals (e.g., charts, maps, diagrams, photos, models and gestures) while speaking.

indicators.text: Participate in presenting to a large audience, such as at a school assembly or school sporting event.

outcomes.statement: Produce a variety of written non-fiction and fiction Dakota texts to express ideas, extend knowledge of the world, achieve objectives and for enjoyment.

indicators.label: a

Produce a variety of written Dakota texts (e.g., comic strips, websites and letters) related to big ideas such as:
- governance;
- heroes; and,
- aspirations.

indicators.text: Complete an autobiography with relevant details (e.g., relations, community and interests).

indicators.text: Write a message to convey the details (e.g., time and location) of an appointment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compose a written message requesting information on topics related to future plans (e.g., post-secondary education and advocacy opportunities).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Express personal opinions on familiar topics (e.g., reconciliation and stewardship) in a persuasive text.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Research, organize and present information in expository texts on topics such as:
- biography of a Dakota hero;
- how the Dakota way of life has changed; and,
- the importance of the land to Dakota people.

indicators.text: Write a letter requesting support for language revitalization in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how Dakota teachings can be passed down through generations by listening to guest speakers and land-based knowledge keepers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the common language characteristics of each Dakota community from Oc̀eti Ŝakowiɳ (the Seven Council Fires).

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how language evolves to fit societal norms.

indicators.label: i

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k

indicators.text: Explore initiatives that support the revitalization of Dakota communities, culture and language.

indicators.text: Reflect on personal linguistic and cultural identity.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and demonstrate dance technique and related protocols within a range of cultural contexts, including First Nations and Métis.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Refine and integrate the dance techniques needed to perform a particular dance type andstyle (e.g., ballroom as a type of dance including waltz, foxtrot or tango styles; ballet as a type of dance including classical or contemporary styles; powwow as a type of dance including grass or fancy styles; modern as a type of dance including Graham or contact improvisation styles; Indian classical type of dance including Bharatanatyam Kathak or Kathakali styles).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply, with guidance, technique and strategies for safe execution of dance movements (e.g., lifts).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Implement and lead warm-up and cool-down in dance class.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate body and spatial awareness while executing dance technique.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Embody elements of dance and adapt to the changes and complexities of the dance making process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply, independently, body alignment specific to the selected dance type and style (e.g., Métis dance type including jigging or square dance styles, hip hop dance type including breaking or locking styles; powwow dance type including Grass or Fancy dance styles).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Integrate technique associated with different dance types and styles to create new work.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of techniques and protocols associated with First Nations dances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore Métis dances as forms of artistic expression and social connection in communities and research competitive dance (e.g., square dance clothing designs, Métis sash colours and designs and their meaning, the number of changes that can be done).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Execute technique with precision in all dance types and styles studied.

outcomes.statement: Create solo, duo or group dances that convey personal vision or social commentary.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create movement or dance composition inspired by personal experience, social issue or recognized Canadian dance maker.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use another art form (e.g., drama, visual art, music) or discipline (e.g., science, social studies, physical education) as inspiration for dance making.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate purposeful use of dance elements and choreographic form in dance-making process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research Canadian choreographers’ methods and practices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate a Canadian dance maker’s (e.g., Michael Greyeyes, Robin Poitras, Peggy Baker) ideas and movement style into a dance composition.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create dance with a focus on social justice (e.g., reconciliation) and cultural diversity in a Canadian context.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Adapt choreography for a range of abilities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate collaboration, problem solving and clear communication during the dance-making process.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design overall vision including production components such as space, attire/regalia, lighting, sound, set and props, working with a range of resources (e.g., found objects).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Collaborate and demonstrate leadership with peers, teacher, community members during dance-making process.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Keep a record of dance-making ideas and choreography using traditional or invented notation.

outcomes.statement: Perform solo, duo or group dances that convey personal vision or social commentary.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform movement or dance composition to convey personal experience.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform movement or dance composition that has a focus on social justice (e.g., reconciliation) and cultural diversity in a Canadian context.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform dances inspired by the work of recognized Canadian dance makers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Collaborate, problem solve and communicate clearly during rehearsal and dance performance (e.g., making adjustments in the moment, dealing with unforeseen technical difficulties).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Rehearse and refine composition to convey the dance maker’s vision.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform a choreographed dance composition.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate one’s optimal level of physical and artistic abilities when dancing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create criteria for evaluating performance

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply peer and teacher feedback during rehearsal process to improve performance.

outcomes.statement: Examine how dance deepens one’s insight into self and expands relationship with community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on how dance has impacted one’s life (e.g., growth, perspective, agency, relationship to world, cultural identity, personal experience).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Establish mindful and/or contemplative exercises (e.g., written reflection, video, blog) as a daily dance practice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on and articulate how dance impacts student voice in relation to the world.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership (e.g., lead dance class for lower grade level, plan seniors’ centre movement class) in developing and sharing dance work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and research (e.g., interview) Canadians whose lives and work inspires own dance expressions, interpretations and/or dance making.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Connect and apply training methods and practices (e.g., medicine wheel, wellness wheel, sports medicine, somatic practices/Pilates) to promote mental and physical health and well-being.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use dance to promote compassion and empathy for the human experience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide evidence of active and critical engagement in community through dance.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how dance has created a sense of community in the classroom, school, local and national community (e.g., powwow, hip hop, Ukrainian communities).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze how own dance can address larger questions of human existence and perspectives (e.g., identity-related inquiry questions such as Who built me? Where am I from? Where am I going? What is my purpose? What is my self-worth?).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Take personal risks in developing and sharing dance work.

outcomes.statement: Respond critically and constructively to dance compositions, in progress and complete, using form-specific terminology and rationale.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and organize criteria, individually or collectively-developed, to analyze and assess dance compositions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Articulate goals and intentions for dance, using discipline-specific terminology.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide rationale for contextual and environmental production decisions (e.g., lighting, staging, sets, props in a theatre; site-specific permits, safety considerations, sound, technical requirements).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Seek and apply feedback from others during dance-making process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique own, peers’ and others’ dance compositions, in progress and finished, identifying and articulating strengths and areas for improvement.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Using a framework appropriate to the dance type and style, assess dance compositions (e.g., footwork in Fancy dance, movement of roach in Grass dance, isolations in hip hop, use of turnout in ballet).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Respond to dance compositions on an emotional, associative and formal intellectual level.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify potential for extended growth or future work based on feedback from self, peers and others (e.g., guest dancer/choreographer).

outcomes.statement: Analyze how dance challenges and influences personal and collective thinking about Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine Canadian social, environmental and political issues and their influence on current dance compositions (e.g., dance as social or political commentary).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare personal and collective thinking, perspectives and biases about societal issues before and after viewing and responding to dance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and reflect on ways that dance raises awareness, challenges thinking and inspires change with regard to issues such as treaty rights, land usage, immigration, diversity, war, ethics, human rights, water rights, disease, racism, gender and sexual diversity, suicide.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Transfer understanding of a dance maker’s work related to a Canadian social, environmental and/or political issue into own dance compositions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: View, analyze and respond to dances that reflect Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take part in, analyze and respond to dances that reflect Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

outcomes.statement: Examine the issues, questions and concerns of appropriation of voice in dance and the arts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the boundaries of cultural appropriation (e.g., what dances and/or elements of dances are appropriate?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate questions concerning appropriation of voice in dance and the arts

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research examples of controversy in dance and the arts regarding appropriation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Survey students, community members and artists regarding their perspectives on the issues.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate and/or discuss questions surrounding appropriation (e.g., When does portrayal cross the line into perpetuating stereotypes? Who can participate in culture-specific dances? When does borrowing become cultural appropriation in dance? When can culturally specific elements such as regalia designs be incorporated in dance? Is hip hop dancing cultural appropriation?).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how Indigenous perspectives and ways of knowing, including local cultural knowledge, impact the creation of traditional and contemporary dance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage, digitally or in-person, with Indigenous Elders, Knowledge Keepers, community leaders and/or dancers to understand the impact of Indigenous practices and perspectives related to dance making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine Indigenous perspectives on traditional and contemporary dance, drawing where possible/appropriate on the experience of students and expertise community members.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the ways of knowing and learning (e.g., dances passed down/gifted) that are applied to learning traditional and contemporary First Nations and Métis dances.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze how the work of contemporary and traditional First Nations dances and dance makers (e.g., Michael Greyeyes, Floyd Favel Starr) and Métis dances and dance makers (e.g., Scott Dance 10, 20, 3049Duffee, Krystle Pederson) are influenced by relationships to land, tradition, community and impacts of colonization (e.g., Truth, Dance and Reconciliationdocumentary, treaty education outcome SI12 -investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the Spirit and Intent of treaties).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how dance and dance makers influence and respond to social, political and cultural contexts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how Saskatchewan and other Canadian Indigenous peoples’ experiences and worldviews are expressed through dance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine protocols related to the teaching, learning and presenting of dances of Saskatchewan and other Canadian Indigenous peoples.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine topics related to gender and sexual diversity (e.g., two-spirit individuals) in dance.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct research (e.g., digital, live, interview) on a contemporary First Nation, Inuit or Métis dancer or dance maker in Canada and report on such things as: philosophy or focus, subject or themes presented, discipline specific or interdisciplinary work, and the potential influence of traditional practices (e.g., ask questions such as Do traditional practices and/or Elders influence the work you create? Does your culture influence the subject matter or themes of your work?).

outcomes.statement: Develop understanding of dance within a Canadian social context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine choreographers who investigate specific social ideas through dance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine choreography that is reflective of social commentary and make connections with development of own work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate choreographers’ approaches to creating social activism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use social commentary in a way that reflects the idea of a professional artist.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how dance can transmit or question values and beliefs.

outcomes.statement: Develop understanding of dance within a Canadian historical context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how social messages are communicated through time, identify what makes them memorable and use this information in own work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the significance of the evolution of dance types, styles and specific choreography throughout history and discuss how the work is connected to social activism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the synergies and evolutions of dance in response to current cultural globalization.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate choreographers as activists throughout history, and identify how own dance composition relates to these ideas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine dance rituals and ceremonies in a variety of Canadian belief systems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the role of dance within Indigenous societies across Canada, specifically pre-contact and post-colonial.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Pose questions about how different belief systems view dance (e.g., repression, affirmation).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate why certain dance compositions were considered to be controversial at different times in Canadian history.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore ways that skills and competencies learned from dance apply to careers one is interested in pursuing.

indicators.text: Investigate and identify careers that would suit one’s strengths, beliefs and interests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss transferable skills learned from dance to the career students are interested in pursuing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore a dance/movement opportunity one might pursue in one’s own life.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Establish a plan for lifelong participation in dance or movement.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
