outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore earth-science related career paths in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of occupations that require a background in earth science through research and/or participation in events such as a career fair or job shadow. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the connection between topics in Earth Science 30 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which earth-science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people involved in earth-science related jobs. (S, A)

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compare the roles and responsibilities of various earth science professionals as they engage with a specific project. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role of regulatory (e.g., Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Saskatchewan [APEGS]) and non-regulatory (e.g., Saskatchewan Geological Survey, Saskatchewan Mining Association, anadian Geophysical Union and the Canadian Water Resources Association) bodies that support earth scientists. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in, and reflect on, an earth-science related field experience. (K, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to earth science occupations through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or orally. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use acquired knowledge to develop a plan to attain a job of personal interest in the earth science field. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore a topic covered in Earth Science 30 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Earth Science 30that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Earth Science 30. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a topic of interest related to biology. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Participate in and reflect on a field experience related to one or more topics of Earth Science 30. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying concept related to an Earth Science 30 topic. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Debate an issued related to earth science, including developing materials to support the arguments for and arguments against a position. (A, K, S).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Consider natural disasters in the news and discuss causes of these phenomena and their impacts on the human environment and natural environment. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Produce a profile of the earth beneath their feet by locating oneself on the geological profile of Saskatchewan and relating this to the geological history of your area. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Examine the multi-disciplinary nature of earth science.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Construct a representation of the major fields of earth science and the major topics of study within each field. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between the characteristics of the four major Earth spheres (i.e., atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss why earth scientists consider interactions between and within two or more of Earth's spheres when they study earth processes. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Outline possible interactions between two or more of Earth's spheres within the context of a particular event and/or issue. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine why earth scientists utilize a systems approach by considering boundaries, inputs, outputs and feedback loops when investigating an earth science issue. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of how earth scientists collect evidence using analytical, field, theoretical, experimental and/or modeling studies. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify how earth scientists draw upon principles and processes from scientific fields such as biology, chemistry, computer science, geology, mathematics, and physics in order to address their questions. (STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify issues and events in Saskatchewan that might be studied from an earth science perspective. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize how historical and contemporary observations, including those made by First Nations and Métis peoples, can contribute to a greater understanding of Earth's processes. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess how earth science processes and principles are applicable to the study of other planets and celestial bodies. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify the significance of contributions made by Canadians to the field of earth science. (K, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine the evidence for and the importance of plate tectonics theory in explaining the processes that produced Earth's major surface features.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of plate tectonics as the unifying concept in earth science. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the key principles and driving forces of plate tectonics theory including how the theory subsumes ideas related to continental drift. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the development of the continental drift hypothesis, including the evidence (e.g., fossil, mineral, ancient climates and continental shape) scientists used to support this hypothesis. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the scientific belief that the movement of tectonic plates was responsible for the formation and break up of continents (e.g., Pangea, Rodinia and Gondwana) over geological time. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the formation of geological features (e.g., ocean trenches, mid-ocean ridges, transform faults, mountain ranges and island arcs) associated with convergent, divergent and transform boundaries, with referenceto the asthenosphere, lithosphere and mantle convection. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Correlate the world distribution of mountain ranges, volcanoes and earthquakes with the location, boundaries and movement of lithospheric plates. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Model the movement of lithospheric plates over geologic time and relate this to the geologic history of Saskatchewan. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze data,using tools such as satellite photos and the Global Positioning System (GPS),to determine the rate of relative lithospheric plate motion. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Predict the locations of future plate boundaries based on current lithospheric plate movement rates and compare with scientific predictions. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Consider which celestial bodies (e.g., Mars, Europa and exoplanets) could have or could not have geological features that might be explained by plate tectonics. (K)

outcomes.statement: Analyze how geologiests use the fossil record and relative and absolute dating methods to determine the geological history of Earth and to construct the geologic time scale.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss why geologists consider the geologic time scale as an important framework for understanding changes to Earth's crust, life forms, climate and continental positions over time. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the paradigm shift from catastrophism to uniformitarianism has influenced scientific thinking about Earth's geological history. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the importance of the fossil record as evidence to support scientific understanding of geological time and evolution. (STSE, A, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize that the nomenclature (e.g., eon, era, period and epoch) and major divisions of the geologic time scale are based on scientists' interpretation of the fossil record. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline the major geological and biological events that occurred during a particular eon, era, period or epoch of the geologic time scale. (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the consequences of catastrophic events such as asteroid impacts (at Cretaceous-Tertiary [K-T] boundary in Saskatchewan), glaciation and volcanism on the fossil record. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Contrast absolute and relative dating principles and techniques and the benefits of each. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of the key concepts of relative dating, including the law of superposition, principle of uniformitarianism, principle of original horizontality, principle of cross-cutting relationships, principle of inclusions and components, principle of faunal succession, principle of lateral continuity, and unconformities. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe how and why scientists use radiometric dating techniques to determine the absolute age of rocks. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Contrast absolute and relative dating principles and techniques and the benefits of each. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss how scientists revise the geologic time scale in response to new geological and fossil evidence. (STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide examples that show geologists can learn about Earth's formation and early history by studying other objects in the solar system. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the composition of Earth's atmosphere and factors that influence changes in the composition in the short and long term.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the history of Earth's atmosphere, including the origins and sources of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases (e.g., argon, carbon dioxide, neon, helium and methane) and the composition of those gases in today's atmosphere. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Model the role of atmospheric layers in insulating Earth and protecting Earth's surface from extra-terrestrial dangers such as ultraviolet light, solar wind and meteors. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how factors such as the oxygen and carbon dioxide balance in the oceans influence the composition of Earth's atmosphere. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how earth scientists use data such as ice composition, tree growth, sedimentary content and landforms to infer the composition of ancient climates. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of notable climatic events (e.g., volcanic activity, Great Oxygenation Event, Snowball Earth events and asteroid collisions) in Earth's history, the impacts of those events on the composition of the atmosphere and their correlation with the fossil and rock record. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the function and operation of various technologies (e.g., Earth orbiting satellites, drones, weather balloons, rocketsondes and radiosondes) used to gather data about the composition of the atmosphere. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine, using archived data, whether the frequency and severity of extreme weather events (e.g., tornadoes, hurricanes and blizzards) is changing locally, nationally and globally. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the effects of El Niño and La Niña on Saskatchewan and predict their effects on future seasons based on historical data. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Hypothesize what changes were present or would need to occur to other planet's atmospheres in order to sustain life on those planets. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize that methane measurements in Mars may provide evidence of anaerobic bacteria similar to those found on Earth. (K)

indicators.label: k

outcomes.statement: Investigate the characteristics of the hydrosphere and how hydrospheric processes impact the atmosphere, biosphere and lithosphere.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Outline the distribution of the hydrosphere in groundwater, surface water, oceans, glaciers and the atmosphere. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the types of evidence scientists gather to determine if water is or was present on other planets and celestial bodies. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the technologies (e.g., acoustics, imaging, buoys and underwater vehicles) and processes scientists use to learn about the hydrosphere. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how factors such as porosity and permeability influence the storage and movement of groundwater. (S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Model the movement of groundwater, including the locations of reservoirs and flows, in a hypothetical or actual groundwater system. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of how groundwater works as an erosional agent, resulting in Karst topographic features such as sinkholes and caverns. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how groundwater storage and flow, along with the depth of the water table, are key considerations affecting the location and maintenance of buildings and infrastructure, including drinking water supplies. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of the ways in which rivers and streams erode, transport and deposit sediment to shape stream valleys and create depositional landforms such as deltas, levees and alluvial fans. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the importance of glaciers in the hydrologic cycle and Earth's climate. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Consider how extended periods of glaciation, including potential Snowball Earth events, have impacted feedback loops related to the biosphere and other components of the geosphere. (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore how Earth's oceans affect climate through heat storage and transfer. (K)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Correlate the locations of the large wind-driven surface ocean currents and thermohaline circulation on Earth. (S, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe the ways in which changes in factors such as ocean salinity, ocean temperature and surface winds influence the processes of ocean convection and thermohaline circulation. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of climate change on the ability of oceans to moderate temperature, absorb carbon dioxide and resist acidification. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Examine the role of governmental and non-governmental organizations in studying the effects of human activities on one or more components of the hydrosphere. (S, STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Examine the processes that lead to the formation of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks and minerals.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose scientific questions about the characteristics and formation of rocks and minerals. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics geologists use to determine whether an Earth material is a mineral. (K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the three primary methods of mineral formation (i.e., precipitation of mineral matter, crystallization of molten rock and deposition resulting from biological processes). (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Observe and classify mineral samples using standard physical properties (e.g., cleavage, fracture, crystal form, hardness, lustre, colour, magnetism and streak). (S, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate among the three main rock groups (i.e., igneous, sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic) by their processes of formation, including the roles of time, heat and pressure. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Outline the basic transitions inherent in the rock cycle, and the forces that disrupt equilibrium to cause these transitions. (K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Classify igneous rocks according to criteria such as method of formation (i.e., intrusive or extrusive) and mineral composition (e.g., felsic or mafic). (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how geologists can infer how an igneous rock was formed by examining its texture (i.e., intrusive or extrusive). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe how the general mechanisms of mechanical and chemical weathering processes, erosion and deposition contribute to the development of sedimentary rocks. (K, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the major features of continental, marine and transitional depositional (sedimentary) environments through structures such as grain size, bedding, ripple marks, mud cracks and fossils in various sedimentary rock formations. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how the agents of metamorphism (i.e., heat, pressure, directional stress and chemically active fluids) influence the formation of metamorphic rocks. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of foliated and non-foliated metamorphic rocks. (K, S)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain why locations where igneous activity and metamorphic rocks occur correlate with plate boundaries and plate movement. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Correlate the location and composition of depositional layers to major events such as volcanic eruptions, glaciation, flooding, mountain building and metamorphism. (K)

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Create, and validate with the help of others, a resource such as a field guide for a specific mineral or rock group. (S, A)

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Research the ways in which society makes use of sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks for various purposes such as art, architecture, industrial materials and energy resources including petroleum, natural gas, potash and uranium. (STSE, S, A)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes and technologies used to locate and extract mineral resources and fossil fuels locally, provincially and globally.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the location, method of extraction, uses and economic impact of major fossil fuel and mineral (e.g., gold, diamond, rare earth elements, copper, zinc, kaolin, coal, potash, uranium, sodium, sulfate and salt) resources locally, provincially and/or globally. (STSE)

indicators.text: Identify the surface and sub-surface geologic features associated with major mineral (e.g., gold, diamond, rare earth elements, copper, zinc, kaolin, potash, uranium, sodium sulfate and salt), building stone, aggregate and fossil fuel resources of Saskatchewan. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Recognize the importance of water for various mining techniques such as solution mining and enhanced oil recovery. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the operation of various surface and sub-surface resource extraction technologies and processes and their associated environmental impcts for mining and resources such as oil sands, shale oil and potash. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Research and investigate solutions to economic and environmental issues (e.g., managing mine tailings and pollutants, reclaiming open pit mining sites, ecological impact of pipelines, resource depletion and maintaining water quality) relatedto the extraction of geological resources in Saskatchewan(STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze surface geography as a product of deposition, weathering, erosion and mass wasting processes

indicators.text: Observe, describe and locate common landforms (e.g., moraines, potholes, drumlins, buttes, coulees, dunes, oxbow lakes and river valleys) of Saskatchewan. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how specific landforms are a consequence of depositional and denudation processes (e.g., weathering, erosion, and mass wasting). (K)

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the importance of chemical weathering to soil quality and formation, atmospheric carbon dioxide and geochemical cycling. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how scientists use stratigraphic columns to infer sea level rise (transgression) and sea level fall (regression) over geologic time. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Speculate on the possible involvement of erosional processes in the development of geographic features found on Mars and other celestial bodies. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: i

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how data gathered by technologies such as Earth orbiting satellites and drones can document changes in land forms and help to identify potential surface geological hazards. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Interpret and/or create a map of geological, civic and/or environmental data using a geographic information system (GIS) to correlate surface geography with human land use.(S, STSE)

units.note: Course-level objectives printed under "General Objectives of Economics 30".

items.text: By studying Economics 30, the student should develop:
an understanding of the nature of Economics.
some ability to use certain Economics process skills.
an understanding and appreciation of the nature of the Canadian economy.
an understanding and appreciation of the nature of the Saskatchewan economy and its interrelationship with the Canadian economy.
an understanding and appreciation of the nature of the inter-national economy and its interrelationship with the Saskatchewan and Canadian economies.
an understanding of the role of the individual as a participant in the Saskatchewan, Canadian and international economies.
To give students an overview of the basic economic concepts of scarcity, choice and the marketplace.
Scarcity; wants; choice; capital goods, consumer goods; market; Gross National Product; producers; consumers; free goods; economic goods; utility and opportunity cost.
To gain an understanding of production, the reasons for specialization in our economy, and the interdependence of people, institutions and regions.
items.section: B. Production, Specialization and Exchange (Unit Two)

items.text: Specialization; interdependence; exchange; factors of production (1and, labor, capital, entrepreneurship); payment for factors (rent, interest, wages, profit); surplus, staple (primary products); barter; private property; and public property.
items.section: B. Production, Specialization and Exchange (Unit Two)

items.text: To assist students to gain an understanding of the organization, the operation and the problems of business institutions. *Units identified in parentheses refer to those in Economics 20.
Types of business organization (sole proprietorship, partnership, co-operative, corporation).
To give the student an understanding of the process of collective bargaining and the role unions play in the economy.
To provide the student with an understanding of the role of the market in the determination of prices and quantities.
items.section: E. The Role of the Market (Unit Five)

items.text: Market; price; supply; demand; consumer price index; and profit.
items.section: E. The Role of the Market (Unit Five)

items.text: To provide students with an understanding and appreciation of the role of money and financial institutions in the Canadian economy.
Banks; inflation and deflation; credit; currency; financial institutions; money; money supply; capital; cash flow; cash reserve; deposits; and savings.
To give students an understanding of the nature of a well-thoughtout savings and investment plan.
Risk; short-term investments; long-term investments; stock exchange; liquidity and capital gain.
To assist students in acquiring an appreciation of the role and importance of international trade in the Canadian economy. To provide an understanding of the nature of barriers to trade.

Foreign trade; comparative advantage; natural advantage; absolute advantage; balance of payments; protectionism; foreign investment; imports and exports--visible and invisible; tarrifs; and foreign exchange.
To give students an understanding of the role of government in the economy.
items.section: I. Role of Government in the Canadian Economy (Unit Nine)

items.text: Government revenue; government expenditures; taxation; income redistribution; government regulation; business cycle; monetary policy; and fiscal policy.
items.section: I. Role of Government in the Canadian Economy (Unit Nine)

items.text: To give students an understanding and appreciation of our own and alternative economic systems.
Capitalism; communism; private (or free) enterprise; socialism; and mixed economy (or mixed enterprise).

outcomes.printedWith: Module 20E: Programmable Logic Controllers (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 20D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices when working with PLCs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the typical components of a PLC with those of a desktop computer.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of PLCs in industrial and manufacturing environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages of using PLCs rather than other technologies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize how the logic of a computer laddering system evolved into the software for PLCs.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Understand how PLCs communicate with themselves and the equipment to which they are connected.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine how timers and counter circuits can be used in PLCs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Troubleshoot timer and counter circuits using the input/output (I/O) racks.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Wire a motor circuit, with safety devices, controlled by a PLC.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Program a PLC.

outcomes.statement: Investigate resistor-capacitor (RC) circuits.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24C: Resistor-Capacitor Circuits (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 23B and 24B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the charging and discharging process of a capacitor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the function of RC circuits, including the role of the time constant.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how to combine resistors and capacitors to control charge and discharge time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct and test RC circuits.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of applications of RC circuits.

outcomes.statement: Analyze electronic circuits that contain negative-positive-negative (NPN) and positive-negative-positive (PNP) transistors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 26B: Transistor Theory B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 24A and 26A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics and applications of transistor amplifier circuits (i.e., common-emitter, common-collector and common-base).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Draw schematic diagrams showing correct biasing (i.e., polarity and voltage level) of an NPN and PNP transistor in a simple
- common-emitter circuit;
- common-collector circuit; and,
- common-base circuit.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Troubleshoot an altered
- common-emitter amplifier circuit;
- common-collector amplifier; and,
- common-base amplifier.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how a small change in base voltage causes a large change in collector voltage in common-emitter and common-collector circuits.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how a small change in emitter voltage causes a large change in collector voltage in a common-base circuit.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the purpose and application of various types (e.g., direct, resistive-capacitive, impedance and transformer) of coupling.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the function of transistors in operational amplifier (op-amp) circuits.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and operation of op-amps.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of applications of op-amps in electronic circuits.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the purpose and operation of junction field effect transistors (JFETs) and insulated gate field effect transistors (IGFETs).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Draw a schematic diagram of a properly biased N-channel and P-channel JFET.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Follow safety precautions when handling and using an IGFET.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the input and output voltage values of inverting and non-inverting op-amp circuits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Construct, test and explain the operation of circuits that use an op-amp such as:
- a voltage comparator;
- a timer; and/or,
- a voltage regulator.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Observe the waveforms and plot response curves for low-pass, high-pass and band-pass active filters in op-amp circuits.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the operating characteristics of integrated circuits (ICs).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 27B: Integrated Circuits B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 27A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List advantages and disadvantages of using ICs rather than conventional circuits.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze conventional circuits to determine how ICs may replace some or all of a conventional circuit.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the common logic families for ICs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret datasheets to determine physical and electrical characteristics, features and applications of specific ICs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between transistor-transistor logic (TTL) and complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) ICs.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the intellectual property issues related to IC products and layout designs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of improved manufacturing processes on IC design.

indicators.text: Provide examples of applications of microcontrollers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the limitations of a microcontroller, including maximum current limits and input and output voltage ranges.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Interpret datasheets to determine characteristics, features and applications of specific microcontrollers and/or microprocessors.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique different microcontrollers for functionality and uses.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the purpose of different types of analog and digital input/output pins that may be found on a microcontroller.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how to program a microcontroller to perform specific functions or tasks.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate how microcontrollers read and interpret data from different types of inputs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate how microcontrollers control various output devices.

indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices when working with PCBs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe different methods (e.g., chemical etching, photo etching, silk screen, CNC and proto-board) of PCB fabrication.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine an appropriate layout design for the chosen method of fabrication according to industry standards (e.g., appropriate use of space on the PCB and minimizing jumper wires).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use appropriate processing procedures (e.g., processing PCB in chemical etchant and drilling holes) to preserve conductive material for the chosen method.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Test the PCB, using a multimeter, for electrical continuity to match design layout.

indicators.text: Troubleshoot defective filters.

indicators.text: Explain how inductive reactance is created in a circuit.

indicators.text: Determine the inductive reactance of a circuit.

indicators.text: Construct and test RL circuits.

indicators.text: Compare impedance in alternating current circuits with resistance in direct current circuits.

indicators.text: Determine the impedance of circuits.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how series and parallel resonance occur in circuits.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the resonant frequency of inductor-capacitor (LC) or RLC circuits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe factors affecting the Q and bandwidth of a resonant circuit.

indicators.text: Determine the bandwidth of resonant circuits.

indicators.text: Draw circuit diagrams and explain the operation of band-pass, band-stop, low-pass and high-pass filters.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80C: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Assess potential workplace hazards and injury prevention strategies related to emergency services.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4B: Workplace Safety – Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Categorize examples of potential hazards that emergency services personnel may encounter.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze statistics related to workplace injuries for emergency services personnel in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the purpose of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the need for, and importance of, proper-fitting PPE and clothing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research employer responsibilities pertaining to PPE (e.g., training employees on the usage, limitations, care, maintenance, proper disposal) in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Examine the state of psychological health and well-being among emergency services personnel in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Psychological Health and Well-being (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the correlation between personal psychological preparedness and the ability to respond effectively in an emergency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research sources of stress (e.g., traumatic events, shift work, separation from family, public disrespect) commonly experienced by emergency services personnel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify mental health challenges such as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), major depressive disorder, general anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder and alcohol use disorder commonly experienced by emergency services personnel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine statistics related to the prevalence of psychological health challenges among emergency services personnel in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the personal feelings, symptoms and behaviours commonly associated with various psychological health challenges.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research statistics related to suicidal ideation, plans and attempts among emergency services personnel in Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of psychological health challenges faced by emergency services personnel on self and others (e.g., family, co-workers, friends).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the purpose of, and steps associated with, the Critical Incident Stress Debriefing process as a traumatic intervention tool commonly used among emergency services workers.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate self-care strategies (e.g., writing in a journal, talking to others such as family and co-workers about feelings and experiences, practising breathing and relaxation techniques, maintaining a healthy diet, getting adequate sleep and exercise) that support mental health and well-being of emergency services personnel.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research ways in which others (e.g., family, co-workers, friends) can support emergency services personnel facing psychological health challenges.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss characteristics (e.g., registered, licensed, evidence-based) of a credible source for psychological support.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify credible Saskatchewan and Canadian sources that offer supports for emergency services personnel experiencing psychological health challenges and for their family members.

outcomes.statement: Examine the storage, maintenance and use of portable fire extinguishers.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Portable Fire Extinguishers (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics, uses and limitations of the three main types of portable fire extinguishers (water, CO2, dry chemical).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the cost and availability of fire extinguishers for various locations (e.g., home, school, work).

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Examine the relationship among the various parts of a fire extinguisher.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the importance of, and steps for, safely storing, inspecting (e.g., monthly, yearly), testing and maintaining a portable fire extinguisher.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the service life of a traditional and disposable fire extinguisher and the factors that might put them out of service.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the process for safely disposing of a fire extinguisher.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the use of the Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep (PASS) method for safely operating a fire extinguisher.

outcomes.statement: Explore firefighting theory.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Firefighting Theory (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the three basic elements of fire known as the fire triangle (i.e., oxygen, heat, fuel).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explain the principle of fire extinguishment through cooling, smothering or starvation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate types of fire extinguishing agents (i.e., water, foam, dry powder, carbon dioxide, wet chemical).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research other ways to extinguish a fire using common objects or materials such as dirt or sand, a blanket or baking soda.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the effectiveness and limitations of each agent in extinguishing all classes of fire.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Demonstrate or explain use of effective methods for applying various extinguishing agents, such as:
- rain on;
- roll on; and,
- bank down.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recommend extinguishing agents for a variety of fire-burning scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Assess the use of personal protective equipment and clothing in firefighting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Personal Protective Equipment and Clothing for Firefighting (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 4B and 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hazards (e.g., excessive heat, smoke, dust, fumes) commonly faced by firefighters.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate types of firefighting PPE and clothing (e.g., gloves, boots, undergarments, helmets, face shields, hearing protection, respiratory protection).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe when, where and how specific pieces of firefighting PPE and clothing are deployed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the evolution and use of PPE technology in firefighting.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine characteristics and features of firefighting PPE and clothing that make them effective.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess challenges (e.g., restricted visibility, weight, heat tolerance, weather) associated with use of a variety of firefighting PPE and clothing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the procedures to donning and doffing of firefighting PPE in a variety of circumstances including darkness.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine the selection of PPE appropriate for a variety of firefighting scenarios.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the impacts (e.g, medical, psychological) of incorrect use of PPE in firefighting.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of pre-incident planning for individuals, families, businesses and the local community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Pre-incident Planning in Firefighting (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the importance of pre-incident planning for individuals, families, businesses, and the local community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe pre-incident planning as it relates to firefighting.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of pre-incident planning for individuals, businesses and the community.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Locate the muster points at the school.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify muster points within the home and community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a pre-incident plan for a building/structure (e.g., home, school) within the community.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate processes for recording, storing and sharing pre-incident plans within the community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the role of a fire safety officer as it relates to pre-incident planning.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the identity and the role of the local fire safety officer.

outcomes.statement: Explore the relationship between fire behaviour and the selection and use of fire suppression techniques.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Fire Behaviour and Suppression (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research deployment techniques used for a variety of extinguishing agents.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between fuel type and the quantity and types of extinguishing agents available.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify factors that impact the speed of fire development, such as the characteristics of fuel involved and ventilation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the information contained within a pre-incident plan that assists firefighters in determining appropriate firefighting attack techniques on the scene of a building/structure fire within the community.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the availability and distribution of water in the community and surrounding area for the purpose of firefighting (e.g., via water hydrants or tanker trucks).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the terms flashover and backdraft.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine methods to prevent and manage flashover and backdraft.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the B-SAHF indicators of fire behaviour (i.e., Building, Smoke and Air track, Heat, Flame) that help firefighters locate a fire and respond appropriately.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify various ventilation techniques that could potentially aid in fire control scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Investigate various fire apparatuses, equipment and tactics commonly deployed by firefighters.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Firefighting Apparatuses, Equipment and Tactics (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe characteristics of, and common uses for, various types of ladders used in firefighting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain circumstances for using a variety of laddering techniques.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the seven basic knots (i.e., overhand safety, clove hitch, half hitch, bowline, figure 8 on a bight, figure 8 follow through, becket-bend, water) commonly used by firefighters.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the firefighting applications for each type of knot.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the proper usage of hand tools (e.g., axes, shovels, fire rakes) for fire-fighting support tasks.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine firefighting uses for items commonly found on a fire truck.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of firefighters’ awareness of the contents and organization of a fire truck.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss factors that help firefighters determine the best way to conduct a forcible entry into a building (e.g., cutting a hole, going through an opening such as a door or window).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research factors for selecting, placing and handling handlines and master stream appliances for applying water to a fire.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the proper procedure for carrying and rolling a fire hose and for connecting fire hose couplings.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Plan the deployment of a fire attack strategy that includes identification of command and suppression functions of all officers and firefighters involved for various given scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Examine fire ground safety practices and procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Fire Ground Safety (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define fire ground safety.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Reflect on ways to work safely as a firefighter, such as:
- wearing a safety vest for greater visibility;
- choosing clothing appropriate for weather conditions; and,
- selecting the proper PPE.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of the buddy system for firefighting.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the meaning of a mayday call in a firefighting situation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate firefighter responses to a mayday call.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe proper techniques for carrying or dragging an injured person to safety.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the importance of fireground awareness, including the initial observation of a firefighting scene, for the safety of self and others.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the role and function of an incident safety officer at a fire incident scene.

outcomes.statement: Examine rural and remote firefighting realities in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Rural and Remote Firefighting (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 15

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between wildland fuels (e.g., vegetation such as grass and trees) and built fuels (e.g., human development such as buildings).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify wildland fuels common to the local area and other regions in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research statistics related to the occurrence of wildland fires in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine factors that contribute to wildland fire development, such as wind, topography and drought.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess firefighting challenges commonly presented by wildland fires and the possible tactics for fighting them.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify factors rural and remote firefighters face in providing service in emergencies, such as distance to call, weather conditions, availability of water and availability of personnel.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine staffing structures and compensation of rural and remote fire departments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore ways in which firefighters interact and communicate with local police and EMS services during scene calls.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the role of the Saskatchewan Public Safety Agency (SPSA) in wildland firefighting.

outcomes.statement: Assess the use of personal protective equipment and clothing in Emergency Medical Services.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Personal and Protective Equipment in Emergency Medical Services (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 4B and 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hazards (e.g., bodily fluids) commonly faced by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine environmental hazards (e.g., extreme cold, rain, snow) and the impacts of these hazards on the effectiveness of EMS personal protective equipment (PPE) and clothing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate types of EMS PPE and clothing (e.g., gloves, gown, medical grade mask, goggles, uniform, boots, hearing pro) utilized by EMS personnel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the different grades of medical masks (e.g., medical, N-95, N-100) and when different grades of masking are required by EMS personnel.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the methods of fitting specialty masks (e.g., N-95, N-100).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe when, where and how specific pieces of EMS PPE equipment are used.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe characteristics and features of EMS PPE and clothing that make them effective and safe.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess problems (e.g., restricted visibility, weight, maneuverability) associated with a variety of EMS PPE and clothing.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate the process of donning and doffing PPE (e.g., gloves, mask, gown) in a variety of circumstances.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine protocols EMS personnel follow if they are exposed to contaminated bodily fluids.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate equipment and methods commonly used by Emergency Medical Services personnel.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 26: Equipment in Emergency Medical Services (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research equipment commonly found in Emergency Medical Services (EMS) vehicles in Saskatchewan (e.g., stretchers, IV pumps, blood pressure kit).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of the equipment used in EMS.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the equipment commonly used by EMS personnel on ambulance (e.g., airway kit, cardiac monitor, pediatric kit).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify equipment commonly used on emergency scenes by EMS personnel in a variety of scenarios (e.g., breathing emergency, traffic collision, severe bleeding).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the evolution of emergency medical services, including the use of ambulance services, in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research equipment used for breathing emergencies (e.g., nebulizer, intubation kit, bag valve mask).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research safe lifting techniques utilized by EMS personnel.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the evolution of emergency medical services, including the use of ambulance and air ambulance services, in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the situational application of the various types of transport equipment (e.g., stretcher, stair chair) used by EMS personnel.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate a basic understanding of human anatomical structure and function.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define and apply key anatomical position and directional terms such as anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, superior, inferior.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the location of the major structures and primary functions of the eleven human body systems (e.g., respiratory, circulatory, digestive, nervous).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the location of the bones in the human skeletal system.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the functions of the skeletal system (e.g., protection, movement, formation of blood cells).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the location of the major muscles of the human body.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the functions of the muscular system (e.g, movement, posture, heat generation).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the segments of the spine (e.g., cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacrum, coccyx) and identify the structure and function of each segment of the spine.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of injury on the different segments of the spine.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research procedure and stabilization methods EMS personnel utilize if a spinal injury is suspected.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Practise spinal immobilization methods to move patients safely.

outcomes.statement: Investigate emergency scene management protocols in emergency medical services.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 5B and 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j

outcomes.statement:
View, listen to, read, comprehend, and respond to a variety of grade-appropriate First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts that address:
- identity (e.g., Define the Individual, Negotiate the Community)
- social responsibility (e.g., Shift Centres, Blur Margins), and
- social action (agency) (e.g., Understand Beliefs, Initiate Action).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore topics and contemporary and traditional visual, oral, multimedia (including digital) and written First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts that present different viewpoints and perspectives including those that reflect the diversity of Canada and its citizens' diverse personal identities, worldviews, and backgrounds (e.g., community, culture, values, spirituality, socio-economic status, language, ability, age, gender, appearance).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze and respond to a variety of First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts representative of various time periods and of the diverse cultures and regions of Canada in order to extend understanding of the ideas, themes, and issues explored in the texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts to identify particular perspectives presented, and the forms and stylistic means used to communicate those perspectives.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze how historical, regional, cultural, political, and social contexts and events influence the presentation and interpretation of ideas, issues, and themes in First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify connections between personal experiences and prior knowledge of language and texts to develop interpretations of a variety of First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Respond personally and critically to perspectives and styles of a variety of First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts and explain how the study of those texts enhances understanding of self, others, and Canadian identity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze ways in which language and texts reflect and influence the values and behaviours of people and diverse communities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the various elements of style used in First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts, and explain how the elements help communicate meaning and enhance the effectiveness of the texts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian texts raise awareness about a variety of regional issues, ideas, cultures, events, and people, and promote social and personal change.

outcomes.statement: View and evaluate critically information and ideas obtained from First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian visual and multimedia texts including an advertisement, news broadcast, poster, and film.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View and respond to grade-appropriate visual and multimedia texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian artists and authors from various cultural communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select deliberately and use effectively a variety of before (page 27), during (page 28), and after (page 29) strategies to construct and confirm meaning when viewing texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use language cues and conventions (page 24) of a variety of informational and literary texts to construct and confirm meaning when viewing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate critical viewing behaviours:
- Determine what the text is representing
- Identify and analyze how the text was constructed
- Identify the purposes, intended audiences, messages, points of view, and techniques of the text
- Infer the assumptions, interests, beliefs, and values embedded in the text, and the credibility and purpose of the author
- Identify and analyze speaker's, artist's, or author's tone, attitude, and bias
- Analyze how the text uses argument, images, placement, editing, and/or music for effect and impact
- Evaluate and critique the persuasive techniques including emotion and propaganda.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate critically information (i.e., whose voice is heard, whose is not) obtained from viewing a visual or multimedia text.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain and evaluate the effectiveness of persuasive strategies and techniques in a range of visual and multimedia texts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Infer point of view and biases explicit in visual and multimedia texts.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze, compare, and critique different visual and multimedia presentations of the same ideas, information, or issues.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess the accuracy and balance of information presented in visual and multimedia texts.

outcomes.statement: Listen to, comprehend, and develop coherent and plausible interpretations of grade-appropriate literary and informational texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian speakers and authors from various communities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to, respond to, and interpret oral texts created by First Nations, Métis, Saskatchewan, and Canadian speakers and authors from various cultural communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select deliberately and use effectively a variety of before (page 27), during (page 28), and after (page 29) strategies to construct and confirm meaning when listening to texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use language cues and conventions (page 24) of a variety of informational and literary texts to construct and confirm meaning when listening.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate critical listening behaviours:
- Concentrate, focus, and attend
- Filter distractions and recognize factors that interfere with effective listening, including personal biases
- Identify the thesis of a speech and determine the essential elements that develop the thesis
- Recognize speaker's values, perspective, biases, and tone
- Analyze explicit and implicit messages/concepts, viewpoints, theme, and tone
- Recognize overall plan or organization including transitional expressions
- Distinguish between emotional appeal and reasoned argument
- Evaluate and verify facts and arguments
- Identify logical fallacies in oral arguments
- Identify key allusions and symbols
- Use effective note making strategies and a variety of written or graphic forms to organize and share ideas acquired from what was listened to
- Prepare and ask relevant questions, and respond appropriately
- Analyze the overall effectiveness of the presentation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline and summarize an oral presentation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate proficiency in reflective, critical, empathetic, and appreciative listening.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare and contrast interpretations of oral texts with the interpretations of others and research points of contention.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide appropriate feedback in a variety of situations including discussions and informative, persuasive, and artistic presentations.
