outcomes.printedWith: Module 17B: Occupational Health and Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the general duties of self-employed persons as outlined in the Saskatchewan Employment Act.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the benefits to employers and employees of the Saskatchewan Workers Compensation Act and the Meredith Principles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., protecting the health and safety of employees, creating a positive work environment and the costs [e.g., to the injured worker and to the business] associated with a workplace injury or incident) for having a safety plan within a business.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Role-play situations where employees, supervisors and managers effectively deal with health and safety concerns within the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities as they pertain to health and safety in the workplace in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Explore entrepreneurship as a career pathway.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Entrepreneurship as a Career Pathway (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Critique common misconceptions about entrepreneurs, such as:
- Entrepreneurs can be successful only if they have access to lots of money.
- Entrepreneurs set their own hours and vacation schedules.
- Entrepreneurs work alone.
- Entrepreneurs take huge risks to be successful.
- Entrepreneurs are wealthy.
- All it takes is one good idea to be a successful entrepreneur.
- Every entrepreneur needs a post-secondary business degree to be successful.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research typical earnings for entrepreneurs in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., media showcasing successful entrepreneurs and increased attention to social entrepreneurship) why entrepreneurship is becoming more widely accepted as a viable career pathway.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Debate the idea that being an entrepreneur is better than working for someone else.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on personal interest in, and suitability for, entrepreneurship as a career pathway of choice.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Construct a personal plan or a plan for another individual aspiring to be an entrepreneur, considering factors such as
- a supportive network of allies;
- membership in, and support from, professional organizations and associations; and,
- education, training and learning opportunities.

outcomes.statement: Construct a detailed business plan for a proposed start-up.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19B: Planning a Start-up B (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between a business model canvas and a business plan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., obtaining financing and planning a start-up or expansion) for preparing a written business plan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze prepared business plans to identify and describe common components (e.g., executive summary, company description, market analysis, financial projections, operational plan, succession plan and conclusion) of a business plan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine characteristics (e.g., written in plain, easy-to-understand language; research-based; well-defined market; and, realistic) of an effective and well-written business plan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop a written business plan for a proposed start-up.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Present the business plan to potential investors or supporters.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on feedback received from potential investors or supporters.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Make required adjustments to the business plan.

outcomes.statement: Execute, conclude, evaluate the success of, and report on, the start-up.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20B: Executing and Concluding a Start-up B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 40-60 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the need for revisiting, updating and revising a business plan throughout the life of a business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Launch and operate the start-up.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Reflect regularly on business progress and success by answering questions such as:
- What has worked well thus far?
- Are sales goals being met?
- Do we have enough supplies to meet production demands?
- What needs adjustment and why?
- How can productivity be improved?
- What has been accomplished in the business to date?
- Where is the business at financially? Is there a cash-flow problem?
- What have I personally contributed? How else can I contribute?
- What have I learned about business and what it takes to successfully operate a business?
- What have I learned about myself?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain what a pivot is and why a pivot strategy is important for business success.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Adjust business operations and the business plan as required throughout the life of the business.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Maintain detailed records (e.g., financial and inventory) throughout the life of the business.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Prepare a final written report (e.g., shareholders’ report) that summarizes operations and success.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present the final written report to others such as supporters and investors.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on business and personal successes and challenges resulting from the operation of the start-up.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Complete an income tax return for self or for various scenarios.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the role of an income tax specialist (e.g., an accountant) in helping individuals and businesses make sound financial decisions to minimize taxes.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the viability of one’s chosen career to support one’s desired future lifestyle.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17B: Lifestyle and Career B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 17A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the earning potential of one’s chosen career to the costs associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss ways (e.g., increase income and reduce expenses) to align the earning potential of one’s chosen career with the costs associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Suggest opportunities (e.g., side businesses, e-commerce, buy-and-sells, odd jobs, raises, promotions and bonuses) for earning additional income to support one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Suggest ways to reduce expenses associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate advantages and disadvantages (e.g., flexibility of hours, worker benefits and sick days) associated with one’s chosen career.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how one’s career path may involve multiple occupations or job loss (e.g., due to natural disaster, economic downturns, layoffs or medical issues) that require resilience and adaptability to overcome.

outcomes.statement: Investigate leaves from work in Saskatchewan and their potential impact on finances.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Leaves from Work (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the availability of, and compensation associated with, several leaves (e.g., sick, disability, maternity, parental and leave of absence) in a variety of work settings in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages associated with each type of leave.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how one applies for a variety of leaves.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of each type of leave on one’s finances.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose a plan for maintaining financial security in the event of a leave or extended absence from work.

outcomes.statement: Assess the value of retirement planning as part of a personal financial plan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Retirement Planning (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6B and 15C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate different types of pension plans (e.g., Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Old Age Security (OAS) program, Saskatchewan Pension Plan (SPP), group and private).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the risks and rewards associated with various types of pension plans.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research approaches for investing in pension funds commonly used at different life stages (i.e., adolescence, early adulthood, middle adulthood and later adulthood).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain processes for contributing to a variety of pension plans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the features of “defined contribution,” “defined benefit” and “target benefit” pension plans.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and verify CPP and other pension deductions and contributions on a variety of pay stubs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) in contributing to one’s retirement income.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) in retirement planning.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how various perspectives (e.g., cultural, religious and community) affect one’s retirement planning.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the future of pension plans and the resulting impact on retirement planning given factors such as people living longer, increasing health costs and the sustainability of pension plans such as CPP.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Compare potential earnings on retirement funds when one starts saving for retirement at varying ages (e.g., 20, 30, 45 and 50).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Debate the question, ‘Should I be debt free when I retire?’

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Design a spending plan that includes planned retirement savings or investments.

outcomes.statement: Explore options for funding post-secondary education and training.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Funding Post-secondary Education and Training (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify common options (e.g., savings, loans, apprenticeships, co-operative education programs and working while taking more time to complete a program) for funding post-secondary education and training.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the role of scholarships and bursaries in funding post-secondary education and training.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the role of student financial assistance programs, including student loans and grants, in funding post-secondary education and training.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the income tax benefits associated with post-secondary student loans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore features of the student loans and grants program specifically for Indigenous students and others (e.g., students with disabilities; students with dependents; mature learners; and students who are, or have been, Crown wards).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the availability and the function of federal government programs related to Registered Education Savings Plans (RESPs), as well as the Canada Education Savings Grant and the Canada Learning Bond, in funding post-secondary education and training.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research eligibility criteria, the application process and the financial benefits of participating in the Graduate Retention Program in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore strategies and debt management tools for repaying student loans upon graduation from post-secondary education and training, including programs such as the Repayment Assistant Plan (RAP).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Calculate the costs associated with a variety of post-secondary pathways.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research funding options and design a financial plan for a post-secondary pathway of interest or for a fictitious scenario for the first five years beyond high school.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the history of credit.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22C: History of Credit (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 22A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the origins of credit including the use of credit during ancient times, the middle ages, fur-trading days and present day.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the historical, cultural and contemporary significance of credit contracts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the history of interest rates and their inter-relationship with world events.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of historical events (e.g., colonization, signing of treaties, the Great Depression, civil and world wars and recessions) on credit.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how past economic events such as the Debt Crisis of the 1980s, the Dotcom Crash of 2000-02 and the Housing Bubble and Credit Crisis of 2007-08 can have a lasting effect on economic conditions.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the process of negotiating and obtaining a mortgage.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Mortgage (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 22D and 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain what a mortgage is and its main purpose.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between mortgage and non-mortgage debt.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify terms in a mortgage contract such as the APR, prepayment penalty, appraisal fee, closing costs, prepayment privileges and portability.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine consumer and lender rights and responsibilities related to mortgages.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how gross debt service ratio (GDSR) impacts one’s ability to obtain a mortgage.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the role of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) in helping Canadians purchase a home.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of mortgage default insurance and determine current CMHC requirements for it.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the availability of and requirements for mortgage default insurance offered by other Canadian companies such as Genworth Financial or Canada Guaranty.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of mortgage life insurance which a mortgagor may also consider purchasing.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research various ways of obtaining a mortgage (e.g., through a bank, credit union or mortgage broker).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare interest rates associated with different types of mortgages available through various lenders.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Research the circumstances under which paying a mortgage prepayment penalty may be advisable.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Research how to obtain mortgage financing by using the equity in one’s home (e.g., 2nd mortgage, Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC)) or the Registered Retirement Savings Plan Home Buyers’ Plan.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Debate the advantages and disadvantages of consolidating other debt such as money for renovations or new furniture, or closing/appraisal fees, into a mortgage loan.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to plan for unforeseen events such as rising interest rates, job loss, death of a partner or economic recession that may affect one’s ability to make mortgage payments.

outcomes.statement: Examine the processes of and alternatives to personal bankruptcy in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 26B: Handling Debt Problems B (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 26A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the advantages and disadvantages of alternatives to filing for personal bankruptcy (e.g., consolidation loans, credit counselling, debt repayment program and consumer proposal) in Saskatchewan, including the impact on one’s credit report.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the factors that may lead one to file for personal bankruptcy.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Discuss the:
- benefits (e.g., eliminating creditor phone calls and eliminating the fear of repossession or foreclosure) of bankruptcy;
- disadvantages of bankruptcy, including the existence of a permanent, public record; and,
- effects of declaring bankruptcy on self and others, including family.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the costs associated with, and the steps for, filing for personal bankruptcy in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine assets that are seized and assets that are protected in a bankruptcy proceeding in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Distinguish between debts that will be eliminated and debts that will remain after declaring bankruptcy in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss myths often associated with bankruptcy (e.g., you will lose everything, bankruptcy will ruin your financial future and you can claim bankruptcy on student loans).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes for buying and leasing a vehicle.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 28B: Vehicles - Leasing vs. Buying (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 28A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the costs ofowning and operating a vehicle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of buying versus leasing a vehicle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate the costs of buying versus leasing using lease calculation and owner’s calculation formulas.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine an individual’s ability to afford a vehicle using strategies or guidelines such as the 20-10 rule and total loan cost.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the consequences of relying primarily on the monthly payment amount to determine affordability of a vehicle loan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore finance options for vehicle loans and leasing vehicles from a variety of providers (e.g., car dealership and bank).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the advantage and disadvantages of buying or leasing a new andused vehicle.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate where and how (e.g., through dealerships, privately and online) vehicles might be purchased.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a down payment in financing a vehicle purchase or lease.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the process of trading in a vehicle to purchase another.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research how vehicles depreciate and ways to help a vehicle hold value.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Define the concept of negative equity and discuss situations (e.g., accident and length of ownership) that may result in negative equity on a vehicle loan.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore the consequences of trading in a vehicle with negative equity to purchase another, and doing so too frequently.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Research and compare insurance and warranty options for vehicles.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Discuss the repercussions of financing a vehicle on access to credit for future purchases.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Apply decision-making strategies or approaches to a variety of scenarios that include the option to purchase or lease a new or used vehicle.

outcomes.statement: Assess factors involved in renting a home.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 28C: Housing - Renting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 28A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of renting and renting-to-own a home.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List the types of home rental properties available within one’s or another community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss factors that may influence one’s selection of a specific rental property.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the suitability of various rental properties to meet the needs represented by several scenarios.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the components of a typical rental agreement in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the rights and responsibilities of landlords and tenants in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a plan for accommodation for the first five years beyond high school.

outcomes.statement: Assess factors involved in purchasing a home.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 28D: Housing - Purchasing a Home (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 28A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List the types of homes (e.g., condominium and house) available for purchase within one’s or another community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Calculate the true costs including expenses such as mortgage payments, utilities, property taxes, condominium fees, insurance and ongoing maintenance associated with owning a home.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define the concept of being “house poor.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss factors one should consider prior to purchasing a home.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a checklist of items a buyer may use to evaluate a prospective home for purchase.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ways (e.g., privately, through a real estate professional and through a real estate service such as ComFree) a home can be purchased in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate programs such as the Home Buyers’ Plan for purchasing a home.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify mortgage lenders locally or within Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Pose questions to ask when shopping for a mortgage.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Debate the issue of obtaining a mortgage for the maximum pre-approval amount.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify closing costs typically paid by the buyer and the seller in a real estate transaction.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Propose the steps a potential buyer could use to manage the home buying process for various scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Compare various investment vehicles.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 29E: Investment Vehicles (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 29D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between an investment vehicle and an investment type.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics and benefits of investment vehicles such as a Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP), Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP), Tax Free Savings Account (TFSA) and Registered Education Savings Plan (RESP).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine an appropriate investment vehicle for various scenarios.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the tax implications of using various investment vehicles.

outcomes.statement: Research ethical and socially responsible investment opportunities.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 29F: Ethical and Socially Responsible Investing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 29D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the concepts of ethical and socially responsible investing and compare the advantages and disadvantages of each.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss factors that influence an individual’s investment goals and decisions as they pertain to ethical and socially responsible investing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on personal goals and priorities for ethical and socially responsible investing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify local, provincial, national and international investment opportunities that align, and also those that do not align, with one’s personal goals and priorities for ethical and socially responsible investing.

outcomes.statement: Construct an investment portfolio that includes short-, medium- and long-term investment goals.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 29G: Investment Portfolio (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 5 and 29A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Determine the investor profile for oneself or for an individual in a given scenario using an investor profile assessment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the risk tolerance for oneself or for an individual in a given scenario.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe investment goals for oneself or for an individual in a given scenario.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the features of various investment types (e.g., stocks, bonds and mutual funds).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the reasons for diversifying an investment portfolio to support short-, medium- and long-term goals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between risk/return and diversification of investments.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research and compare features of different types of investment strategies and styles such as the Couch Potato, market timing, dollar-cost averaging, leverage investing, short selling, index investing, Value/Growth and Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRIP).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of developing and managing one’s own investment portfolio compared to working with a financial advisor.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify and evaluate services that assist individuals with investing.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the risk and relationship between inflation and rate of return.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research the concept of “buying low and selling high.”

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assess the financial implications (e.g., capital gains) of acquiring and disposing of capital assets.

outcomes.statement: Examine the processes for purchasing insurance policies and for filing insurance claims.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 30B: Insurance - Application of Insurance Policies (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 30A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the processesforpurchasinga variety of insurance policies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss when filing an insurance claim may be necessary.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the steps for filing various insurance claims.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles and responsibilities of various stakeholders (e.g., insurance broker, actuary, agent, adjuster and investigator) involved in the administration of an insurance policy.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore potential legal consequences related to insurance fraud.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design scenarios for which insurance claims could be filed.

outcomes.statement: Collaborate to plan and implement a fundraising project in one’s community or school.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 31C: Charitable Fundraising Project (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 31B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess various registered charities,non-profit organizations or worthy causes to select a beneficiary for the fundraising project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate ideas for the project and determine the best option.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop a project plan that includes components such as goals, timeline, target audience, budget, a list of responsibilities, communication or marketing plan, and process for making the donation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Implement the plan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on the personal and community impact of the completed project.

outcomes.statement: Explore economic factors that impact personal or community financial decisions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 32: Micro-Economics (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe life events or circumstances (e.g., job loss, living common law, single parenting and becoming a parent) that may influence one’s personal financial goals and decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the impact that different economic systems including traditional, market, command and mixed economies may have on personal finances.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify stages of the economic life cycle and how they may affect personal financial decisions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify economic trends in sectors (e.g., manufacturing, agriculture, natural resources, energy and banking) that drive the Saskatchewan and Canadian economies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain and simulate economic principles including supply and demand, scarcity, incentives, elasticity, opportunity cost, diminishing marginal utility and diminishing marginal productivity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify Saskatchewan and Canadian policies that may impact personal or community financial decisions.

outcomes.statement: Examine the impact of investing on the local, provincial and national economies.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 33: Macro-Economics (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research investments that have the potential to stimulate economic growth.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the potential effects of limited investment in an economy.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and explore the relationship between unemployment, inflation, and Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as key indicators to a country’s economic performance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between investment spending, money supply, and economic growth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the role and responsibilities of the Bank of Canada in regulating interest rates in Canada.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research and assess the impact of each stage of the economic life cycle on Saskatchewan and Canadian markets.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between economic factors such as interest rates and economic conditions (e.g., recession, depression and bull market) and investment relative to a country’s economic growth.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the local, provincial, national and international economic consequences of historical events such as The Great Depression, 2008 debt crisis, signing of the treaties in Canada, colonization of Canada, andcivil and world wars.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the generational impact on the handling of finances resulting from historical events.

outcomes.statement: Investigate foreign exchange.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 35: Foreign Exchange (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the factors that determine the value of the Canadian Dollar relative to foreign currencies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the current exchange rate of the Canadian Dollar relative to a variety of foreign currencies such as the British Pound, Euro, United States Dollar, Chinese Yuan Renminbi, Mexican Peso and Indian Rupee.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the equivalent value in a variety of foreign currencies for a given number of Canadian Dollars using an online currency converter.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the equivalent value in Canadian Dollars for a given value in a variety of foreign currencies using an online currency converter.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine processes for and costs associated with sending money internationally.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how money can be earned from currency trading and discuss the associated risks and rewards.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Participate in a work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 81B: Work Study Placement (Optional) · Suggested Time: 25-50 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 80A, B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply relevant skills and abilities during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Document knowledge and awareness of labourstandards, safety, workplace ethics, rights and responsibilities, occupational health and safety, and networking observed during the work placement.

outcomes.statement: Relate one’s work placement experience to personal and career goals.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 82B: Work Study Follow-up (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 81A, B

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Reflect on the attainment of personal and learning goals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Update personal career documentation (e.g., resume, portfolio) following the work placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In appreciation prepare a letter, note, card or other communication for the work placement employer.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and/or revise personal and career goals based on the work placement experience.

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of safe food handling, preparation and storage.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of personal hygiene and using personal protective equipment (e.g., gloves) for food safety.

indicators.text: Discuss causes of food borne illnesses.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine safe food temperature zones for various foods (e.g., poultry, egg dishes, pork, beef).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the two types of contamination (i.e., direct and indirect/cross contamination).

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k
l

Research and compare the three categories of contamination:
- biological (e.g., bacteria or viruses);
- physical (e.g., objects that enter any stage of food preparation); and,
- chemical (e.g., cleaning products and naturally occurring).

indicators.label: n

indicators.label: o

outcomes.printedWith: Module 52: Food Policy (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 50

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify information (e.g., food guides, school nutrition guidelines, advisory councils) used to develop regional and/or national food policies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore perspectives and land-use policies that influence the growing, gathering, hunting and harvesting of food, including numbered Treaties and Métis hunting and fishing rights (e.g., Morin and Daigneault decision).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the roles and responsibilities of Canadian government agencies and food companies in food labelling (e.g., regulations, nutrition facts, health claims, terminology, ingredients, calories, allergies, preservatives).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how food promotion and marketing strategies are influenced by legislation, regulations and policies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Predict how current and future trends in food and nutrition could impact legislation, regulations and policies.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine opportunities and challenges faced by First Nations and Métis people in Canada in relation to Treaty and land-use rights and selfgovernance of food policy.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Inquire into local regulations and guidelines for home-based food businesses such as catering, food trucks, meal delivery, food kits and food market vendors.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the importance of food policies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research school or division food policies.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate what supports are available for Saskatchewan schools to create, update and implement food policies.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the use of policy and its effect on food security/insecurity locally, provincially and nationally.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Participate in a work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 81B: Work Study Placement (Optional) · Suggested Time: 25-50 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 80B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply relevant skills and abilities during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Document knowledge and awareness of employment standards, safety, workplace ethics, rights and responsibilities, occupational health and safety, and networking observed during the work placement.

outcomes.statement: Relate one’s work placement experience to personal and career goals.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 82B: Work Study Follow-up (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 81B

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Reflect on the attainment of personal and learning goals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Update personal career documentation (e.g., resume, portfolio) following the work placement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare a letter, note, card or other communication for the work placement employer, expressing appreciation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and/or revise personal and career goals based on the work placement experience.

outcomes.statement: Examine general safety requirements within the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2B: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify standard safety equipment and processes used within the different areas of forestry (e.g., harvesting, production and reforestation).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between provincial and federal health and safety rules and guidelines as applied within forestry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify potential hazards and necessary precautions within the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Examine occupational health and safety requirements in Saskatchewan’s forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3B: Occupational Health and Safety in Forestry (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify health and safety legislation and requirements common to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of environmental health and safety training for those working within the forestry industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or avoid damage to materials and equipment through safe work environments in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss appropriate actions that should be taken if an injury or accident occurs, such as whom to contact and first-aid procedures.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify prevention strategies for forest sector injuries in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Classify appropriate safety equipment for jobs found within forestry.

outcomes.statement: Investigate forest fire management.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Forest Fire Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify language used within forest fire management (e.g., fire status, contained, values protection, monitored and cultural values of the landscape).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a controlled burn in forest fire management (e.g., impact on plant diseases and prevention of wildfires).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the impact forest fires have on wildlife.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify agencies that collaborate and share resources to assist with forest fire management in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate different forest fire management strategies and factors used to prioritize fires (e.g., location of fire, communities, infrastructure, timber and industry).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the six levels used to rank forest fires and how they impact response strategies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research how First Nations and Métis communities have used natural fire management in the past and present day.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the knowledge of Elders and Knowledge Keepers on natural forest fire management used in First Nations and Métis communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on forest fire management techniques (e.g., controlled burn, natural forest fire management) and how these techniques may differ based on worldviews (e.g., First Nations and Métis).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze how public perception or media portrayal of forest fire management has changed over time (e.g., Smoky the Bear campaign).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the existence of old and very old forests in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the impact of fire prevention in provincial and national parks.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss how fire history maps from 1945 to the present in Saskatchewan and Canada help inform forest fire management today.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of silviculture within the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Silviculture (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11, 12, 13

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define silviculture and describe how it differs from forestry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Summarize different natural and artificial silviculture techniques.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise growing techniques including bare-root, container seedlings or broadcasting seeds.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment to determine what factors (e.g., soil pH, moisture, sunlight and carbon dioxide) impact growing conditions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research silviculture practices such as natural regeneration, fire, thinning and rotation ages, by different companies in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify reasons for reforestation and afforestation practices used in Saskatchewan (e.g., shelterbelts, wildlife habitat protection, decreasing erosion and increasing biodiversity).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain ecological requirements (e.g., soil and moisture) and management implications (e.g., growth rates, yield, wildlife impact, height and diameter) for a chosen tree species (e.g., spruce, aspen and pine).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how emulating natural disturbances (e.g., wind, fire, insects and disease) is accomplished in silviculture.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how harvesting practices have changed over the years (e.g., move from geometric shapes of clear cuts, leaving intact islands or retention structures to maintain diversity, clear cut to maintain even aged and pure stands) because of silviculture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how the Indigenous worldview (i.e., humans are keepers of the land and all living creatures are connected) relates to current silviculture practices.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of ecosystem-based management on forestry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Ecosystem-based Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize factors (e.g., human impact, fire, insects, disease and climate change) considered in ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the benefits of using ecosystem-based management on forests, the Earth, communities, businesses and economies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research how ecosystem-based management is used within the forestry industry (e.g., woodland caribou habitat connectivity to forestry).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how ecosystem-based management contributes to sustainable development and biodiversity protection.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how ecosystem-based management is used within provincial and national parks in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of heavy equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Heavy Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify heavy equipment (e.g., buncher, skidder, bulldozer, scraper and rolling equipment) used in various areas of the forestry industry (e.g., harvesting, reforestation, milling and pulping operations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements for heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of routine inspections and maintenance of heavy equipment in the safety of employees and life of the equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the historical evolution of heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of heavy equipment on the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research innovations in heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry on a heavy equipment operator in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of light equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Light Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between light and heavy equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the types and application of light forestry equipment (e.g., axes, hatchets, winches and water pumps).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate light equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements (e.g., safety boots, eye and ear protection) of various light forestry equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate storage, transportation and shipping regulations for forestry light equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of maintenance and routine inspections of light equipment in the safety of employees and life of equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how light equipment is used in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore how mapping and remote sensing are used for forest protection and sustainability.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Mapping and Remote Sensing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how different types of maps (e.g., base, topographic or contour, soil type, geologic, forest stand or type and road) benefit the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between mapping and remote sensing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of using current remote sensing techniques (e.g., GPS, aerial laser 3D mapping and real-time satellite imaging) in forest exploration.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how mapping is part of the planning process in sustainably harvesting forest products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the benefits of Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping and how it can provide information to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe how mapping can support the evaluation of forest structure and age.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate how mapping can be beneficial in fire management and prevention.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how forest mapping can show the relationship between common biogeochemical cycles (i.e., carbon, water, phosphorus and nitrogen).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the three main ways remote sensing and mapping can be applied to the forestry industry (i.e., reconnaissance mapping, commercial forestry and environmental monitoring).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes and applications of measuring a forest.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Measuring a Forest (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the conducting of a forest survey, the type of information gathered and the purpose for collecting data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between forest samples and forest populations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the goals and techniques for conducting a forestry survey.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss what technology and equipment are used to measure a forest and conduct a forestry survey.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collect boreal forest measurements (e.g., diameter, circumference and height of trees and distribution of species) accurately and reliably.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply appropriate safety procedures and use of equipment when taking forest measurements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select appropriate and efficient ways to organize data collection (e.g., chart, table and technology) for analysis.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze collected data to determine the condition and distribution of tree or wildlife species in the forest.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how forest ecosystems and climate are linked.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Climate Change (Optional) · Suggested Time: 9-11 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how climate and weather influence Saskatchewan forests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history of forests and how glaciation and climate have shaped them to what they are today.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discover how the increase in human population and resources directly impact forests.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how a forest can be a carbon source or a carbon sink and how that can affect climate change.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how forests store carbon and are an important part of the carbon cycle to balance greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the earth maintaining a carbon balance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) and its significance in providing information on climate change.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact forestry has on the Saskatchewan economy.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Forestry Economy (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify forestry industry products (e.g., pulp and construction material) that are manufactured in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define gross domestic product (GDP) as it relates to the forestry industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the contribution of forestry on the GDP over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the role of marketing in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the marketing of forest products over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research how technology has impacted marketing, products and production practices within the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how different worldviews influence marketing, production and profit sharing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how First Nations forestry partnerships share profits within their communities.

outcomes.statement: Complete a project to compare the portrayal of the forestry industry in society with information obtained from a trip to a company, community or organization.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Forestry Excursion (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan an excursion with a company, First Nations community, tribal agency or government organization that is connected to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the portrayal of a topic within the forestry industry that will be compared during the excursion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collect information about a topic within forestry (e.g., treaty education, reforestation, harvesting, wildlife, mapping, remote sensing, forest fires and conservation) as it applies to the location, community, company or government organization visited or studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare how the forestry industry was portrayed with the in-person information gathered.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on a personal experience in an area within forestry studies (e.g., treaty education, land-based education, harvesting, reforestation, climate change and sustainability).

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of financial decision making including analysis of:
- renting, leasing, and buying
- credit
- compound interest
- investment portfolios.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of simple interest and compound interest.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations that involve compound interest.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Graph and compare the total interest paid or earned over different compounding periods for the same annual interest rate, principal, and time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the total interest to be paid on a loan given the principal, interest rate, and number of compounding periods for the loan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the total cost of a loan under a variety of conditions (e.g., different amortization periods, interest rates, compounding periods, and terms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve contextual problems that involve compound interest.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, using technology, different credit options that involve compound interest, including bank and store credit cards and special promotions, and provide justifications for the credit option.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and describe examples of assets that appreciate or depreciate relevant to one's self, family, and community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare renting, leasing, and buying of large cost items and generate reasons for considering each choice.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Solve situational questions related to the costs of renting, leasing, and buying (including questions that require formula manipulation).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Solve, using technology, situational questions that involve cost-and-benefit analysis.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of two or more investment portfolios, and make recommendations for selection based upon this analysis.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the total value of an investment when there are regular contributions to the principal.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Graph and compare the total value of an investment with and without regular contributions.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Apply the Rule of 72 to solve investment problems and explain the limitations of the rule.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Investigate and report possible investment strategies that could be used to achieve a financial goal.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of long-term and short-term investment options.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Investigate and compare small investments over a long term and larger investments over a shorter term.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of inductive and deductive reasoning including:
- analysis of conditional statements
- analysis of puzzles and games involving numerical and logical reasoning
- making and justifying decisions
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, verify, explain, and apply strategies to solve a puzzle or win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- simplify the original problem
- work backwards to develop alternative approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and correct errors in a solution to a puzzle or in a strategy to win a game.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation on a puzzle or game and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze an "if-then" statement, make a conclusion, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e

units.note: Course-level objectives printed under "OBJECTIVES OF GEOGRAPHICAL STUDIES".

items.text: The intent of this course in geography is to.acquaint and explain to the student the basic distributions of physical and cultural phenomena over the earth's surface. Through analysis of these distributions, and some of the societal processes, an understanding of the environment, society and economy of the different regions of the world should be achieved. Further, the study of geography should lead to an appreciation of the fact that the world is one, that no region exists in isolation, that, today, all parts of the world are interdependent. To ensure the attainment of the above, the geography program should foster in the students the development of the following understandings, skills and attitudes:

items.label: a
items.text: There is no split between "physical geography" and "regional geography". Geography is a chorologicai science (i.e. deals with distribution) which needs and uses the facts of many sciences to arrive at an understanding of differences between regions.

items.label: b
items.text: Geography is unified by its method and viewpoint and not by its subject matter. Much of its subject matter may be contained in other disciplines -- in history, in physics, in geology, in economics, etc. -- but its viewpoint is distinctive; it is the regional viewpoint.

items.label: c
items.text: The regional viewpoint infers the recognition of differences and of similarities between areas across the earth's surface. Regions are distinguished on the basis of definite criteria, both physical and cultural.

items.label: d
items.text: Classification of phenomena (physical or cultural) into categories of greater or lesser degree of generalization should lead to the understanding of real variation in their occurrence and hence to an appreciation of regional distribution.

items.label: e
items.text: In recognizing relationships occurring between different classes of phenomena, e.g. areas of dense population coinciding with great natural resources, one must be careful to differentiate between cause and effect relationships and those relationships which are accidental.

items.label: f
items.text: The major device for demonstrating regional differences and distributions is the map. In addition the geographer uses a variety of descriptive devices including statistical diagrams of many kinds.

items.label: a
items.text: To read with comprehension in the field of geography.

items.label: b
items.text: To analyze, interpret and evaluate data provided in many forms (statistical, map, or other).

items.label: c
items.text: To discover geographical relationships and to recognize regional differences.

items.label: d
items.text: To present, orally and in writing, in organized fashion, the results of geographical research.

items.label: e
items.text: To use, and construct where possible, the various tools of geography including globes, maps, charts, and graphs.

items.label: f
items.text: To make case studies, 1ocal or other, and thus develop understanding of relationships between environment and human activities.

items.label: g
items.text: To undertake geographical studies, including elementary field work, of the local area to achieve first-hand understanding of the fundamental approach of the geographer.

items.label: a
items.text: Recognition that the.state of knowledge is not finite, that new methods of research and new concepts are continually evolving, that understanding of the world in which we live is very incomplete.

items.label: b
items.text: Willingness to undertake research with an open mind and to arrive at generalizations based on unbiased appraisal.

items.label: c
items.text: Willingness to recognize that cultural differences across the world are the result of geographical, historical and societal factors rather than a result of "racia1" dissimilarities.

items.label: d
items.text: A willingness to recognize that regions of similar physical environment may be occupied by very dissimilar economics and societies and that these dissimilarities are a result of numerous factors including stage of cultural and technical development, together with differences in the objectives of the peoples concerned.

items.label: e
items.text: A willingness to understand that no region exists in isolation, that all parts of the world are inter-related and interdependent.

notes: This guide predates foundational/learning objectives. Course-level objectives are given type "foundational" and the unit "Understandings"/"Objectives" type "learning"; printedHeading keeps the heading as printed. "Content", "Suggested organization of content", "Suggested activities", references and resources are not extracted.
Numbered or lettered entries are separate items ("label" keeps the number or letter); unnumbered text is one item per paragraph.

The six units of this 1969 tentative course outline print only a numbered topic outline (topics and sub-topics, with teacher and student references); there are no "Understandings to be developed" or unit objectives, so the units have no items. The outline is on PDF pages 10-18.

outcomes.statement: Justify the importance of proper sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3C: Sanitation, Disinfection and Sterilization (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the terms sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the three levels of infection control (i.e., sanitation, disinfection and sterilization).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe contamination and decontamination.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate the purpose and application of antiseptic versus a disinfectant.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify given scenarios as sanitizing, disinfecting, or sterilizing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Classify single-use implements versus multi-use tools.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the different levels of disinfection (i.e., high, intermediate and low level) and describe situations when each level is appropriate.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare different techniques for sanitizing, disinfecting and sterilizing instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate techniques for sanitizing and disinfecting instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate different processes for disinfecting, sanitizing and sterilizing non-porous items (e.g., glass, metal, electric files, linen).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between a chemosterilant and a high level disinfectant.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare labels on chemicals for proper use and disposal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique sanitation practices when performing a service (e.g., manicures, pedicure, facial, makeup application, cut and style).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: i

indicators.label: j
