outcomes.statement: Improvise in a jazz style on an instrument showing understanding of applicable jazz theory.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: To deepen understanding of jazz style, analyze musical events within a solo or composition (e.g., shout chorus, form, dynamics, pitches, changes, articulation).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Play and/or transcribe recorded music of recognized performers through methods such as:
- play blues heads and simple and more complex jazz tunes by ear
- sing roots of the chord progression of the solo
- call and response with the teacher (or other students)
- sing and/or play along with solo
- sing the solo being studied without listening to the recording at the same time
- notate the solo including elements such as form, chord changes, pitches, rhythms articulations, and dynamics
- start with short sections, such as a few bars or a single lick, and gradually increase the length and complexity of the selection.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create simple, short three or four note jazz licks and develop these licks by methods such as:
- transposing
- transforming
- adding single notes
- decorating
- connecting licks with segments of scales.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate improvement and growth in the presentation and construction of improvised solos in a performance setting.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ideas, new concepts, and a variety of styles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Demonstrate through writing, describing, and/or playing, the understanding of jazz theory including:
- II-V-I and I-VI-II-V chord progressions
- turnarounds
- modes of major and minor scales
- blues form
- rhythm changes
- 32-bar song form (AABA).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Improvise to show a personal, clear understanding of the function of guide tones within a musical form or chord progression.

outcomes.statement: Infuse, independently, the understanding of jazz theory into personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse, and perform music in a jazz style in solo, small group, or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Integrate the understanding of the different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement, and tone that help create a jazz style, and apply this knowledge while music making.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize and define musical forms emphasizing rhythm changes in music that is listened to and/or performed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, implement, and evaluate a personal plan to improve the individual performance process and to enhance knowledge and understanding of jazz (e.g., as part of the process of improvement, include recording and listening back to the performances, practices, and/or rehearsals).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Integrate knowledge of conventions regarding jazz articulation, and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Integrate into performance knowledge of standard notation conventions such as note durations up to 16th notes, codas, D.S.s, and dynamic markings.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize and describe the standards of notation in jazz music that are different from traditional "classical" notation (e.g., falls, doits, turns, and hats, as well as notation conventions such as how off-beat quarter notes should be written).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Show proficient use of jazz vocabulary to relate jazz theory to personal musical practice, learning, and performance (see Jazz Glossary).

outcomes.statement: Show growth in individual instrumental techniques and knowledge of the elements of music and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate and record technical development and develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate technical inquiry questions and take action on the findings of the inquiry (e.g., "What can I do to get better?" or "How could I change this performance, paper, or arrangement?").

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Play with a tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Having internalized the key concepts of playing expressively, demonstrate this knowledge through playing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Play a full range chromatic scale.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Play major, dorian, mixolydian, and blues scales in all 12 keys, two octaves when possible.*

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Play both whole tone scales and all three diminished scales.*

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Sight-read music at one level below the general level of the music being performed by the ensemble.
*For students playing drum set, teachers may substitute other technique directly related to set playing, although the drummers should know the scales on mallets and perform the set techniques in addition to the mallet technique.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond as a jazz performer when playing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, and time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., their tone, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond to the ensemble's response to the student's responding to them (e.g., when the lead player starts to play out or articulate a certain way, does the band follow and does the lead player recognize it?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including his/her gestures, cues, tempo, expressions, and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room, and adjust playing accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, to their presence (or not), body language, expressions, and their reaction to the music (e.g. applause, cheering, being asked to play quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form, and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music (written or not written) by reading the music and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo and group jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy, and/or change the personal emotional state of the performer to synchronize it with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know, predict, and/or anticipate what is next or might be next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music

outcomes.statement: Listen to jazz as a jazz performer when not personally playing the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and independently analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key, and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the development of the jazz music (head, arrangement, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on the structure of the chord progression and the potential development of the chord progression.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and and other elements of well-known players and/or groups.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify performers and/or groups on recordings just by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one instrument from the beginning to the end of the musical selection (e.g., Did the player play the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she play that the student also might be able to play?)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on the melody, bass line, fills (including drums and percussion) background lines, chord progression, roots, and sing along with the recording.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage, and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Independently analyze jazz music in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually identify, experiment with, and purposefully use strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common chord progressions including but not limited to blues, rhythm changes, AABA, II-V-I, I-VI-II-V, in music performed and/or listened to (including progressions that break from the norm).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the time signature on first hearing a piece of music, including odd metre times such as 7/8, 7/4, 11/8, and simpler time signatures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Clap on 2 and 4 on first hearing a piece of music in an appropriate time signature.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Internalize and demonstrate the pattern of strong and weak beats that are identified with the time signatures.

outcomes.statement: Listen to performances of jazz music and individually develop and apply criteria to use in critical evaluation of one's own and other's work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers, (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? What do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble do not?).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and implement a plan for improvement (personal and group) based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Upon first hearing a musical selection, describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g. style, period, composer, culture, performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Broaden knowledge of the skill and components of listening actively, continue to develop listening skills, and recognize that listening contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era, and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate knowledge of, and personal implementation of, the skills, techniques and attitudes necessary for successful ensemble performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Know the functions of all the sections within the student's ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the instrument that the student plays in the ensemble (e.g., comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo chairs in the horns, and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Individually attend to melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy, and articulation in the preparation and performance of jazz.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Play in tune with good balance and tone and know the intonation tendencies of the student's instrument.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership as a performer by offering help, ideas, and guidance to other performers during rehearsal/practice.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate a `professional' attitude towards conduct, focus, and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials, and presentation of products.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critically examine and assess the student's own individual work and personal contributions to group projects/performances.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Be accepting of appropriate critiques from others and work towards implementing the solutions to that critique.¿

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know the value of individual practice, know how to practice, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student's personal practice skills, and implement a plan to improve.

outcomes.statement: Aurally distinguish the different eras, genres, styles, and feels of jazz by listening to and/or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually listen to recordings of jazz, develop a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods, and place, and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: On first hearing, categorize jazz music into styles, genres, periods, and/or place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore aspects of jazz such as history, performers, styles, and eras through a variety of media with a focus on Canadian or Saskatchewan jazz artists.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate awareness of jazz music by suggesting listening and/or performing opportunities for the ensemble.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Experience through listening and/or playing "free jazz" (jazz music which is free from restraints such as key, form, metre, and changes).

outcomes.statement: Explore jazz music and its performers and educators and their influence in the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine roles that jazz artists might have beyond being performers and identify individuals who fit those particular roles (e.g., Oscar Peterson/teacher, Wynton Marsalis/educator and Louis Armstrong/ambassador).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: A number of jazz artists have First Nations or American Indian heritage. Discuss possible reasons why this is not widely known (e.g., older performers Mildred Bailey and Dave Brubeck spoke to this, younger players such as Sharel Cassity and Julia Keefe have a different outlook).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify influential players of the student's instrument, investigate why these performers are so influential, listen to their music, and give special attention to performers from Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the First Nations/American Indian heritage of jazz performers such as Oscar Pettiford, Art Farmer, and Jim Pepper and the effect of this heritage on their music and lives.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of jazz on contemporary First Nations music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Research career avenues in jazz and music in general.
See online resources for lists of performers.

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence of jazz on current popular music styles with an emphasis on the music of Canada and Saskatchewan as possible.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of jazz in `pop', `rock', and other current music (e.g., the use of jazz themes and rhythms in hip-hop, rap, funk), and the influence of these current styles on jazz.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify or explore the statement that the jazz music of past eras lives on, not only in recordings but also in "ghost bands", and with new, younger artists playing in the style of the greats of the past.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how Canadian and international copyright laws affect the lives of those who work in the jazz field.

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 3 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Research roles and responsibilities of interior designers and interior decorators.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Exploring Interior Design and Interior Decorating (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between interior design and interior decorating.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the qualifications of interior designers and interior decorators.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of the types of problems that interior designers solve and those that interior decorators solve.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the roles of interior designers and interior decorators, how they differ from each other and how they differ from the role of architects and other related professions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the client-focused nature of interior design and interior decorating.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how interior designers and interior decorators work together and with clients.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how interior designers and interior decorators influence how clients think, feel and act in spaces.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Discuss the need for interior designers and interior decorators to recognize and apply safe and fair work practices, including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying (e.g., professional code of ethics).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss risk mitigation and how it can prevent injuries at work.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify potential workplace health and safety hazards (e.g., excessive computer use, improper ergonomics for workspace) and methods to mitigate risk.

outcomes.statement: Examine the elements of design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Elements of Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between the elements and principles of design.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Describe various effects that can be achieved by manipulating line.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the effect of form and how it can be used efficiently in interior design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how space can be manipulated to create specific feelings.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare how visual and tactile textures can be applied to design and decorating.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the role of lighting such as ambient, task, accent and natural, in design and decorating.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how colour can be used to impact people’s moods, feelings and behaviours.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate how colour systems (e.g., colour wheel) show relationships between colours.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Differentiate among the basic attributes of colour (e.g., hue, value, intensity).

indicators.label: k
l
indicators.text: Examine how different types of patterns (e.g., naturalistic, organic, geometric, abstract, metamorphic) can be used in design and decorating.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Predict how changing one or more elements of design can impact other elements in a specific space.

outcomes.statement: Examine how interior designers and decorators incorporate principles of design to create appealing and functional spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Principles of Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how interior designers and decorators apply the elements of design using the principles of design.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Provide examples of formal (e.g., symmetrical), informal (e.g., asymmetrical) and radial forms of balance in a room or accessory.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between proportion and scale.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research how different proportion systems (e.g., golden mean, Le Corbusier’s Modulor) can guide design.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of the effective use of scale in different types of spaces.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how different types (e.g., alternation, progression, repetition, transition) of rhythm can be used effectively in design.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe how emphasis creates focal points in a space.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how to achieve harmony through a balance of unity and variety.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop and apply criteria to evaluate specific designs based on the principles of design.

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence of culture in interior design and decorating.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Cultural Influences (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how design is human-centered (e.g., focus on people, functional, aesthetic).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how cultural and global influences impact interior design and decorating.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Recognize influences of First Nations, Métis and Inuit cultures on interior design and decorating choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of the influences of various cultures globally on interior design and decorating choices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between cultural appropriation and cultural appreciation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain ethical cultural appreciation (e.g., buying from ethical sources, buying from the maker, avoiding misuse of sacred symbols) in interior design and decorating.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how to celebrate cultural influences in interior design and decorating.

outcomes.statement: Analyze design processes common to interior design and decorating.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Design Processes (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of creativity in design processes.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Outline the major stages (e.g., inspiration, ideation, implementation) of design thinking as they might apply to interior design or decorating.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a visual, such as a flowchart or concept map, illustrating how the design process is non-linear and iterative.

outcomes.statement: Develop client profiles based on their needs, wants and preferences.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Client Profiles (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between needs, wants and preferences.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the type of information (e.g., family, lifestyle, style preferences, storage requirements, budget, sensory considerations) interior designers or interior decorators should seek from the client to develop a client profile.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how an individual’s physical (e.g., safety, shelter) and psychological (e.g., love, privacy, belonging, success) needs can influence their design and decorating decisions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how the client’s budget helps to prioritize their needs and wants.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Conduct research on client’s needs, wants and preferences related to specific interior design and decorating projects.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a visual representation of physical and physiological needs and wants from a client perspective.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare how client profiles might differ for new house builds, co-housing, renovations or commercial projects.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop client profiles for real or imagined clients and real or imagined interior design and/or decorating projects.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how an individuals’ housing needs and wants change over a lifetime.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore considerations (e.g., aging, health changes, sensory) for accessibility when remaining in the same home.

outcomes.statement: Explore tools and techniques used to present interior design and decorating ideas.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Design Presentation (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of using various visual formats to present design ideas to clients.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the range of drawing equipment (e.g., pen and paper, digital) interior designers and interior decorators use to create and communicate their ideas and plans.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate common architectural drawing conventions such as scale, line weights, dimension lines, section views, elevations and plan views.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of architectural symbols and conventions commonly used in floorplans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify common abbreviations, alphabets of lines and symbols commonly used in blueprints.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the role of sketching to develop initial interior design and decorating ideas.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how to use digital rendering tools to construct technical drawings.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Read, interpret and construct technical drawings.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create presentation models for client review.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the role of concept boards, material boards and style boards in presenting different aspects of interior design and decorating projects to clients.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify components commonly included on various (e.g., concept, material, style) presentation boards.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Communicate intended concepts for design or decorating projects using written, verbal and visual presentation techniques.

outcomes.statement: Examine how interior designers and decorators incorporate inclusive design approaches to meet client needs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Inclusive Design Approaches (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among accessible design (e.g., wide door openings, roll under countertops), adaptable design (e.g., upgradable, expandable, dividable) and universal design (e.g., open floor plan, lever handles) approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate socially inclusive designs that support clients living with various physical, cognitive and intellectual conditions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of accessibility (e.g., visual impairment, hearing impairment, limited mobility, cognitive and intellectual conditions) designers and decorators should consider when creating safe, aesthetically pleasing spaces and meeting clients’ needs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore potential challenges related to accessibility when designing and decorating residential and commercial spaces.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how individuals’ accessibility needs may change over time.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the need for adaptable housing to meet occupants’ changing accessibility needs through different stages of life.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the impact accessible design, adaptable design and universal design have on physical and psychological health and well-being.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of how principles of universal design ensure current and future accessibility for residents in different types of spaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate options and benefits for retrofitting a defined residential or commercial space to meet various accessibility needs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the drawbacks and benefits of adaptable housing models such as flexible housing, multigenerational housing, accessory and secondary suites.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the role of legislation (e.g., National Building Code of Canada, Accessible Canada Act, The Uniform Building and Accessibility Standards Act) and standards (e.g., CSA B651-12 Accessible Design for the Built Environment) regarding accessibility.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Apply one or more design approaches to plan a residential or commercial space that fosters inclusivity and access for all (e.g., gender identity and expression, ability, age, culture).

outcomes.statement: Examine the process of space planning for interior design projects.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Space Planning (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the goals of space planning for interior design projects.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of typical public (e.g., entry, living room, dining room, meeting room), private (e.g., bedrooms, bathrooms) and work (e.g., kitchen, laundry, office) zones in residential and/or commercial spaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of how public, private and work zones are arranged in relation to each other in residential and/or commercial spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the need to consider safety when planning and designing spaces, considering things such as stairs, rails and balconies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of how public and private zones are connected (e.g., stairs, halls, archways) in residential and/or commercial spaces.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Create bubble diagrams to analyze the zones and the relationships between zones for a client’s space.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Construct concept boards to present potential space plan ideas to clients.

outcomes.statement: Examine the principles of sustainable design for interior design and decorating.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Sustainable Design (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the primary goals of sustainable interior design.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Research the role of rating systems such as Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED®) in promoting sustainable design for residential and commercial projects.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the role of the WELL Building Standard™ in promoting features for buildings, interior spaces and communities that support human health and wellness.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Discuss how renovating existing spaces can contribute to environmental sustainability.

outcomes.statement: Examine the characteristics of various types of housing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Housing Types (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of common detached house types (e.g., bungalow, bi-level, two-storey, split level and 1 ½ storey).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate different types of houses found locally, regionally, nationally and globally.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how zoning bylaws affect choices of housing types.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the advantages and disadvantages of different configurations (e.g., apartments, row houses, mobile homes, single family detached dwellings, duplexes, homes on wheels, tiny homes, co-housing) of living units.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how the layout of different types of housing influence interior design and decorating options.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design a floor plan for a specific house type.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop assessment criteria in consultation with peers and instructor to assess floor plan of a specific type of space.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss own and peer’s floorplan to provide feedback on the strengths and areas of improvement.

outcomes.statement: Examine the characteristics and evolution of housing styles.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Housing Styles (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how housing has evolved to meet human needs using available materials.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how the evolution of housing styles is related to geographical influences as well as historical and economic events during the time in which the housing was constructed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare traditional Indigenous housing styles common to North America with those brought by immigrants from various cultures (e.g., English, Spanish, Scandinavian, German, Dutch, French).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how traditional Indigenous housing has influenced current housing styles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of classic traditional (e.g., Georgian, Federal, Greek Revival, Southern Colonial, Victorian), modern (e.g., Prairie Style, Arts and Crafts, Tudor, Spanish Revival, International) and postmodern (e.g., contemporary, ranch, split-level, solar, earth-sheltered) housing styles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of various housing styles found locally, regionally, nationally and globally.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how the exterior style of houses can influence interior design and decorating decisions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine how the elements and principles of design apply to the exterior appearanceof a building.

outcomes.statement: Explore how residential and commercial building codes apply to interior design applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Building Codes (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of standardized regulations (e.g., zoning bylaws, building codes) in providing requirements that ensure the safety, health and well-being of occupants, builders and the community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the responsibilities an interior designer has regarding awareness of government regulations such as building and fire codes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify current national and provincial legislation, such as the National Building Code of Canada, National Fire Code of Canada, National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings, Accessible Canada Act, The Fire Safety Act, The Uniform Building and Accessibility Standards Act and municipal building bylaws, that regulate residential and commercial construction.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of the bylaws and regulations that might apply in specific contexts, such as an office, kitchen, single family home, hotel room, classroom or restaurant.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Assess the construction and purpose of building components in residential or commercial spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Building Components (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the function of each of the major building components (e.g., floors, walls, windows, doors, stairs, roofs) found in residential and commercial spaces.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the different building components collectively define interior spaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the types of questions interior designers may have with respect to each major building component (e.g., Is the wall load bearing? Can a stairwell be moved or reconfigured? Is there plumbing or wiring in the wall?).

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Create a visual representation (e.g., drawing, model, digital rendering) of building components that can be used in a variety of residential and commercial spaces.

outcomes.statement: Examine the characteristics of residential and commercial building materials.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Building Materials (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the history of building materials from various eras.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss factors (e.g., strength, durability, performance, aesthetic appearance, maintenance) that influence the choice of building materials.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of how wood, glass, steel and concrete are used in residential and commercial buildings.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the characteristics and environmental impact of a variety of materials (e.g., wood, glass, steel, concrete) used in design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of building materials such as earth, recycled wood or plastic composite lumber, straw bales, insulating concrete forms and recycled steel.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prepare a cost estimate of materials used to construct or renovate a defined residential or commercial space.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a materials board to present potential material choices for a residential or commercial project to clients.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the life cycle of building products and materials.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how to use technical sheets, safety data sheets and pictograms from the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) to obtain information about product safety.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine short- and long-term health concerns related to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) released from building materials and household products.

outcomes.statement: Examine the characteristics of energy efficient buildings.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Energy Efficient Buildings (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the history of energy efficient buildings and building technologies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of constructing and retrofitting buildings to improve energy efficiency.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of energy efficient housing models such as self-sufficient, earth-sheltered, active and passive solar and net-zero.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Outline factors to consider when assessing a building for energy efficiency.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Describe the operation and benefits of active and passive energy management systems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research available financial incentives to retrofit residential spaces to improve energy efficiency.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create, using drawing skills, computer-aided design programs or model- making, an innovative energy efficient space considering factors such as passive or active energy sources, windows, appliances and sustainable construction materials.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop assessment criteria in consultation with peers and instructor to assess an innovative energy efficient space.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss own and peers’ energy efficient designs to provide feedback on the strengths and areas for improvement.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Review current codes (e.g., National Energy Code) and their impact on design.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how social and environmental conditions and new technologies influence housing design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Housing Designs of the Future (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research how social conditions have influenced housing design over the ages.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Predict how changes in social conditions may affect future housing design (e.g., socially inclusive housing).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how current and historical environmental conditions (e.g., areas prone to floods, areas prone to fires) can influence future housing design.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Predict how new technologies and construction materials may impact future housing design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the potential of 3-D printing to meet future housing demands.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a futuristic invention or innovative technology and describe or demonstrate how it would be used in the home.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how design principles apply to outdoor spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Designing Outdoor Spaces (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore how interior designers might collaborate with landscape designers or landscape architects to design outdoor spaces.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify factors that influence choices of natural and manufactured landscape elements for outdoor spaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of landscaping suitable for public, private and work zones in outdoor living spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the use of natural elements in exterior spaces in both commercial and residential design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how to use a balance of soft scape and hard scape elements in landscaping residential or commercial properties.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how designers can apply principles of sustainability to outdoor spaces.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore three-season and four-season room designs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate weather sustainable materials used to furnish outdoor spaces.

outcomes.statement: Explore commercial interior design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Commercial Interior Design (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of common types (e.g., office, hospitality, healthcare, retail and education) of commercial interior design projects.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain ways in which commercial interior design differs from residential interior design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify historical and contemporary trends in commercial interior design.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the complexity of designing interiors for healthcare facilities, referencing issues such as life safety systems, patient focus, emerging technologies, waiting rooms, nursing stations and family and visitor areas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of corporate style and branding in office, hospitality and retail interior design projects.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare how interior design differs among types of retail spaces such as malls, boutique shops and big-box stores.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify major issues to consider when designing educational facilities.

outcomes.statement: Explore the characteristics of interior materials, treatments and finishes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Materials, Treatments and Finishes (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how interior decorators use materials, treatments and finishes to personalize spaces.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine a variety of design trends (e.g., shabby chic, farmhouse, industrial) represented in decorating and design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of how seasonal trends are implemented in residential and commercial spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze factors (e.g., client tastes, life cycle, flammability, infection control, decorative theme, energy conservation, maintenance, budget) to consider when decorating residential or commercial spaces.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify common styles of wall, ceiling and floor treatments for decorating residential and commercial interiors.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of common types of wall treatments (e.g., paint, wallcoverings, cladding).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the characteristics and potential environmental impacts of common soft (e.g., carpet, resilient flooring) and hard (e.g., wood, tile, concrete) flooring materials.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the characteristics, including energy efficiency, of common window treatments (e.g., blinds, shutters, curtains, drapes, shades).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Estimate the quantity, cost of materials or finishes and labour to decorate a particular area in a commercial or residential space.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Construct a style board of potential materials, treatments and finishes to present to clients.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research various levels of legislation and programs (e.g., LEED® Indoor Environmental Quality credits, LEED® Canada-CI for commercial interiors) that encourage the responsible use of materials and finishes.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify potential health, safety and welfare considerations (e.g., allergic reactions, sickness, fire hazard), when decorating residential or commercial spaces that can result from the inappropriate selection of interior materials, particularly flammable and combustible materials and those that emit toxins and toxic fumes.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain how to use technical sheets, safety data sheets and pictograms from the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) to obtain information about product safety.

outcomes.statement: Analyze furniture options for decorating residential and commercial spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Furniture (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how decorators select and place furniture to help shape and define space.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common types of furniture (e.g., chairs, sofas, tables, desks, beds, workstations, indoor/outdoor) to consider for residential and/or commercial settings.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between the standards of construction, quality and features of residential furniture and those of commercial furniture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine factors to consider (e.g., location, durability, source of materials, style, cost, colour, comfort) when selecting residential or commercial furniture.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research options to acquire new, used or custom-made furniture locally, regionally, nationally and globally.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Contrast processes for purchasing residential and commercial furniture.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the history, construction, design and function of various types of furniture from select time periods (e.g., ancient civilizations, Middle Ages, Renaissance, Neo-classical, Modern).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of various furniture styles (e.g., early American, Queen Anne or Shaker) and influences (e.g., Greek, Renaissance or Baroque).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how ergonomics informs furniture planning decisions to optimize human well-being.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of various floor plans and furniture configurations on traffic flow and focal points.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the purpose and function of law in societies.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the influence of societal worldviews on the organization of historical and contemporary legal systems (e.g., Indigenous legal systems, Sharia law, Mosaic law, Hammurabi’s law code, Law of the Prairie).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Debate whether the primary function of law is to create order or provide freedoms for members of its society.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Predict the consequences of a society without laws.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why the rule of law is a fundamental principle in democratic societies and relate it to examples in Canadian society.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify examples of ways in which law is a part of everyday life in Canada.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the difference between equality and equity as they relate to the concepts of justice and the application of laws.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Examine how the historical roots of law in Canada stem from Indigenous legal systems, British common law and the Civil Code of Québec (1991).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare the purposes and functions of law and the justice system in Canadian society today with traditional Indigenous approaches to law and justice (e.g., restorative vs. punitive justice).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Debate criteria for just laws and systems of justice and apply to scenarios and case studies.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine safeguards (e.g., impartial and independent judiciary, jury of one’s peers, right to counsel, presumption of innocence, courts of equity, right to appeal) in law that should protect Canadians from abuse of power by the state and ensure fairness.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine the role of judges in the Canadian judicial system.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how and why laws change over time.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how diverse worldviews can influence the creation of, or change, a law.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Summarize the process of how new laws are created in Canada at the local, provincial and federal levels.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the law-making roles and powers typically associated with the executive, legislative and judicial branches of provincial and/or federal governments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how the idea of cooperative federalism works in relation to legislation, regulation, funding and administration.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the diversity of First Nations, Métis and Inuit traditional restorative practices (e.g., talking circle, humour and shaming for minor offences, banishment for serious offences and value restoration over punishment).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the evolving legal relationship between First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples and non-Indigenous Canadians, including treaty relationships and truth and reconciliation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine promises made in treaties and legal cases related to treaty land entitlement claims in Canada.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how differing cultural understandings of treaties between the Crown and First Nations peoples lead to ongoing negotiation and dialogue to resolve outstanding issues.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain various provisions in Canadian law (e.g., Articles 2, 23, 29, 33 in the Charter) that may be used to accommodate the diverse interests and needs of individuals and groups.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the motivation and impact of individuals or organizations who have influenced the evolution of law in Canada.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Predict possible changes to Canadian laws regarding emerging issues and support these predictions.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Create a plan that includes strategies to affect changes to current laws in Canada at the local, provincial and federal levels.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore the origins of Saskatchewan's Language Act and examine the impact of this legislation on the work of the provincial legislature.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the historical context for the inclusion of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (Charter) (1982) in the Constitution Act (Constitution) (1982).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate how the Charter attempts to seek balance between the rights of the individual versus those of society and apply to specific scenarios and case studies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the structure and content of the Charter, including its jurisdiction, its enforcement, how it can be amended and the difference between Charter rights and Charter freedoms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the limits of the Charter's jurisdiction as it only applies to the relationship between the state and the citizens.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why the “reasonable limits clause” and the “notwithstanding clause” exist and justify situations when they can be applied.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Justify how the Constitution and the Charter's protect existing rights, inherent Indigenous rights and minority language educational rights.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Assess scenarios and case studies that illustrate how courts interpret laws in light of the Charter to shape and inform current laws.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how groups or individuals (e.g., Indigenous people, treaty rights holder, gender and/or sexually diverse, minority languages) struggle to have their rights recognized and protected.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the steps one might take if they believe their Charter rights have been violated.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the elements and processes of Canadian criminal law.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between elements of criminal law and civil law such as purpose, role of the courts, procedures, outcomes, enforcement of sanctions, onus and burden of proof.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss what constitutes a crime according to the Criminal Code of Canada (1985).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the types of offences (e.g., indictable, summary and hybrid) in the Criminal Code of Canada (1985) and identify in a variety of cases.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Outline the different types of court jurisdictions in Canada and describe the anticipated progress of a criminal procedure through the Canadian courts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the roles and responsibilities of institutions (e.g., police, courts, judiciary, correctional system, legal and paralegal professionals, victim services, community-based justice organizations) within the criminal justice system.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the different levels of policing (e.g., municipal, RCMP, Indigenous police services, conservation officers and highway patrol officers, sheriff department) available in Saskatchewan communities and justify the roles, responsibilities and limitations of powers.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the mens rea vs. actus reus in a variety of case law.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the various defences (e.g., threshold test, air of reality test and reasonable doubt) available to defend against criminal charges and evaluate the applicability of a defence given a particular case.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify factors to ensure the judicial process is fair to the accused (e.g., presumption of innocence, right to jury, trial of peers).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the purpose and use of processes available in the Canadian justice system, including presentence reports, victim impact statements and restorative practices.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Model the process (e.g., investigation, arrest, voir dire, trial, sentencing, appeals) of a criminal procedure.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Differentiate between federal penitentiaries and provincial correctional facilities, including various levels of security within, length of sentence and programs available (e.g., substance abuse intervention, sex offender treatment, literacy development, work experience, treatment courts).

outcomes.statement: Critique the impact and effectiveness of the Canadian justice system.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore possible root causes of crime (e.g., addictions, violence, abuse, trauma, poverty, gangs).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess how shifting worldviews have contributed to changes in understanding of right and wrong and the effects on legal systems/criminal justice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how certain actions are criminalized or decriminalized using a variety of cultural perspectives.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the various goals (e.g., rehabilitation, reparation, sense of responsibility, acknowledgement of harm done, deterrence) of sentencing and justify appropriateness in given situations.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss alternatives (e.g., parole, probation) to incarceration available to convicted offenders in relation to rehabilitation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the various sentences (e.g., discharges, suspended sentences, conditional sentence orders, incarceration, electronic monitoring, community service hours) possible within the Canadian justice system and evaluate the appropriateness of a sentence given a particular case.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how rehabilitation, reparation, sense of responsibility and acknowledgement of harm done to victims and communities are reflected in the goals of restorative justice.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Debate if imprisonment is an effective way to change long term human behavior

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine factors that contribute to the over-representation of Indigenous people in the justice system.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the purpose, process, limitations and importance of Gladue factors on the determination of a sentence.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Justify the appropriate use and effectiveness of plea bargaining in the criminal justice system.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine the effectiveness of various correctional models (e.g., custody, maximum-security, minimum-security) and programs (e.g., substance abuse intervention, sex offender treatment, literacy development, work experience, treatment courts).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Analyze the purpose, impact and validity of crime statistics.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the Jordan decision (2016) as a measure to improve the effectiveness of the Canadian justice system.

outcomes.statement: Analyze interactions between participants in the Canadian justice system and the community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the impact of crime on the community (e.g., victims and their families, offender after serving sentence, family of the offender, workplaces).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique how the Canadian justice system responds to people in challenging circumstances (e.g., poverty, mental health issues, language and cultural barriers, victims of trauma).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine systemic barriers (e.g., racial profiling, court wait times, cost and availability of legal resources) in the Canadian criminal justice system.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare public perception versus patterns and statistics regarding sentencing and corrections.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore supports available for offenders integrating back to the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine ways to assess levels of recidivism and impact of integrating back high risk offenders in the community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyse government responses in light of wrongful imprisonment and other miscarriages of justice and justify appropriateness of response in given situations.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of the interrelationship between law enforcement agencies and communities.

outcomes.statement: Examine the elements and processes of dispute resolution in Canadian civil law.

indicators.text: Analyze intentional and unintentional tort cases while considering the possible defences.

indicators.text: Describe the remedies (e.g., punitive damages, special damages, general damages, injunctions) available under tort law and identify methods of enforcing civil judgments.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80B: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act,2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for injury prevention to ensure safety in the automotive workplace.

indicators.label: a

indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury or material and equipment damage as a result of unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Inspect and utilize protective devices on equipment.

indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE), such as safety goggles, hearing protection, gloves and footwear, and appropriate PPE cleaning procedures.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify potential health concerns when PPE is not used properly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the correct fire extinguisher for different classifications (i.e., A, B, C, D and K) of fires and how to use the extinguisher correctly (i.e., PASS - Pull Aim Squeeze Sweep).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the importance of a clean workplace and methods used to maintain a clean workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Locate, identify and explain the correct use of safety equipment (e.g., eye wash station and first aid station) in the workplace.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify, label, store and handle hazardous materials according to Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices, including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.text: uses social interaction skills to enhance group learning tasks;

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: uses various strategies to resume and sustain conversation;

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: asks follow-up questions to check for understanding;

indicators.label: s
indicators.text: obtains feedback on tasks;

indicators.label: t
indicators.text: monitors own anxiety about learning tasks, and takes measures to lower it if necessary;

indicators.label: u
indicators.text: provides personal motivation for learning by rewarding self when successful;

indicators.label: v
indicators.text: uses a buddy system in learning Michif; and,

indicators.label: w
indicators.text: seeks help from Elders in Michif language and cultural learning.

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with accuracy (accuracy is primarily the grammatical system of a language).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: creates a variety of basic sentences using accurate grammar;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: uses complex sentences and phrases but not without error;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses idioms, and basic and specialized vocabulary from course content, to communicate ideas;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: uses understanding of the varying sound systems of different dialects to understand them better; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: reads factual texts or concrete information from a cultural study or prose that is relatively straight forward.

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with proficiency (proficiency involves the ease with which communication is expressed or received).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: produces several sentences of spoken, coherent discourse, with relative detail and precision, in spontaneous situations;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: produces a variety of lengthy texts on topics, providing details to support the main point;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: communicates thoughts, ideas, and feelings for specific purposes and audiences through a variety of verbal and visual media;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: listens to and reiterates what another speaker has said, though the listener may need passage repeated or explained; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: sustains conversations for up to 15 minutes.

outcomes.statement: communicate meaningfully with coherency (coherency relates to the connectedness of information, thoughts and ideas within communication)

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: uses complex and compound sentences to hold ideas in discourse together;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: uses linking devices throughout the discourse, though not with complete agreement;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses sentences and questions that contain learned vocabulary and familiar language structures in different forms;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: adjusts language to suit audience and purpose;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: uses the appropriate level of formality with people in a variety of contexts; and,

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: uses a wide range of interaction patterns to deal with routine and non-routine transactions and interactions.

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow them to get and give information.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: exchanges information and opinions about moral dilemmas and issues affecting them personally;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: listens actively to others, in discussions and group work, and solicits and offers ideas;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: attempts to reformulate the ideas of others in discussions and group work to enable consensus;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: seeks, in discussions and group work, the input of those who are experienced in the area of discussion;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: exchanges ideas and thoughts on topics of personal interest; and,

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: asks and answers questions using complete sentences.

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow them to socialize and celebrate.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: appreciates the spontaneous humour in social situations;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: carries on a simple conversation with another speaker, and uses appropriate register;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: uses appropriate register at community events, such as introducing a speaker;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: uses language of avoidance; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: demonstrates and explains an understanding of special symbols and objects used during celebrations and ceremonies, including their meaning and foundation in traditional narratives.

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow them to interpret discourse

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: engages in previewing or hearing activities that orient students to the discourse, such as providing background knowledge, recalling what is already known;

indicators.label: b

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow them to research.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: consults with community Elders, and identifies a research need or purpose to gather information on the Michif culture;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: formulates research questions;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: identifies possible sources of information, including people, written texts and media texts;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: practices and approaches cultural resource people with appropriate protocol for collecting information;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: gathers and records information;

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: processes and adapts information;

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: scans for relevant information;

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: evaluates information critically;

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: organizes information in ways to fit the need or purpose of task;

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: prepares a report or presentation (written, visual, using technology);

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: follows protocol for acknowledging sources; and,

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: explores effective forms for recording and presenting or using research findings, such as incorporating technology, visual presentation, a magazine article, or written report.

outcomes.statement: perform language functions that allow them to produce discourse.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: gives reasons and information to support a point of view on an issue, such as the position taken on learning languages, the position taken on political Involvement;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: gives advice; e.g., write a letter of advice to themselves, to a younger brother, to a cousin; and,

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: retells a traditional moral narrative orally with a focus on developing the main character; e.g., his/her strengths and weaknesses, his/her dilemma, the problem, the resolution, the lesson.

outcomes.statement: assess personal strengths and needs as a Michif speaker and contributions made to the community of learners.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: identifies with guidance what proficient Michif speakers do;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: reflects on what they learned;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: reflects on what they would like to learn more about;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: reflects on what they might do on their own to learn more as a result of previous learnings; and,

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: reflects on who they might approach to learn more about the Michif language.

outcomes.statement: assess personal strengths and needs within the development of their own language skill, and set goals for future improvement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: reflects on and identifies through the Michif world-view and language;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: recognizes speaking, listening and viewing as useful tools to clarify thinking, communicating and learning;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: evaluates the quality of own contributions to group process and sets goals and plans for further development; and,

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: develops and uses criteria for evaluating self, goals, and projects.

outcomes.statement: assess personal strengths and needs within the development of their own language learning as they relate to self, family and community and set goals for future improvement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: assesses own and others' work for clarity, accuracy, and impact;

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: monitors personal communication goals;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: reflects on attainment of personal goals for effective language learning and use;

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: reviews, refines, through reflection, feedback and self-assessment;

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: determines personal inquiry and researches strengths and language goals;

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: reflects on new knowledge of Michif and its value to self and the wider community;

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: determines personal inquiry and learning goals; and,

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: reflects on, analyzes, and assesses strategies used while learning Michif.
