Interpret direct and inverse square law relationships, as illustrated by Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation.
Determine the gravitational force on an object at various distances, expressed in multiples of Earth radii, from the centre of the Earth.
Explain how the gravitational mass of an object within a known gravitational field can be derived.

units.name: Optional Unit VI: Fluid Mechanics
factorsEmphasized: D8 limitations of science and technology
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: Perform a variety of activities involving fluid mechanics.
Explain a variety of common phenomena by applying the principles of fluid mechanics.
Solve problems related to fluid mechanics.
Appreciate that an understanding of the basic principles of physics can be useful in understanding common and practical life experiences.

Strengthen their knowledge and understanding of how to compute, measure, estimate and interpret mathematical data, when to apply these skills and techniques, and why these processes apply within the particular framework of physics. (NUM)
Promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences and objects in physics in meaningful contexts. (CCT)
Develop a contemporary view of technology. (TL)
Use a wide range of possibilities for developing their knowledge of the major concepts within physics. (COM)
Access knowledge. (IL)
Define the following terms: density, relative density (specific gravity).
Recognize that density is a characteristic property of matter.
State the SI unit for density.
Solve problems based on an understanding of density.
Apply concepts of length, mass, area, volume (etc.) to specific tasks.
Define the following terms: pressure, standard atmospheric pressure, barometer, absolute pressure, gauge pressure.
Demonstrate an understanding of accepted usage of units for pressure.
Recognize other non-SI units for pressure that are in common use.

Recognize that the historical development of ideas in science has often led to the adoption of accepted standards and conventions. (e.g., Torricelli's mercury column used to measure atmospheric pressure.)
Solve problems related to pressure in fluids.
Distinguish between absolute pressure and gauge pressure.
Define the following terms: manometer, hydraulics, hydraulic lift.
State Pascal's principle.
Give some examples which illustrate Pascal's principle.
Explain why the output force on a hydraulic lift exceeds the input force.
Solve problems involving Pascal's principle.
Define the following terms: buoyant force, apparent weight.
State Archimedes' principle.
Explain what factors would need to be considered in determining whether or not an object will float.
Solve problems relating to Archimedes principle.
Define the following terms: streamlining, turbulence, whirlpools, eddies, drag.
Compare streamlined and turbulent flow.
Give some examples of streamlined objects.
Explain why an incompressible fluid moving into a region having a different cross-sectional area will undergo a change in speed.
Recognize the causal relationship between the change in speed of a fluid and the accompanying change in pressure.
Provide an operational definition of Bernoulli's principle.
Transfer an understanding of Bernoulli's principle to practical examples and common experiences.
Solve problems involving Bernoulli's principle.

units.name: Optional Unit VII: Electromagnetism
factorsEmphasized: D3 impact of science and technology
D9 social influence on science and technology
F1 longing to know and understand
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: Explore the interrelationship between electricity and magnetism.
Apply an understanding of concepts dealing with electricity and magnetism to common experiences and practical applications.
Recognize the importance of safety when working with electrical equipment.
Perform a variety of activities to investigate electromagnetism.
Consider some of the implications of increased energy demands in the future.
Understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize physics. (COM)
Promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences and objects in physics in meaningful contexts. (CCT)
Appreciate the value and limitations of technology within society. (TL)
Meet their own learning needs. (IL)

Define the following terms: ferromagnetic, soft ferromagnetic, hard ferromagnetic, compass, magnetic field, magnetic lines of force, north- seeking pole, angle of declination, south- seeking pole, angle of magnetic dip.
Describe some of the similarities that exist between electricity and magnetism.
Explain how a compass works.
State the Law of Magnetic Poles.
Recognize that conventions are determined by arriving at a consensus among scientists.
Recognize the importance of using conventions to communicate information in science.
State some important properties of magnetic lines of force.
Suggest a plausible explanation for the movement of the earth's magnetic field over time.
Apply an understanding of magnetism to common experiences and practical applications.
Investigate important uses of magnets in different technological applications.
Define the following terms: magnetic permeability, ferromagnetic.
State that the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor depends on the direction of current flow through the conductor.
Illustrate that the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor forms a series of concentric circles.
Recognize the effect that increased distance away from the conductor has on the strength of the magnetic field.
State Ampere's Rule (right-hand rule) for a straight conductor.
Use the right-hand rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field lines or the direction of the current for a straight conductor.
Explain that the strength of the magnetic field can be intensified by coiling the conductor into a loop.
Describe the shape of the magnetic field formed in the region outside of a solenoid.
State Ampere's Rule (right-hand rule) for a solenoid.
Apply the right-hand rule for a solenoid to determine the direction of the current through the coil or the magnetic polarity of the coil.
Recognize that the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid can be increased enormously by using a core with a high magnetic permeability.
Identify other factors which affect the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid.
Transfer an understanding of electromagnetism to practical applications.
Solve problems relating to electromagnetism.
State the motor principle.
State the right-hand rule for force on a conductor.

Apply the right-hand rule for force on a conductor to determine the direction of force experienced on the conductor, the direction of the external magnetic field, or the direction of current flow through the conductor.
Apply the motor principle to explain important applications such as electric meters or electric motors.
Identify the main components of an electric motor.
Explain how an electric motor works.
Recognize important differences in the design of A.C. and D.C. motors.
State several factors which affect the speed of rotation of an electric motor.
Define the following terms: induce, induced field, inducing field.
Identify the conditions which must occur before a current can be induced within a conductor.
Recognize that maximum current is induced when the direction of movement of the conductor is perpendicular to that of the external magnetic field.
Explain that the interaction between the induced and inducing magnetic fields produces a temporary change in the external magnetic field.
State Lenz's Law.
Recognize that Lenz's Law is consistent with the Law of Conservation of Energy.
Apply Lenz's Law to investigate electromagnetic induction.

units.name: Optional Unit VIII: Atomic Physics
factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
D3 impact of science and technology
D4 science, technology, and the environment
D8 limitations of science and technology
D9 social influence on science and technology

items.text: Recognize that physics is an ongoing human endeavour.
Recognize the need to remain informed on current research in science.
Realize that scientists need to inform society of any real or potential abuse of science.
Appreciate that research is still needed into the uses of nuclear energy.
Recognize that people are constantly being exposed to various forms of radiation.
Recognize that, although exposure to radioactivity is inevitable, it should be minimized.
Recognize the potential hazards associated with exposure to certain types of radiation.
Assess whether or not certain positions regarding the use of nuclear energy are based on a good understanding of physics.
Recognize the need to become informed about the facts and issues surrounding the use of nuclear energy.
Understand the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of physics. (PSVS)
Use a wide range of possibilities for developing their knowledge of the major concepts within physics. (COM)
Develop as "strong sense" critical and creative thinkers. (CCT)
Become actively involved in decision-making related to technological developments. (TL)
Develop a positive disposition to life-long learning. (IL)
Define the following terms: atomic number, isotope, radioisotopes, nuclear binding force, average binding energy, nuclear mass defect, nuclear binding energy, photon.
Use the atomic number of an element to determine the number of protons in a nucleus.
Infer the number of electrons in a neutral atom from the atomic number of an element.
Use the atomic mass number and the atomic number to determine the number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Recognize that isotopes of an element have similar chemical properties, but different physical properties.
Give an example of an element which contains isotopes and show how those isotopes differ from each another.
Explain that the average atomic mass of an element takes into account the relative proportions of its isotopes found in nature.
Explain some of the important characteristics of the Bohr model of the atom.
Identify, interpret, or explain the use of quantum numbers in orbital theory.
Show how the Bohr model of the atom offered explanations for some physical phenomena, while failing to provide a suitable explanation for others.
Explain how photons are used to describe the wave-particle duality of light.
Explain that quantum theory helps to explain the photoelectric effect, the Compton effect, and other important physical principles which earlier theories did not account for adequately.
State that quantum theory describes a region surrounding the nucleus which has the highest probability of locating an electron.
Describe some of the electron orbital descriptions provided by quantum theory.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Define the following terms: transmutation, alpha decay, beta decay, gamma decay, neutrino, disintegration (decay) series, nuclide charts, background radiation, decay constant, half-life.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Demonstrate an understanding of a nuclear transmutation process.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that in a nuclear decay series, nuclear transmutations take place until a stable nucleus results.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain that in alpha particle decay an element with a lower mass is formed.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain that atomic mass number is conserved in alpha and beta particle decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain that mass is not conserved in alpha and beta particle decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that in beta particle decay the beta particle released originated in the nucleus of the atom, not in the electron orbital. A neutron disappears, and in its place a proton and an electron appear.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Develop general expressions for alpha and beta decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Identify alpha, beta, and gamma decay from generalized expressions or nuclear equations.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain that energy is released during a nuclear transmutation.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that mass is not conserved in nuclear reactions.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain why mass is not conserved in a nuclear reaction.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Determine the amount of nuclear binding energy which holds a nucleus together by comparing it to the nuclear mass defect that occurs in a nuclear reaction.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Write equations representing nuclear decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Balance nuclear equations correctly for atomic number and atomic mass number.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Determine missing or incomplete information from a partially balanced equation for nuclear decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Interpret information about a nuclear disintegration series from a nuclide chart.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain what background radiation is and where it originates.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that in trying to measure or observe important physical phenomena, the presence of "noise" may make it difficult to do.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that each radioactive nuclide emits radioactivity at its own characteristic rate.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that the rate of radioactive decay for a given nuclide is related to the energy change that accompanies the transformation. (They are related, but one does not depend on the other.)

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Explain that the rate of radioactive decay is directly proportional to the amount of radioactive material present.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that the decay constant is a measure of the rate of radioactive decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that the rate of decay of a radioactive nuclide is also measured and expressed by its half-life and its mean life.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Determine the decay constant from the half-life and vice versa.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: State the correct units for half-life

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: State the correct unit for the decay constant.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that it is not possible to determine when an individual nucleus within a radioactive sample will undergo decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that it is possible to determine the length of time needed for a certain proportion of the nuclei within a radioactive sample to decay.

items.topic: B. Half Life and Radioactive Decay
items.text: Recognize that the expressed relationships for the radioactive decay are based on statistics and probability, and on the examination of the behaviour of a large number of individual situations.
Define the following terms: fusion, thermonuclear, plasma, magnetic confinement, inertial confinement.
Describe what happens during a fission reaction.
Explain that nuclear fusion occurs within the sun and the stars.
Recognize that scientists believe that nuclear fusion is possible under extremely high temperatures.
State that fusion reactions produce no long-term waste products.
Recognize that the fuel needed for a fusion reaction is abundant.
Compare fusion and fission.
Explain one possible way of sustaining a fusion reaction.
Suggest the potential that fusion has for providing an abundant supply of energy.
Describe an application of nuclear energy (other than fusion reactors).
Identify the type of fuel used in that application.
Recognize the role that Saskatchewan and Canada play in that specific application of nuclear technology.
Identify some of the main uses of the specific application of nuclear energy.
Identify some of the safety precautions that need to be taken in the application being considered.
State some of the facts that supporters of nuclear energy use to substantiate their position for the use of that application.
Identify some of the concerns that critics raise regarding the use of nuclear energy for the specific application.
Suggest what potential concerns regarding the environment emerge as a result of the use of nuclear energy for the application being considered.
Develop a position which either supports or rejects the use of nuclear energy for a specific application.
Defend a position which either supports or rejects the use of nuclear energy for a specific application.

outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI TPS

indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Physics 30. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a topic of interest related to physics. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of relativistic principles and quantum mechanics in our world.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the development of quantum mechanics and relativity, including perspectives of key scientists such as Albert Einstein, Maxwell Planck, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Thomas Young and Stephen Hawking. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate how Newtonian mechanics, quantum mechanics, relativity and emerging theories describe the universe on different scales. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Distinguish between the theories of general and special relativity with respect to space and time (e.g., curvature of space-time, time dilation, length contraction and relativistic mass). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider the implications of inconsistent time with respect to a frame of reference (e.g., time travel and the twin paradox). (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the impact of scientific understanding of relativity on the development of technologies such as the Global Positioning System, atomic clocks and communication systems. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of phenomena such as the photoelectric effect, Young's double slit experiment, black body radiation and Compton scattering to understanding the quantum nature of light. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of conducting observations while investigating wave-particle phenomena and objects at a quantum-scale. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine Planck's constant experimentally or using simulations and discuss its implications for quantum mechanics. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the photoelectric effect including the influence of various frequencies and energies of electromagnetic radiation. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the ongoing debates within physics regarding contradictory and differentiated interpretations (e.g., Collapse, Pilot Wave, Many Worlds and Copenhagen) of quantum mechanics. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Assess the effects of radioactivity and applications of nuclear technology on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the contributions of women (e.g., Harriet Brooks, Marie Curie, Lise Meitner, Chien-Shiung Wu, Mileva Maric and Ida Noddack) from various cultures to the development of scientific understanding of radioactivity. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify natural and artificial sources of radiation on Earth and throughout the universe. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics (e.g., composition, penetrating power, speed and potential danger) of alpha, beta and gamma radiation. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent nuclear reactions involving alpha, beta and gamma decay using words, diagrams and equations. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain that some isotopes undergo natural radioactive decay, and that half-life is a measure of the rate of radioactive decay. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the short- and long-term implications of radiation on living things, including the effects on different types of tissues and cells. (A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how the difficulties in detecting effects of radiation on living things lead to lack of agreement among scientists and others about those effects. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the weak nuclear force and its role in beta decay. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Model the process of nuclear fission, including conditions necessary for a chain reaction. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the amount and rate of energy released in various man-made fission reactions (e.g., nuclear energy production, nuclear weapons, nuclear propulsion and satellites). (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the process of nuclear fusion and the difficulties in harnessing nuclear fusion as an energy source. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the characteristics of the strong nuclear force and its role in maintaining atomic stability. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of mass defect and $e=mc^2$ and why this particular equation has gained such prominence in society. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze societal and environmental impacts of applications of nuclear technologies such as medical isotopes, food irradiation, smoke detectors, industrial radiography, pesticide tracers, nuclear weapons, nuclear reactors and nuclear waste disposal. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: b

outcomes.statement: Analyze the motion of objects and interactions between objects using momentum concepts, including the law of conservation of momentum.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore how impulse and momentum concepts apply to motion-related technologies in fields such as sports science, transportation and space science. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Derive the formula for impulse from Newton's second law of motion. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how changing the net force applied to an object or the amount of time the force is applied affect the momentum of an object, with reference to the formula $F\Δt=m\Δv ↖ {→}$. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples that show how momentum is or is not conserved in everyday situations. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment or simulation, including collecting, analyzing and interpreting data, to determine the extent to which momentum is conserved in elastic and inelastic collisions. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems using the law of conservation of momentum in one- and two-dimensional interactions (e.g., head-on collisions, glancing collisions, rocket launches and explosions). (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze applications (e.g., neutrino detection, Large Hadron Collider, crash test dummies and personal safety devices) of the law of conservation of momentum. (STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Investigate gravitational fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the value of the concept of fields and field theory and the meaning of field strength in understanding the effects of non-contact forces (i.e., action at a distance). (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the gravitational force and its effect on large-scale phenomena throughout the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore phenomena such as gravitational lensing, dark matter, universal expansion and contraction and time dilation as they relate to gravitational fields within the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Relate gravitational field strength near Earth's surface, and variations in that field strength, to the accepted value of acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish, qualitatively and quantitatively, between weight and mass. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain variations in gravitational field strength as a function of inverse-square dependence. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the relation between common misconceptions about perceptions of weightlessness in microgravity environments and people's understanding of gravitational field strength. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research how scientists use an understanding of microgravity environments to further scientific understanding in fields such as biotechnology, fluid physics, materials science, combustion science and fundamental physics. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems involving gravitational field strength using $g={Gm}/r^2$ and Newton's law of universal gravitation $F=G{m_1m_2}/r_^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the nature of scientific collaboration and contribution in researching questions related to emerging topics such as gravitational waves and the graviton. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Investigate electric and magnetic fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that electric fields act on point charges, including action at a distance and following the inverse-square law to determine strength of field. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Draw and describe electric field lines for like and unlike point charges and plates separated by a distance. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how the electric field strength at a point varies according to the inverse square of the distance between two charges, with reference to the equation $E={kQ}/d^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems related to Coulomb's law $F = k{q_1q_2}/d^2$, including electrostatic equilibrium in one- and two-dimensions. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe current scientific thinking regarding the electromagnetic force, one of the four fundamental interactions. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize how our understanding of the interrelationships between magnetic and electric fields has led to the development of technologies such as generators and electromagnets (e.g., moving charged particles create a magnetic field, interaction of electric and magnetic fields). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Represent magnetic fields using magnetic field lines. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent the direction of the magnetic field around current-induced conductors, including linear wires and wire coils, using the right hand and/or left-hand rules. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the characteristics of Earth's magnetic field, including the effects of short- and long-term changes to the field. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the direction of positive, negative and neutral charges moving in natural (e.g., solar flares and aurorae) and man-made (e.g., particle accelerators and MRI's) magnetic fields. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate a prototype of a technology (e.g., electric motor, generator or electromagnet) to demonstrate principles of electromagnetism. (K, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze ways in which natural and technological sources of electric and magnetic fields can influence society and the environment (e.g., changes in animal migration, health concerns and increased communication). (K, STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Extend understanding of angles to angles in standard position, expressed in degrees and radians.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sketch angles in standard position including positive and negative degrees.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate and describe the relationship between different systems of angle measurements, with emphasis on radians and degrees.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sketch, in standard position, an angle measuring 1 radian.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Sketch, in standard position, any angle measuring $ kπ $ radians where $ k∈Q $.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for converting between angle measures in degrees and radians (exact value or decimal approximation).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for determining all angles that are coterminal to an angle within a specified domain (in degrees and radians).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the general form for all angles that are coterminal to a given angle (in degrees and radians).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the radian measure of an angle in standard position and the length of the arc cut on a circle of radius $r$, and solve situational questions based on that relationship.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the unit circle and its relationship to the six trigonometric ratios for any angle in standard position.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Derive the equation of a circle with centre $(0,0)$ and radius $r$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Derive the equation of the unit circle from the application of the Pythagorean theorem or the distance formula.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and generalize the six trigonometric ratios in terms of $x$, $y$, and $r$, using a point that is the intersection of the terminal arm of an angle with the unit circle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, and apply strategies for determining the six trigonometric ratios for any angle given a point on the terminal arm of the angle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, with technology, the approximate value of the trigonometric ratios for any angle (in radians or degrees).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies, including using the unit circle or a reference triangle, for determining the exact trigonometric ratios for angles whose measures are multiples of $0°$, $30°$, $45°$, $60°$, $90°$ (when expressed in degrees), $ 0, π/6, π/4, π/3 $, or $ π/2 $ (when expressed in radians).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain and apply strategies (with or without the use of technology) to determine the measures, in degrees or radians, of the angles in a specified domain that have a particular trigonometric ratio value.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain and apply strategies to determine the exact values of the other trigonometric ratios, given the value of one trigonometric ratio in a specified domain.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Sketch a diagram to represent the context of a problem that involves trigonometric ratios.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Solve situational questions using trigonometric ratios.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the graphs of the primary trigonometric functions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Sketch, with or without technology, the graph of $y= \sin x$, $y= \cos x$, and $y= \tan x$.
Sketch, with or without technology, the graph of

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, and explain strategies for determining the transformational impact of changing the coefficients a, b, c, and d in $y=a \sin b(x-c)+d$ and $y=a \cos b(x-c) + d$ on the graph of $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies to sketch, without technology, graphs of the form $y=a \sin b(x-c)+d$ or $y=a \cos b(x-c) + d$.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Write equations for given graphs of sine or cosine functions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify, with justification, a trigonometric function that models a situational question.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how the characteristics of the graph of a trigonometric function relate to the conditions in a situational question.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve situational questions by analyzing the graph of trigonometric functions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of first- and second-degree trigonometric equations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Verify, with or without technology, whether or not a value is a solution to a particular trigonometric equation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for determining algebraically the exact form of the solution to a trigonometric equation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the approximate solution in degrees and radians of a trigonometric equation in a restricted domain.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the general solution of trigonometric equations to the zeros of the related trigonometric functions limited to sine and cosine functions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the general solutions for trigonometric equations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze solutions for given trigonometric equations to identify errors, and correct if necessary.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of trigonometric identities including:
- reciprocal identities
- quotient identities
- Pythagorean identities
- sum or difference identities (restricted to sine, cosine, and tangent)
- double-angle identities (restricted to sine, cosine, and tangent)

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the difference between a trigonometric identity and a trigonometric equation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Verify numerically (using degrees or radians) whether or not a trigonometric statement is a trigonometric identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "If three different values verify a trigonometric identity, then the identity is valid".

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine, with the use of graphing technology, the potential validity of a trigonometric identity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the non-permissible values of a trigonometric identity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for proving trigonometric identities algebraically.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain and apply strategies for determining the exact value of a trigonometric ratio by using sum, difference, and double-angle identities.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an understanding of operations on, and compositions of, functions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of a function that is the sum, difference, product, or quotient of two functions whose graphs are given.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Write the equation of a function that results from the sum, difference, product, or quotient of two or more functions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the domain and range of a function that is the sum, difference, product, or quotient of two other functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Write a function as the sum, difference, product, or quotient (or some combination thereof ) of two or more functions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the composition of two functions: $\table f(f(x)); f(g(x)); g(f(x))$

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for evaluating a composition of functions at a particular point.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching the graph of composite functions in the form: $\table f(f(x)); f(g(x)); g(f(x))$ where the equations or graphs of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are given.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Write a function as a composition of two or more functions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Write a function by combining two or more functions through operations on, and compositions of, functions.

outcomes.statement: Extend understanding of transformations to include functions (given in equation or graph form) in general, including horizontal and vertical translations, and horizontal and vertical stretches.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare and analyze various graphs of transformations of the function $y = f(x)$, and generalize about the effect of the placement of different coefficients on the original graph of $y = f(x)$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching transformations of the graph of $y = f(x)$ to give the graph of $y-k=af(b(x-h))$.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Write the equation of a function that has undergone specified vertical translations, horizontal translations, vertical stretches, and/or horizontal translations of the function $y = f(x)$ for which the equation is given.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of functions, relations, inverses and their related equations resulting from reflections through the:
- x-axis
- y-axis
- line $y=x$.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generalize and apply the relationship between the coordinates of an ordered pair and the coordinates of the corresponding ordered pair that results from a reflection through the x-axis, the y-axis, or the line $y=x$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for sketching the reflection of a function $y = f(x)$ through the x-axis, the y-axis, or the line $y=x$ when the graph of $f(x)$ is given but the equation is not.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for sketching the graphs of $y=-f(x)$, $y=f(-x)$, and $x=-f(y)$ when the graph of $f(x)$ is given and the equation is not.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for writing the equation of a function that is the reflection of the function $f(x)$ through the x-axis, y-axis, or line $y=x$.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for sketching the inverse of a relation, including reflection across the line $y=x$ and the transformation $(x,y)⇒(y,x)$.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the inverse relation, given the graph of the relation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining if one or both of a relation and its inverse are functions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine what restrictions must be placed on the domain of a function for its inverse to be a function.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "If a relation is not a function, then its inverse also will not be a function".

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the equation and sketch the graph of the inverse relation, given the equation of a linear or quadratic relation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the domains and ranges of a relation and its inverse.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Develop and apply numeric, algebraic, and graphic strategies to determine if two relations are inverses of each other.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate an understanding of logarithms including:
- evaluating logarithms
- relating logarithms to exponents
- deriving laws of logarithms
- solving equations
- graphing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between powers, exponentials, logarithms, and radicals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express a logarithmic expression as an exponential expression and vice versa.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine, without technology, the exact value of a logarithm such as $log_2 8$.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how to estimate the value of a logarithm using benchmarks (e.g., since $log_2 8 = 3$ and $log_2 16 = 4$, $log_2 9$ is approximately equal to $3.1$ ).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Derive and explain the laws of logarithms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply the laws of logarithms to determine equivalent expressions for given logarithmic statements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the approximate value of a logarithmic expression (e.g. $log_2 9$).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve exponential equations in which the bases are powers of one another.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve exponential equations in which the bases are not powers of one another.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for solving logarithmic equations and verify the solutions.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain why a value obtained in solving a logarithmic equation may be extraneous.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve exponential growth or decay, such as loans, mortgages, and investments.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving logarithmic scales, such as the Richter scale and pH scale.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of exponential functions of the form $y=a^x,x>0$ and report about the relationships between the value of a and the domain, range, horizontal asymptote, and intercepts.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without the use of technology, the graphs of exponential functions of the form $y=a^x,x>0$.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Explain the role of the horizontal asymptote for exponential functions.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching transformations of the graph of $y=a^x,x>0$.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of logarithmic functions of the form $y=log_b x,b>1$ and report about the relationships between the value of b and the domain, range, vertical asymptote, and intercepts.

indicators.label: s
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without technology, the graphs of logarithmic functions of the form $y=log_b x,b>1$.

indicators.label: t
indicators.text: Explain the role of the vertical asymptote for logarithm functions.

indicators.label: u
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching transformations of the graph of $y=log_b x,b>1$.

indicators.label: v
indicators.text: Demonstrate graphically that $y=log_b x,b>1$ and $y=b^x,b>0$ are inverses of each other.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of polynomials and polynomial functions of degree greater than 2 (limited to polynomials of degree $≤ 5$ with integral coefficients).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply long division for dividing polynomials by binomials of the form $x-a,a∈I$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare long division of polynomial expressions by binomial expressions to synthetic division, and explain why synthetic division works.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Divide a polynomial expression by a binomial expression of the form $x-a,a∈I$ using synthetic division.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the linear factors of a polynomial expression and the zeros of the corresponding polynomial function.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Generalize, through inductive reasoning, the relationship between the remainder when a polynomial expression is divided by $x-a,a∈I$ and the value of the polynomial expression at $x=a$ (The Remainder Theorem).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain and apply the factor theorem to express a polynomial expression as a product of factors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Categorize, with justification, a set of functions into polynomial functions and non-polynomial functions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of polynomial functions to determine the impact of changing the values of the constant term and leading coefficient in the equation of a polynomial function with respect to the graph of the function.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Generalize and apply strategies for graphing polynomial functions of an odd or even degree.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text:
Explain the relationship between:
- the zeros of a polynomial function,
- the roots of the corresponding polynomial equation,
- the x-intercepts of the graph of the polynomial function.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain and apply strategies for determining the behaviour of the graph of a polynomial function at zeros with different multiplicities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without the use of technology, the graph of a polynomial function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions by modelling the situations with polynomial functions and analyzing the graphs of the functions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of radical and rational functions with restrictions on the domain.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the function $y=√x$ using a table of values, and state the domain and range of the function.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply transformations to the function $y=√x$ to sketch the graph of $y-k=a√{b(x-h)}$.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the function $y=√{f(x)}$ given the graph of the function $y=f(x)$, and compare the domains and ranges of the two functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the roots of a radical equation and the x-intercepts of the graph of the corresponding radical function.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, graphically, the approximate solutions to radical equations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sketch rational functions, with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the behaviour (shape and location) of the graphs of rational functions for values of the dependent variable close to the location of a vertical asymptote.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the equation of a rational function to determine where the graph of the rational function has an asymptote or a hole, and explain why.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Match a set of equations for rational and radical functions to their corresponding graphs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the roots of a rational equation and the x-intercepts of the graph of the corresponding rational function.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Determine graphically an approximate solution to a rational equation.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "Any value that makes the denominator of a rational function equal to zero will result in a vertical asymptote on the graph of the rational function".

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of permutations, including the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies, such as lists or tree diagrams, to determine the total number of choices or arrangements possible in a situation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why the total number of possible choices is found by multiplying rather than adding the number of ways that individual choices can be made.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations relevant to self, family, and community where the fundamental counting principle can be applied to determine the number of possible choices or arrangements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and solve situational questions that involve the application of the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Count, using graphic organizers, the number of ways to arrange the elements of a set in a row.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies, including the use of factorial notation, to determine the number of permutations possible if n different elements are taken n or r at a time.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain why $n$ must be greater than or equal to $r$ in the notation $_nP_r$.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve equations that involve $_nP_r$ notation such as $_nP_2=30$.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of permutations possible when two or more elements in the set are identical (non-distinguishable).

outcomes.statement: PC30.13 Demonstrate understanding of combinations of elements, including the application to the binomial theorem.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain, with examples, how to distinguish between situations that involve permutations and those that involve combinations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of ways that a subset of $k$ can be selected from a set of $n$ different elements.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to determine combinations of $n$ different elements taken $r$ at a time in situational questions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why $n$ must be greater than or equal to $r$ in the notation $ _nC_r $ or $ (\table n; r) $.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prove or explain using examples $_nC_r = _n C _(n-r)$ or $(\table n; r) = (\table n; n-r)$.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve equations involving combinations e.g. $_nC_2=15$ or $(\table n; 2)=15$.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore and describe patterns found within Pascal's triangle, including the relationship between consecutive rows.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore and describe the relationship between the coefficients of the terms in $(x+y)^n$, and the combinations.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for expanding $(x+y)^n,n≤4$.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining specific terms within a particular expansion of $(x+y)^n$ given $n∈\ℕ$.
