outcomes.statement: Examine historical shifts in psychology including major theoretical perspectives and research methods related to lifespan development using various culturalperspectives.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine and compare various historical and current cognitive development theories, such as, First Nations and Métis Elders and Knowledge Keepers traditional ways of knowing and westerndevelopment theorists.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore and compare historical shifts within Western European theoretical perspectives of psychology (e.g., psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, evolutionary, sociocultural)using various cultural worldviews.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate developmental psychology as an evolving science.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles of the four dimensions of human development (i.e., biological, cognitive, socioemotional, spiritual) in developmental psychology.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss validity, reliability and ethical issues in various quantitative and qualitative research methods (e.g., experimental, interview, observation, case study) used in psychology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impacts of imposing concepts of Western social sciences on marginalized groups.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how the practice of psychology has been used to maintain power imbalances in institutions across Canada.

outcomes.statement: Investigate theories of nature and nurture and the impact of biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual factors on lifespan development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how biological (e.g., gross and fine motor skills), cognitive (e.g., thinking and memory), socioemotional (e.g., temperament) and spiritual (e.g., personal beliefs, value systems) aspects of development interact to support development of a child.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze aspects of human development that might be attributed exclusively to heredity or inherited factors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how gender identities can influence biological, cognitive, socioemotional and spiritual development during childhood.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how biology, culture and spirituality might influence one’s gender identity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine roles and influences (e.g., morals, prosocial and antisocial behaviour, motivation, discipline philosophies) of families, peers and significant others on lifespan development.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ways individuals’ support systems (e.g., parents, foster parents, extended family caregivers, social, religious and cultural organizations, worldviews) influence thoughts, feelings and behaviour.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how different cultures and perspectives view lifespan development (e.g., First Nations, Métis and Inuit, Black, Asian).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze and compare roles of nature (e.g., hereditary traits, individual abilities and capacities) and nurture (e.g., environmental influences) that shape behaviour with lifespan development.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate how trauma, from historical and current events (e.g., genocide, Residential Schools, Sixties Scoop, effects of poverty, racism), impacts biological, cognitive, socioemotional and spiritual development (e.g., epigenetic, intergenerational) of a child.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence development of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) from conception to five years.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Summarize processes of biological, cognitive and emotional development from conception to birth, infancy and early childhood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate sensory and perceptual systems from birth to five years.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how family’s spiritual views (e.g., values, morals, beliefs) can impact the development of young children.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine stages of pregnancy and complications that can arise.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare effects of healthy and unhealthy lifestyles on fetal development.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine beginnings of personality in infants (e.g., temperament, early socialization, types of attachments, affects of social deprivation, bonding/attachment with parents).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate stages of communication processes and language development in early childhood.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create a timeline of language development from ages birth to five years.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the influences of direct conversation (i.e., adult to child) on language development.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the influences (e.g., child’s use, parent’s use) of technology on childhood development.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate criteria for toys available for young children (e.g., infants, toddlers, preschoolers)that develop gross and fine motor skills.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Design and create a toy for a young child that develops cognition and fine motor skills.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence development of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) from 6 to 12 years.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Summarize and discuss key changes (e.g., biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual) indevelopment of children from 6 to 12 years.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: AnalyzeJean Piaget’s four stages of cognitive development (i.e., sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational) and their relationships to the four dimensions of development.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss Howard Gardner’s theory of Multiple Intelligences and connections to childhood development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how various dynamics of a family have changed throughout history and creatively represent these dynamics (e.g., dramatic role play, song, illustrated timeline, fictional parenting blog).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the influences (e.g., child’s use, parent’s use) of technology on childhood development.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine influences of parent-child interaction during significant life events (e.g., death, adoption, blended families, parental separation/divorce) on childhood development.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine influences of culture on identity development.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the biological, cognitive and emotional benefits of unstructured creative play during childhood.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the influence of biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual dimensions on the development of identity in childhood.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence development of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) from adolescence to early adulthood.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Summarize and discuss key changes (e.g., biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual) in development from adolescence to early adulthood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine issues and challenges in adolescence (e.g., substance misuse, eating disorders, teen parenting, gender identity, teen violence, crime, bullying, self-harm, suicide).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., drama, video, song, visual) demonstrating understanding of key changes from adolescence to early adulthood.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate ways sociocultural environments influence adolescent development.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze influences (e.g., cultural, gender, family, peers, media, poverty) on self-concept.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research how individuals form social perceptions, make sense of behaviours of others and form judgements about other people.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine development of agency (i.e., acting independently and making own choices) and co-agency (i.e., interactive, mutually supportive relationships) in adolescence.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how an individual or groups may encounter obstacles (e.g., racial or gender privilege, ideals of beauty) within mainstream society that can impact their sense of agency and ability to achieve personal goals.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate similarities and differences among stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination and discuss potential impact on adolescent development

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine emotional and social issues and challenges involved in becoming a parent (e.g., values, family genetic history, parenting styles, relationship stability, spiritual beliefs, parent age, finances).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate influences of spiritual beliefs and cultural rites of passage (e.g., birth, intimacy, group behaviour, marriage, death) on individuals.

outcomes.statement: Investigate ways in which biological influences affect thoughts, feelings and emotions in relation to development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify parts and functions of the central nervous system (e.g., brain, spinal cord, neurons) and the endocrine system (e.g., thyroid, pituitary pancreas).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Design a visual (e.g., superhero or villain with nervous system enhancements or flaws) to represent similarities, differences and interconnectedness of the nervous and endocrine systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine ways emotions are connected to biological influences.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the roles of nutrition and physical activity on thoughts, biological and emotional development.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the effects of traditional food diets (e.g., Western, Indigenous, South Asian, African, Mediterranean) vs. processed food diets and their impact on health and emotional well-being

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how injuries, health conditions affecting the nervous and/or endocrine system and substance misuse can influence thoughts, feelings, perceptions and behaviour.

outcomes.statement: Examine cognition as it applies to lifespan development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine various historical and current cognitive development theories (e.g., Vygotsky, Piaget) and traditional Indigenous views of cognitive development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the development of the nervous system and the brain from birth to five years.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine developmental changes in cognition from childhood through adolescence.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate what is meant by “adolescent egocentrism" and its effects on one’s life.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine connections between cognition and memory (e.g., memory tools, dementia, Alzheimer’s, muscle memory).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Distinguish differences among learning styles theories (e.g., visual/spatial, logical/mathematical, kinesthetic) and examine their roles in learning and surrounding controversies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., mind map, cluster diagram, 3D model, mobile, game, song) depicting one’s learning style strengths.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate explanations for elements of cognition (e.g. learning, memory, imagination, judgement, decision-making) shared through oral storytelling.

outcomes.statement: Examine interconnectedness of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) of the whole person through lifespan development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate historical and contemporary perspectives (e.g., First Nations and Métis traditional worldviews, psychoanalytic, behavioural, sociocultural, psychosocial) on human development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of holistic approaches (i.e., interconnected mind, body, spirit, emotion) to lifespan development.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual changes, challenges and benefits during the aging process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of change as one transitions through different experiences (e.g., moving away from home, entering the work force, becoming a parent, retiring) in a lifespan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a written piece (e.g. interview of a senior citizen about their current life, series of personal daily journal entries 50 years in the future, letter to one’s future senior self) that details daily life as a member of the older generation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., essay, letter, comic strip, magazine advertisement) that supports a positive quote about aging (e.g., “Getting old is like climbing a mountain; you get a little out of breath, but the view is much better!”, Ingrid Bergman), based on two dimensions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess influences of childhood traumas (e.g., war, violence, abuse, neglect, attachment issues, exposure to or witnessing substance misuse, family isolation, poverty) on adult development and lifestyle.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze relationships between personality, lifestyle and health and discuss implications for own life.

outcomes.statement: Investigate various sociocultural factors that influence adulthood.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the influences of various lifestyle choices (e.g., nutrition, exercise, substance abuse, how one chooses to handle stress, deceitfulness in a relationship) on the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) during adulthood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research influence of substance misuse on cognitive, biological, spiritual well-being and identify reasons why some people may be susceptible to addiction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research various relationship trends, processes and moral and legal commitments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how adverse childhood experiences (e.g., abuse, death of caregiver, divorce, caregiver incarceration, abandonment) influence choices and behaviour in adult life.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine causes and affects of divorce on couples and their families.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into various cultural influences on one’s perceptions of death and dying.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the meaning of the phrase “living beyond one’s means” and the effects this can have on one’s physical and mental well-being.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine some issues and challenges (e.g., financial, mental and physical well-being, cognition, retirement, relationships) seniors face and consider potential solutions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine stressors parents face and research resiliency and coping skills they can develop to maintain balanced and healthy lives.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the strengths and challenges of becoming new parents at different stages (e.g., 20s, 40s, 60s) of life.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the emotional and physical effects of grandparents becoming primary care givers for their grandchildren and research available community supports

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze the pros and cons (e.g., medical, emotional) of postponing motherhood/pregnancy to establish one’s career.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Debate when old age starts and discuss various cross-cultural attitudes towards aging.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the definition of personality and determine if aspects of one’s personality continue to develop during a lifespan.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Determine the connections between one’s personality, lifestyle, health and relationships.

outcomes.statement: Investigate contemporary developmental psychology issues.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Investigate an issue of personal interest related to pre-adolescence (e.g. , ages 10-12) including biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual aspects.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore issues involved in transitioning from dependent child into independent adult (e.g., living on your own, post-secondary schooling and/or work responsibilities, financial stresses, boomerang children, establishing adult relationships, responsibility to parents/caregivers versus self-responsibility).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and compare current and past studies which reflect various viewpoints and/or theories regarding nature and nurture.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the implications of organ donations and organ transplants for individuals and their families.

outcomes.statement: Design and carry out a detailed exploration of one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Psychology 30using an ethical perspective.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine validity, reliability and ethical issues in various quantitative and qualitative research methods (e.g., experimental, interview, observation, case study) used in psychology.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed inquiry through research paper, display, presentation, performance, demonstration, representation, or video.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Co-construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) and use it to assess the process and products involved in one’s student-directed study.

evidence.observation: “Outcomes at a Glance” lists the Psychology 30 outcomes as one numbered list, with no unit, strand, theme or module headings.

allEvidence.observation: “Outcomes at a Glance” lists the Psychology 30 outcomes as one numbered list, with no unit, strand, theme or module headings.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for injury prevention to ensure safety in the work area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify personal protective equipment (PPE) such as eyewear, clothing, footwear and ear wear that may be needed for the work site, school or home.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply accident prevention principles and techniques, and discuss appropriate actions in case of an injury or accident, such as whom to contact, fire extinguisher locations, emergency exit routes and first-aid procedures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practice good housekeeping and avoid obvious hazards (e.g., touching live wires, extending cords over walking spaces and leaving objects on the floor).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Complete an assessment of all safety and robotics equipment and, in consultation with the instructor, perform maintenance to repair or replace defective or worn parts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

outcomes.statement: Develop and implement a plan to resolve multiple issues present in a device.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Troubleshooting B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and locate all issues present in a device, including programming and physical issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Isolate all issues present in a device.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the cause of all issues present in a device.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop and evaluate a plan to resolve all issues present in a device.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Implement a plan to resolve the issues present in a device.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the resolutions and modify the plan as needed to resolve the issues.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the need for having troubleshooting skills in various careers in the fields of robotics and automation.

outcomes.statement: Incorporate empathy into engineering design processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8C: Design Thinking C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 4-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Construct a problem definition empathizing with the needs and wants of the end user(s) for the project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply empathetic interview skills (e.g., ask why 3 times, encourage stories, ask open ended questions, pay attention to non-verbal cues and look for inconsistencies) to determine the needs and wants of the end user(s).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on whether proposed solutions address actual versus perceived problems.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Share project progress with the end user(s) at regular intervals to elicit feedback and ensure the project is meeting their needs.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe practices when working with electricity and electrical devices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Electrical Safety (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment when working with electrical devices such as a soldering iron.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Review safety procedures (e.g., inspect equipment for damaged or frayed wires, ensure proper grounding and ensure work area is free from liquids) for working with electrical equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Understand the need for circuit protection in an electrical circuit.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify basic electrical hazards in the shop and/or work area.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Inspect all tools and electrical equipment, including extension cords, for hazards before using them.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify safe current and/or voltage values pertaining to equipment safety.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify safe current and/or voltage values pertaining to personal safety.

outcomes.statement: Design and construct a variety of circuits to interface between a programmable control board and a robotic or automated device.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14C: Electronic Components C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List some advantages and disadvantages of using integrated circuits rather than conventional circuits in robotic and automated devices.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between NPN and PNP transistors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and construct a circuit that uses a transistor circuit (e.g., 5-5-5 timer) to control a higher current device.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and construct a motor control circuit (e.g., H-Bridge) using an integrated circuit (IC) or transistor.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and construct a complex circuit that is composed of multiple simple circuits and that contains inputs and outputs.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and construct a servo control circuit using an integrated circuit (IC).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design and construct a circuit, such as a 3D cube, that will allow for the control of multiple light-emitting diodes (LEDs).

outcomes.statement: Explore how fuses are used to protect circuits.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Fuses (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what it means for a circuit to be overloaded.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss what occurs in a circuit that is experiencing a short circuit situation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the use of different fuse types (e.g., plug fuses, cartridge fuses, time-delay fuses and renewable fuses).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how fuses should be wired in an electrical circuit.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Troubleshoot a circuit with a fuse in it using a multimeter.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Calculate the fuse rating for a given circuit.

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of datasheets for providing information about the technical characteristics of electronic components.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Datasheets (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what datasheets (or spec sheets) are and their purposes in robotics construction.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Indicate where datasheets for electronic components can be found.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Extrapolate data from given datasheets.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Using information from a datasheet, determine the proper parameters for a given electronic component to be used in a project.

outcomes.statement: Incorporate internal, external and user-defined libraries to extend the functionality of software.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 32B: Coding - Functions B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 32A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that a library is a compilation of functions that can extend the functionality of software.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss why programming languages make use of libraries.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Utilize internal libraries to reduce the required code necessary for a project.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Import and incorporate an external library to solve a programming problem.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a library to meet a specific need.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how and when to incorporate recursive functions into programs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 32C: Coding - Functions C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 31A, 32B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between the functionality of a loop (i.e., iteration) and a recursive function (i.e., recursion).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize that a recursive function is one that calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the terminating or base condition in a recursive function.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations where it is advantageous to use recursive functions in programming robotic and automated devices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a recursive function to solve a programming problem.

outcomes.statement: Construct and program a device capable of following a complex line, including dotted line sections.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 35C: Line Sensors C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 35B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Program a device to follow a complex solid line, including curves, 90-degree turns, greater than 90 degree turns and T-junctions using input from a line follower sensor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Program a device to make a decision at the end of a line using input from a line follower sensor.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Program a device to follow a dotted line, including curves, 90-degree turns and T-junctions using input from a line follower sensor.

outcomes.statement: Construct and program a device that uses multiple ultrasonic sensors to make decisions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 37C: Ultrasonic Sensors C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 37B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Program a device to make decisions (e.g., navigate a maze and stop when in a dead end or follow a wall around a room) using inputs from multiple ultrasonic sensors.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of how ultrasonic sensors are used in manufacturing environments to automate process control and maximize efficiency.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and construct a device using multiple ultrasonic sensors to perform a task involving manipulating outputs (e.g., change movement based on inputs or alter direction of movement or reach out to touch an object).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate the usefulness of an ultrasonic sensor in various situations.

outcomes.statement: Construct and program a device that uses multiple infrared sensors to make decisions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 38C: Infrared Sensors C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 38B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Program a device to make decisions (e.g., navigate a maze and stop when in a dead end or follow a wall around a room) using inputs from multiple infrared sensors.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Design and construct a device using multiple infrared sensors to perform a task involving manipulating outputs (e.g., change movement based on inputs, alter direction of movement or reach out to touch an object).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate the usefulness of an Infrared sensor in various situations.

outcomes.statement: Customize a transmitter for control of a robotic or automated device.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 43C: Transmitting and Receiving C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 43B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop an understanding of the mapping of a transmitter (i.e., channel controls and trims).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate control of multiple outputs (e.g., servos, motors, actuators and pneumatic devices) from a single transmitter.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Program a transmitter (e.g., reversing channels, speed controls, setting limits and naming) to control a specific robotic or automated device.

outcomes.statement: Explore applications of stepper motors in robotics and automation applications.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 50: Stepper Motors (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the operation of a stepper motor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain when it is appropriate to use a stepper motor rather than a servo.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between voltage level, speed and torque in a stepper motor.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how stepper motors are rated.

Know that the Iroquoian worldview consisted of these basic beliefs:
- spiritual beliefs
- Every expression of life is part of an awesome order known as the Great Mystery.
- All human beings are sacred because each is an expression of the will of the Great Spirit.
- The sacred circle of life means that all life is equal and spiritual, so every part of nature must be used with respect.
- The earth is the mother of all and the spirit that governs it is feminine.
- moral beliefs
- Indian society, beliefs, and ways are good when they obey the Great Spirit.
- Women represent reason, because it is they who produce and educate the child that becomes the adult.
- Women are the head of the household and, as such, are expected to give leadership to society.
- Men should show great physical courage as well as grace and obedience in carrying out their role as protectors of society.
- economic beliefs
- The earth is a gift from the creator which cannot be owned or sold.
- Status was earned by those who could give away the most wealth.
- Trade and peace are the same thing.
- social beliefs
- Freedom is the most prized possession and the preservation of freedom depends upon obeying the law and preserving the freedom of others.
- Society should be communal, cooperative, and sharing.
- Everyone has an equal place in the social circle and everyone protects each other and the society that gives so much.
- political beliefs
- Power should be diffused throughout society so that all may contribute.

Know that the eighteenth century British worldview consisted of these basic beliefs:
- spiritual beliefs

Great Britain was a Protestant nation which:
- accepted that the King was the "defender of the faith";
- rejected any right of control by the Pope over British society anywhere; and,
- believed in an individualistic, personal relationship with God without any intervention by priest or church.
- political beliefs
- Britain should be a monarchy because its supporting institutions (aristocracy, army, gentry, the church) embodied the best traditions for guiding society.
- The monarch, in governing society, is obligated to accept guidance from an elected assembly (Parliament).
- Parliament must be supreme in British society and cannot have its power limited in any way by any other institution.
- —The-behaviour-of-all-individuals-and institutions (including the King) within society must conform to the rule of law.
- economic beliefs

The British government's policies were based on mercantilistic beliefs:
- an imperial system of trade and political power would augment Britain's power and prestige throughout the world;
- colonies should serve the interests of the mother country; and,
- colonies should be taxed to pay for their own defence.

Many British businesspeople accepted the beliefs underlying a market oriented economy:
- private entrepreneurship and less government interference are desirable; and
- competition and profit should guide production rather than government.

Know that the Aboriginal Nations believed:
- Land was not something that could be "owned" because it was a gift from the Creator to be held in trust by one generation for the next generation.
- Treaties were a means through which they could adapt to European influences while maintaining their cultural traditions.
- A treaty was a binding social contract which should define all future relations between themselves and Euro-Canadians.
- The purpose of treaties was to safeguard their rights and would remain binding for "as long as the sun shines and the water flows" (a European phrase).
- In return for these binding treaties, the Aboriginal peoples were prepared to become loyal subjects of the Crown and would respect its laws.

In the treaties, Euro-Canadians had agreed to:
- provide annuities, land, schools, housing, livestock, agricultural implements and training, medical care, and clothing;
- prohibit liquor on reserves; and,
- protect hunting and fishing rights.
- Indian nations would have the right to select the location of their reserves of land.

Know that the Indian nations believed that the treaties were being deliberately misinterpreted by the government:
- "We hear our lands were sold...we don't want to sell our lands; ... no one has the right to sell them".
- The land can only be borrowed not bought.
- If the land was sold, the money should go to the Aboriginal peoples.
- The Treaty right of Plains Indian nations to select contiguous Indian reserves was ignored. (A common Indian territory that would stretch from Gleichen AB in the northwest to Swift Current in the northeast and south to the 49 parallel of latitude was wanted.)
- The government failed to protect the right to hunt buffalo by allowing the buffalo to be destroyed, and then not meeting its obligation to find food for the starving Indian people.
- Needed agricultural equipment, training and guidance was not provided as agreed so the Indian nations could find another living.
- The government denied Indian nations the right to meet together in large assemblies to discuss common problems and devise solutions and ways of pressuring the government.

- A tripolar system occurs when there are three dominating powers. Each of the three powers is forced to work to limit the power of the others by strategically allying with one of the other powers. (Great Britain, France, and Germany prior to World War I.)
- A multipolar system occurs when there are more than three powers who can function as major competing players in the balance-ofpower system. Know that transnational movements achieve power through influence and charisma. They use emotional and spiritual appeals to mobilize large numbers of people in some kind of cause.
Non-governmental Organizations (NGOs) Know that the International Olympic Committee, Red Cross, and Amnesty International are examples of NGOs.
Know that Amnesty International is a good example of an NGO that can publicize and successfully limit the behaviour of a government that is being arbitrary and dictatorial.
International Government Organizations (IGOs)
Know that Canadian governments when developing foreign policy have to resolve ambivalent and contradictory pressures both;
from within and without Canada.
Know that developing foreign policy involves a process of dialectical evaluation in order to weigh the consequences of alternative policies.
Know that Canadians are seriously divided about whether integrating Canada's economy into the North American trading bloc represents capitulation or progress.

Dialectic on the Future of Canadian Culture Know that Canadians are extremely ambivalent about American culture: Canadians vote for American culture with their television dials while expressing a great deal of dislike for it.
Know that Canadian social and foreign policy has never been able to resolve the conflict over access to the international media and protecting and maintaining Canadian culture.
Know that international law is based on a complex mix of legal principles, widely practised customs, basic standards of behaviour, and legally-binding rules, all of which change slowly.
Know that change in nature often occurs catastrophically fast and, therefore, international law will lag and not respond immediately to the crisis.
Know that nations will find themselves in a dilemma where they may wish to act legally but feel forced to use illegal means to prevent a conservation disaster.
Practise using concepts to categorize and classify information.
Practise drawing generalizations and inferences from classified data.

Practise applying the thinking skills of:
- stating propositions (hypotheses) that are testable and guide the search for data;
- collecting data in a systematic manner; and,
- presenting analyses to confirm or disconfirm an hypothesis.
How should a nation in its foreign policy balance its domestic interests against its international responsibilities?

Should nations such as Canada opt for protecting their own self-interest by:
- building up their national power and duplicating, wherever possible, the shady practices of other nations? or,
- working with other nations to strengthen the international system and attempt to pressure nations to conform to standards of international law?
Know that nations have historically reserved the right to define and implement social policies that, they believe, serve their best interests.
Know that other members of the international community (nations, MNCs, etc.) are challenging that right particularly in areas of economic and fiscal policies.
Know that countries like Canada will have to find a balance between maintaining international commitments and protecting national well-being.

Know that many Canadians believe that there is a great deal of poverty in Canada which should be eliminated before Canada sends out foreign aid. Other Canadians argue that Canada is so much wealthier than poor countries that it has the capacity and, therefore, the obligation to help wherever it can.
Know that many people believe Canada's best interests are served by creating a strong defence industry which improves Canada's capacity to defend itself and its economy.
items.concept: Dialectic on the Defence of Canada

items.text: Know that other people argue that using defence and armaments as the basis to build industry and create jobs is wasteful and expensive. This wealth could be better used to create more productive industries while Canada works to create a disarmed, peaceful international community.

Practise drawing generalizations and inferences from classified data.

Practise applying the thinking skills of:
- stating propositions (hypotheses) that are testable and guide the search for data;
- collecting data-in-a systematic manner; and,
- presenting analyses to confirm or disconfirm an hypothesis.
How should a nation in its foreign policy balance its domestic interests against its international responsibilities?

Should nations such as Canada opt for protecting their own self-interest by:
- building up their national power and duplicating, wherever possible, the shady practices of other nations? or,
- working with other nations to strengthen the international system and attempt to pressure nations to conform to standards of international law?
Know that Canadians have always been ambivalent about the size and role of the military in Canada.
Some Canadians believe that Canada should maintain a strong military and a prominent role in international organizations such as NATO and NORAD.
Other Canadians believe that, at most, Canada should have a small military that is trained for peacekeeping so that Canada can play a mediating role in the international community.
Know that making international commitments is always expensive and often risky because of mistakes and entanglements.
Some Canadians argue that Canada's first responsibility is to Canadian self-interest and that of close allies.
Others Canadians believe that Canada's self-interests are best served by taking a leading role in making the relationships within the international community work peacefully and effectively.

notes: Method: page images OCRed with RapidOCR (PP-OCRv6 det/rec small, 200 dpi). Lines are grouped into columns by the table header positions, then split into items by: a list marker, a line ending in . ; : ? !, a line ending in "; and"/"; or", or a line that ends early (the next line’s first word would have fitted). Lines after an item ending in ":" are kept as its sub-list (lines starting "- "). Text is the OCR reading with no correction; hyphenated line breaks are rejoined.
84 items are marked segmentationUncertain (no closing punctuation, or a knowledge objective that does not start with a capital): they may be a fragment of the item before or after.
Items with ocrLowConfidence have at least one OCR line scored below 0.85, or a line that ran across two table columns and was split at the column edge.
Core vs optional: the guides print core material in bold. Bold is not detected here, so content-table items are not marked core/optional.

This 1997 guide has no separate foundational-objectives pages. Each unit has "Core Learning Objectives" summary pages (level "unit-summary") where, by the printed legend, a solid bullet marks a foundational objective of the course and a hollow bullet a core learning objective. Bullets were read from the page image (markers.py: shape and centre fill), not from the OCR text: type "foundational" = solid bullet, "core": true = hollow bullet, "marker" keeps the reading. Bullets that could not be read leave the item as type "learning" without "core". Spot checks on Unit One matched the page, but a few bullets were missed.

Concept labels in the left margin of those pages are in "concept"; indented sub-concept headings (e.g. "Burden of proof") are in "subConcept". The content tables that follow give the full learning objectives (level absent).

outcomes.statement: Research, plan, produce, analyze and resolve a series of works exploring, through independent inquiry, big ideas of personal significance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Brainstorm big ideas for sustained investigation drawing on experiences, interests, visual culture and/or contemporary issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate inquiry questions to guide own investigations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Plan and create works demonstrating personal artistic voice from direct observation, dreams, fantasies, inspirations, combinations of found references and own photographic compositions and designs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Strive for increasingly sophisticated and/or sensitive works that build on existing strengths while challenging current level of technical proficiency.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Connect with artists, including Indigenous, to learn how they speculate, hypothesize, research, test, discover and experiment throughout their career.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Articulate a clear planning, research, production and reflection process to develop a portfolio of work shaped through inquiry and the possibility of real-world applications.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Exercise creative voice and critical decision making to convey an informed perspective and real-world application of selected inquiry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate and critique own art works, with input from peers and teacher, at various stages for technical success and relationship to selected inquiry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research interdisciplinary connections along with cultural and historical examples, including Indigenous, that expand on selected investigation to determine how other disciplines or cultures might respond to same inquiry.

outcomes.statement: Create original works inspired by artists of personal interest while maintaining own intentions and artistic vision.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine works of various personal, social, cultural and historical contexts recording inspirational aspects, visually or in writing, and define intentions for responding artistically to this work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experiment with mashups, collages or mixed media works that demonstrate appropriately placing own work ‘in conversation’ with another artist or style.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate own portfolio for instances of copying and revise derivative works by interpreting, stylizing, layering or abstracting to communicate own ideas in new ways.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Alter significantly several aspects of own work when referencing photographic, illustrative or other work that belongs to another artist using methods such as:
- improvising a mashup of three works while exploring an idea of personal significance
- referring to an inspiration file and sketchbook to alter and combine ideas in new ways.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research legal and ethical concerns in the context of intellectual, virtual and physical property influencing own work particularly when similarities to the work of others is intended.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the concepts of ethics, authenticity and originality along with community norms and values related to art production and marketing, including online, in the context of contemporary art practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Provide rationale for historical, cultural and stylistic references in own work and describe how personal experiences, interests and intentions are depicted in portfolio.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research plagiarism policies of universities, colleges, art schools and art programs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create through multiple lenses, design strategies and perspectives to apply new ways of communicating own views.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Respond knowledgeably and sensitively to the work of others with inventive interpretations to merge and mold to own style and message.

outcomes.statement: Refine and document full range of own creative process (e.g., idea generation, sketches, drafts, maquettes, reference work, source material, research, production, media exploration, critique, refinement) including completed works, providing evidence of critical inquiry.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Connect with artists who create work for a variety of purposes to inquire about creative process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critically analyze and compare own creative process to methods used by practicing artists in order to incorporate relevant aspects to own practice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe and experiment with the fluid, cyclical nature of the creative process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Actively record own practice, experimentation and revision of works up to and including final versions demonstrating, for example:
- preliminary rough drafts, written reflections, artist study
- reasoning and motivations during process
- risk-taking with mixed media, layering and current techniques for creating visual interest and nuanced meaning
- critical responses to contemporary conceptual approaches in art making
- analysis of strengths and weaknesses of own creative process
- how feedback has been applied to elevate works included in presentation portfolio
- documentation of selected aspects of own process through photographs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate evidence of regular exploration and independent thinking through ongoing studio work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate current portfolio and/or sketchbook to assess strengths that can be built on and incorporated into future works.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare for portfolio submission by creating high quality, well composed, high resolution photographs of completed works.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Edit, during post-production, digital images of own work to aid in presenting the clearest, most accurate representation of the work and ensure that images meet the requirements of selected digital submission web application.

outcomes.statement: Cultivate proficiency in manipulating visual, stylistic and conceptual conventions to solve a range of challenging art making investigations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use compositional and design strategies in a variety of ways to convey meaning and create visual interest.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Accentuate personal style and voice when applying image development strategies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Take risks with elements of art, principles of design, and composition/design rules to work beyond the confines of those theories and increase visual impact.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use synectics as a tool to develop creative thinking strategies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate and make revisions to existing works to employ innovative or imaginative visual arrangements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate a unique, personal voice while extending art works beyond common artistic clichés or exercises.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply critical and creative thinking to define ways to work within and push the boundaries of artistic conventions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the philosophy of aesthetics and assess own work for the application of these principles.

outcomes.statement: Prepare and curate an exhibition of own work in a professional and collaborative manner.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Collaboratively research the changing role of the curator in diverse and inclusive institutions and communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how contemporary curatorial work has evolved to include historically-excluded worldviews such as Indigenous, feminist and minorities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe a range of methods of, and purposes for, presenting art to the public.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: View various visual art exhibits in locations such as galleries, land-based environments, pop-ups and community centres, to analyze and discuss how the curated show tells a story.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consider how the public is involved in the exhibition and ways that artists engage viewers to reflect and respond to work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the elements of a marketing strategy that are likely to generate interest in a student art exhibition.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Engage in critical decision making to select and prepare own works for public display.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Plan and develop one or more projects that showcase artwork with the local, school or online community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify and apply gallery conventions of mounting an exhibition such as signing works, matting works, framing works, selecting lighting, designing invitations and catalogues, writing an artist statement, handling and display of art pieces, use of signage, traffic flow patterns, promotion, disassembly and follow-up.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Document exhibition with camera and ensure that digital images accurately represent the original works on display and format of the overall design of show.

outcomes.statement: Utilize creative and systematic investigations to critically analyze, interpret and respond to professional art, orally and in writing, across formats, styles, cultures and time periods.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare/contrast the function and social impact of selected works that explore similar topics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize recognized critical analysis processes in addition to informal and personal approaches to examine how art reflects on and contributes to culture and society.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how perspectives of diverse cultural groups, including Black, First Nations, Métis, and people of colour, are represented in their art forms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the role of audience, critic and consumer by researching initial reactions of critics at the time selected work was produced and the response of the audience of the day in contrast to today’s audience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Deconstruct visual content within a range of works, created for a variety of purposes, to acquire lessons that can be applied to own work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify cultural, political, historical or spiritual factors affecting the work of several artists across disciplines or time periods.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the effect of viewing and deconstructing art on own perspectives, perceptions and biases.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Study works to determine how artists conceptualize and communicate ideas and apply to own work.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Select works to investigate from applied and commercial disciplines including traditional and emerging technologies and practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Make connections to work studied and own creations.

outcomes.statement: Critique works in progress and portfolio development with peers and other experienced reviewers to inform the development of that work and/or lead future work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Collectively choose criteria for reviewing student art including how to determine if work is complete rather than abandoned.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use a variety of formal and informal art appreciation approaches to guide feedback.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how inquiry and research inform inception of own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Refer to documentation of initial ideas and explain how intentions may have evolved through creative process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify own influences, intentions and processes in the creation of non-derivative works and development of personal aesthetic vision.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct portfolio review identifying areas of strength and areas for growth that guide goals for improvement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess and apply select feedback from trusted sources to improve or fully resolve own work.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how own work is situated in current culture and reflects own views.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compose a presentation portfolio (e.g., select items from one’s working portfolio) to best showcase one’s strengths and development as an artist.

outcomes.statement: Appraise current trends and emerging practices to determine how artists produce and embed knowledge within work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore inventive contemporary art (e.g., maker and hacker cultures, game design, video culture, interactive art, land art) to formulate personal definition of art and understand its purposes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Study cultural and historical themes in art (e.g., equality, politics, family, poverty, gender) to learn how artists contextualize or re-contextualize content.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how art uses non-verbal visual language to embed knowledge (e.g., traditional First and Métis ways of knowing, world cultures, historical artifacts) and apply to own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how art that persuades and/or protests is used to affect beliefs (e.g., propaganda, advertising, film, folk art).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze methodologies used by artists as researchers and apply to own inquiry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate examples of interdisciplinary work involving arts and non-arts fields.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine art as a social critique and means of promoting global understanding.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect and identify how the production and consumption of artistic knowledge can positively impact health and well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss aesthetic knowledge in art and principles of universal beauty (e.g., golden ratio).

outcomes.statement: Activate self-advocacy and agency as an emerging artist by connecting with arts professionals, including First Nations and Métis.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Expand entrepreneurship skills by studying art as a business (e.g., copyright, insurance, income tax, art contracts, art dealers, and art suppliers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore and develop skills for pursuing a career in the arts within a work study, apprenticeship or mentorship experience (e.g., local artists, First Nations and Métis artists).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate awareness of post-secondary study in the arts and local and global career opportunities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine criteria used to determine the sale value of art and estimate the sale value of own artwork.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate agency and independence as an emerging artist by maintaining physical studio spaces that are safe and utilizing resources appropriately considering practices that respect the environment and minimize impact.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the financial and other supports (e.g., grants, exhibition space, marketing, community members) available to practicing artists.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create materials to market one’s skills (e.g., compose a résumé and artist statement).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create artist social media presence or website including posts of process, progress and final products.

indicators.text: Investigate ways to apply visual art skills to careers that are seemingly unrelated to the arts.

outcomes.statement: Examine potential hazards in theatre production and apply injury prevention practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4B: Safety in the Theatre: Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore risk assessment as it relates to the work area and how it can prevent injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how an injury might affect an injured worker and others such as the employer, supervisor, work colleagues, family and friends.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, theatre inspections and following safe work practices.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Generate and discuss examples, within the context of theatre arts, of potential workplace hazards and injuries in the four major categories.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare a variety of industry safety guidelines and requirements for different areas of the theatre.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in the school theatre or performance spaces.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate consistent and proper use of personal protection equipment or PPE (e.g., dust or ventilation masks, gloves, closed-toe shoes, clothing) and safety procedures (e.g., correct lifting of heavy objects, organization of storage areas, proper use of tools and equipment) in personal theatre arts experiences.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss and use standard verbal warnings such as “Heads up!” or “Clear!”.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain health and safety regulations that apply to technical theatre occupations and identify employer and employee responsibilities.

outcomes.statement: Examine ways to maintain psychological health and safety in the theatre workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4C: Safety in the Theatre: Psychological Health and Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 4B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the inclusion of psychological health as a safety concern in the theatre.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe potential challenges in achieving life/work balance in theatre arts careers and discuss ways of maintaining personal wellness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how self-employment and project-based contract work may impact one’s mental and physical health both positively (e.g., pursuing one’s passions, opportunities to be creative, a sense of accomplishment, pride in one’s work) and negatively (e.g., periodic financial stress, rejection of project proposals, long hours leading up to and during show runs followed by periods of less work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe practical ways that theatre employees and employers can contribute to a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research accommodations (e.g., modification of work duties, flexible hours, modifications to the work environment) that employees experiencing mental health problems or issues can request.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research sources of support (e.g., Professional Association of Canadian Theatres [PACT], Associated Designers of Canada [ADC], performing arts unions, Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, Canadian Actors’ Equity Association, Theatre Saskatchewan) for psychological health and safety in the theatre.

outcomes.statement: Apply artistic and technical components in set design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Set Design B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and explore techniques (e.g., inspirational image bank, thumbnail sketches, ground plans, models) and aesthetic approaches (e.g., minimalism, selective realism, abstraction) used by set designers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss purpose and processes for drafting ground plans.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Investigate how set design decisions are informed by the thematic interpretation of the play or traditional practice.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the purpose of renderings and explore colour theory, techniques and media (i.e., traditional and digital).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create set design renderings for the same play or scene located in two different performance spaces and build a maquette for one of them, considering physical performance space and aesthetic interpretation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Present set design renderings and maquettes and explain key parts of the decision-making process.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how a rendering informs own design decisions and identify how it impacts decisions of other production team members.

outcomes.statement: Plan and create a set design for a real or imagined multi-set play, musical or devised drama/theatre production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5C: Set Design C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 5B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how physical performance space and artistic interpretation can shape a set design (e.g., sightlines, elevations, symbolism, style).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of manual, mechanized and automated set pieces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the purposes, effects and mechanics of various types of stage machinery (e.g., revolves, scrims, drops, cycloramas, flying set pieces).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare ground plans for selected scenes or full production using hand or digitally-created scaled drawings including elevations, top view and side view.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate design factors such as doorway dimensions, weight, portability, transporting, load in and load out to inform creation of a set design.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a coloured scaled model and/or maquette based on ground plans for selected scenes from a multi-set play, musical or devised drama or theatre piece, real or imagined (e.g., paper or digital project).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research and examine modeling software for digitally-created renderings for set and scenery construction (e.g., creating ground plans, adding furniture and properties, drawing scenic elements).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Discuss advantages that digital media have over traditional rendering methods, such as:
- speed - rendering digitally can be faster than traditional techniques when considering time spent to redo a traditional rendering;
- ease - detailed or photographic looking elements can easily be reworked without having to start over; and,
- duplication - a digitally rendered master image can save different looks as separate images for multiple sets.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the practice of re-purposing materials for theatre sets and discuss benefits of sustainable practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Conduct a cost analysis and ensure that design plans work within a prescribed budget.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Present design including rationale and explanations for design decisions reached in collaboration with production team.

courses.name: Treaty Education

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its outcomes under 3 headings: “Grade Ten: Examining the Canadian context for Treaties”, “Grade Eleven: Assessing Treaty Making from a Global Perspective”, “Grade Twelve: Applying Treaty Understandings to One’s Life”.

courses.problem: The site's outcomes page answers with its “Page Not Found” page (HTTP 200): “The page you are looking for does not exist. If you are trying to access a curriculum, it might have been renewed. Please use the menu above to search for the updated version.” Its curriculum document link (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=481) answers the same “Page Not Found” page; the outcomes are taken from the curriculum document the site's menus link (https://www.edonline.sk.ca/bbcswebdav/xid-8784654_1); see `document`.

units.name: Grade Twelve: Applying Treaty Understandings to One’s Life

items.text: Examine one’s position regarding the importance of the treaty relationship for the social, cultural and economic prosperity of all Saskatchewan and Canadian people.

Analyze data from multiple sources (e.g., oral tradition, National Council on Welfare, Assembly of First Nations, Statistics Canada, Indian and Northern Affairs Canada) to inform personal beliefs regarding the effectiveness of treaties in addressing social, cultural and economic inequities.
Analyze how the media currently depicts the treaty relationship and determine the effects this has on public perception.
Analyze what you believe about treaty relationships, why you believe it, and how you came to believe it.
Investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the Spirit and Intent of treaties.
Interview family, friends and community members to determine values and beliefs in relation to treaties.
Describe ways people could demonstrate the spirit and intent of treaties and treaty principles (e.g., honour, respect, honesty, fairness, ethical space).
Reflect on and discuss personal experiences in honouring treaty principles.
Examine how treaties within contemporary society impact on individual’s lives.
Describe the principles of treaty and understand the importance those principles play.
Evaluate one’s actions according to personal beliefs nurtured through their understanding of treaty making.
Analyze responses to treaties in current federal and provincial government policies.
Synthesize knowledge and appreciation of treaties.
Represent personal understanding of the concept, We Are All Treaty People.
Examine the benefits of treaties as a way of defining and honouring relationships between nations.
Describe various worldviews represented by the signing of treaty.
Examine the importance of decolonization as a process that supports the understanding that We Are All Treaty People.

notes: Treaty Education is organised by grade (10, 11, 12), not by course level, and is meant to be taught within other subjects. `level` gives the matching course level (Grade 10 = 10-level, 11 = 20-level, 12 = 30-level) only so the course can sit beside the others.
Outcome codes are printed with a superscript goal number (TR¹, SI², HC³, TPP⁴, per the page's KEY); the superscript is kept in `superscript`, and `code` is the code as the Ministry CSV lists it.

The site's outcomes page for Treaty Education (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumOutcomeContent?id=481) and its curriculum document link (https://curriculum.gov.sk.ca/CurriculumFile?id=481) both answer the site's “Page Not Found” page (checked 2026-11-21).
Every Grade 10–12 code matches the Ministry CSV (https://www.edonline.sk.ca/bbcswebdav/library/outcomes/csvFiles/481_Treaty_Education_.csv), which lists the codes with empty statements.
